sources.news_title: Disney World Flights Disrupted After Deadly Miami Plane Crash Hits Florida Airports
sources.text:
Labor Day weekend already ranks among the most hectic stretches of the year for anyone flying in or out of Orlando, with families racing to squeeze in one last summer trip to Disney World or Universal before school schedules take over. This year, that usual holiday travel crunch collided with something far more serious. A deadly plane crash in Miami sent ripple effects across the entire region’s air travel network, and Orlando travelers are caught right in the middle of the fallout.
What you need to know:
- The fatal Amazon cargo plane crash that triggered a ground stop in Miami
- How that ground stop turned into hundreds of delayed and canceled flights in Orlando
- What Orlando International Airport has said about receiving diverted flights
- Why the timing during Labor Day weekend makes this especially disruptive for theme park travelers
A Tragedy in Miami Reaches Far Beyond the Runway
According to Click Orlando, federal investigators are currently examining a deadly crash involving an Amazon cargo plane in Miami, and passengers in Orlando are feeling the lingering effects through flight delays and cancellations. The aircraft overran the runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico. During the landing, the jet crossed a road used by warehouse workers and nearby businesses surrounding the airport. Officials confirmed five people died in the crash, with three others critically injured and two more hospitalized with less severe injuries.
The crash forced a ground stop at Miami International Airport for much of the afternoon, and many flights originally bound for Miami ended up diverted to Orlando instead. By late Sunday, more than 160 flights had been cancelled, and nearly 325 more were delayed as a direct result of the disruption.
One Traveler’s Firsthand Look at the Chaos
Cindy Noam, who was scheduled to fly to Miami on Monday, told Click Orlando her flight was delayed for at least an hour because of the fallout. “I received a message saying that my flight might be impacted because of the ground stop, but hopefully they have it all under control now,” Noam said. “It’s very concerning, but I think it’s safer to fly than it is to drive.”
Noam’s experience reflects what a lot of travelers passing through Orlando dealt with this weekend, uncertainty layered directly on top of an already demanding holiday travel schedule.
Why the Timing Made Everything Worse
The flight disruptions hit at almost the worst possible moment, right as airports across the region were already bracing for one of the busiest travel stretches of the year. Orlando International Airport expected 841,577 arriving and departing passengers between Thursday and Tuesday of Labor Day weekend, with Monday alone projected to bring 78,336 passengers through the airport, making it the single busiest day of the entire stretch.
Layering a major diversion event on top of numbers like that created a genuinely difficult situation for both the airport and the travelers moving through it. In response to Sunday’s crash, Orlando International Airport posted directly to social media addressing the situation, stating, “We’re currently receiving diverted flights to support operations at MIA and assist our airline partners. Travelers on affected flights are encouraged to contact their airline directly for the latest information and instructions regarding their journey.”
What This Means for Anyone Flying In for Disney or Universal
For families flying into Orlando specifically to visit Walt Disney World or Universal Orlando Resort this weekend, this kind of widespread flight disruption creates real, practical problems beyond just a stressful airport experience. A delayed or diverted flight can throw off carefully planned park reservations, Lightning Lane selections, dining bookings, and even hotel check-in windows, especially for guests who built tight, single day arrival plans around already limited Labor Day availability.
Given how tightly theme park trips are often scheduled around specific arrival and departure times, even a delay of a few hours can mean missing an early dinner reservation or losing a chunk of a first park day entirely. Guests connecting through Miami specifically, or flying on airlines that had aircraft diverted into Orlando as part of Sunday’s ground stop, should expect potential ripple effects continuing into the following days as airlines work to reposition aircraft and crews back into their normal rotations.
How to Handle Travel Disruptions During a Packed Holiday Weekend
Noam’s own approach to the chaos offers a genuinely useful takeaway for anyone navigating air travel during a weekend like this one. “I’ll tell you, carry on patience. That’s what we need to do is have patience. Especially when you’re traveling on a Labor Day weekend,” she said. Arriving at the airport with extra time built in, exactly what Noam did ahead of her own delayed flight, remains one of the simplest ways to reduce stress when disruptions are already rippling through the system.
For guests specifically traveling to a Disney or Universal vacation this weekend, it’s worth building some flexibility into park plans for your arrival day rather than scheduling anything too tightly right after landing. Checking your airline’s app frequently for real time updates, and reaching out directly to your airline rather than relying solely on airport announcements, can also help you stay ahead of any additional delays tied to the ongoing diversion situation.
Keeping Perspective During a Difficult Weekend
It’s worth remembering that behind all the flight delays and disrupted vacation plans is a genuine tragedy, five people lost their lives in Sunday’s crash, and investigators are still working to determine exactly what happened. While the travel disruptions are a real and valid concern for anyone trying to get to Orlando this weekend, they’re a relatively minor inconvenience compared to what the victims and their families are going through right now.
For travelers still working through delayed or canceled flights this week, staying in close contact with your airline and building extra patience into your plans remains the best way to manage an already difficult situation. If your trip to Disney World or Universal Orlando has been affected by these delays, both resorts have historically shown flexibility with reservations during major regional travel disruptions, so it’s worth reaching out directly if your arrival plans have shifted significantly.
Has your Labor Day weekend travel to Orlando been affected by the flight delays and diversions stemming from Sunday’s crash? Share your experience in the comments, we’d like to hear how you’re navigating your trip and what’s worked for you so far.

sources.text:
Support WBUR
What to know about the cargo plane crash in Miami
Authorities are investigating a cargo plane crash at Miami International Airport on Sunday that killed at least five people after the plane overshot the runway during landing and slammed into multiple vehicles.
We spoke with NPR’s Chandelis Duster for more details.
This segment aired on September 7, 2026.

sources.news_title: Orlando airport receives diverted flights after deadly Miami runway crash
sources.text:
ORLANDO, Fla. — A crash involving an Amazon cargo plane at Miami’s airport Sunday caused delays, cancellations and hours-long ground stop, sending some Miami-bound flights to Orlando International Airport and other surrounding airports.
The plane overshot a runway in Miami and crashed into several cars. The crash claimed several lives and shut down the runway and airport for hours, affecting flights across Florida.
The Greater Orlando Aviation Authority said about 20 flights were diverted to Orlando International Airport.
Greater Orlando Aviation Authority Angela Starke said in a statement, “We encourage everyone who has been diverted to MCO to work with their airline to reach their destination and ask that all passengers have patience during this period."
Starke, senior vice president of Public Affairs, added, "We also ask that outbound passengers please check with their airline before heading to MCO to ensure their flight is on time.”
Some travelers said they spent more money and time rebooking flights after the incident. Others rerouted through Orlando to continue their trips.
Howard Taikeff was traveling from Ecuador to California to visit family and had a layover in Miami on Sunday.
After learning he might not be able to fly out for several days due to the crash, he booked an early Brightline train ticket to Orlando on Monday so he could fly out of MCO instead.
“They said, ‘Well, maybe Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday you’ll get out of here,’” Taikeff said. “So I was in a jam, and I hadn’t slept for a couple of days. So, I decided that I should just go to Orlando.”
Taikeff said the disruption cost him money as he tried to keep his trip moving.
“I can’t hang out in the Miami airport for three days waiting to see if I can get out of here,” he said. “So, it cost me almost probably about $800 for a personal loss, but I must say, this airport in Orlando is fabulous and beautiful.”
Taikeff said MCO was welcoming and inviting after experiencing a stressful environment in Miami following the crash. He flew back to California on Monday afternoon.
Another traveler, Joshuia Drumm, said he was stuck at MCO Sunday night for hours but eventually got a flight back home to South Carolina.
He says he’s choosing to remain positive about the delays.
“I feel like sometimes God will end up making your situation be inconvenient for you, just so that you will be able to slow down and actually be able to pay attention to what really matters," Drumm said. "That's what really happened in that moment for me."
Drumm landed back home after 1 a.m. on Monday.
Mike Slack is a pilot, aviation lawyer and former NASA aerospace engineer. Slack said rerouting planes during an incident like this requires quick coordination between flight crews and air traffic control.
“Each flight crew is going to know what they have in terms of reserve fuel, how much time they have that they can take to get to the airport,” Slack said. “They’ll be conversing about those things with air traffic control, but it’s a tremendous logistical undertaking.”
Slack said runway overruns can be caused by several factors. He said the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigation will determine what happened in Miami, a process that could take six months to a year.
“We see this weather pattern factor in, but a lot of times it’s associated with bad decision-making by the flight crew and possibly, and I think you can’t rule this out, possibly a malfunction of a system on the aircraft that was needed to slow the airplane down,” Slack said.
He said airports like Orlando and Tampa are perfect for responding to a situation like this, when an airport like Miami has to temporarily pause all flights.
“Florida has some good alternatives if something, if Miami goes down. So you have Orlando, which has tremendous capacity to take in aircraft and a lot of space on the ground to keep those aircraft until they're able to get relocated or reposition back to Miami or elsewhere," Slack said. “Some of these airplanes may not ever go to Miami. They may actually, stay in Orlando for a little while, and then they'll be rerouted on another trip. It takes very quick coordination by air traffic controllers.”

sources.news_title: At least five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport
sources.text:
Authorities in Florida on Monday were investigating a plane crash in Miami International Airport that killed at least five people a day earlier.
Five people were also injured in the crash, though it is not yet clear how many of the people killed or hurt were on board the plane or on the ground.
An Amazon Prime cargo plane was landing at the airport around 2 p.m. ET on Sunday when it overran the runway, crashed and rammed into vehicles on the ground, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Amazon says the plane was operated by 21 Air, a contract cargo carrier.
Rosie Cordero-Stutz, the Miami-Dade County sheriff, said that the plane came to rest in a field adjacent to the airport.
Photos from the scene showed the Prime Air plane, a Boeing 767, off the runway, in a parking lot, its wings charred.
In a statement to NPR, the FAA said that Flight 7598 originally took off from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The FAA said it will investigate the crash.
The Miami-Dade Aviation Department said in a statement that the plane overran the diagonal runway and is disabled at the northwest end of the airport.
“What we found was a very complex situation here,” Miami-Dade County Fire Chief Ray Jadallah told reporters on Sunday. Jadallah said the airplane struck a couple of vehicles, requiring extrication of trapped victims. He also said emergency teams were engaged in a search and rescue operation of the pilot and co-pilot.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said over 60 MDFR units had responded. Jadallah said there was a fuel leak from the aircraft, which they were working to mitigate.
On the ground on Monday also were National Transportation Safety Board investigators as they looked into all factors, from potential mechanical failure to environmental variables or flight crew performance.
Following the crash, the FAA on Sunday issued a ground stop on planes until 3 p.m. that was later extended until 5:30 p.m. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop was ordered so that first responders could assess the scene and warned travelers of “significant delays and potential cancellations.”
The closure caused delays, flight cancellations and long lines at the airport with passengers rebooking flights. Miami International Airport said on Monday morning that two of the four runways were back open, but cautioned that it was still dealing with the “impacts of this incident.”
“This is a fast-moving situation and we’re still gathering details. We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened,” said Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel in a post on social media. “Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved. We’re doing everything we can to support those affected.”

sources.news_title: 5 dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes in Miami
sources.text:
Five people were killed Sunday after an Amazon cargo plane overran a runway while landing at Miami International Airport, struck several vehicles and caught fire.
The Boeing 767-300, operated by cargo carrier 21 Air for Amazon, was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, when it went off the runway shortly before 2 p.m., according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
Five other people were injured, including three who remained in critical condition, Miami-Dade officials said. Authorities have not publicly identified those killed or injured.
Video from the airport showed the plane landing before disappearing from view, followed by a plume of black smoke. The aircraft continued beyond the runway and across a road used by workers at businesses surrounding the airport, striking vehicles before bursting into flames. More than 60 fire-rescue units responded to the scene.

sources.news_title: Amazon Cargo Plane Crashes At Miami Airport, Killing Five
sources.text:
A routine landing at Miami International Airport turned into a deadly disaster. What went wrong?
An Amazon Air Boeing 767-300 cargo plane crashed shortly before 14:00 local time after flying in from San Juan, Puerto Rico.
The aircraft overshot the runway, struck vehicles on the ground and caught fire, killing five people and seriously injuring five others.
Miami-Dade Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said rescue crews reached the scene within “seconds” as firefighters worked to free people trapped inside or beneath vehicles.
Three of the injured are reportedly in critical condition.
More than 200 firefighters responded, eventually bringing the flames under control. But a fuel leak remained at the crash site.
Investigators Probe Crash Cause
Flight-tracking data showed the aircraft was travelling at about 129mph as it left the usable runway, while light thunderstorms and gusty winds were reported in Miami.
Still, officials stressed that it is far too early to determine the cause.
The National Transportation Safety Board will lead the investigation, with more details expected after its planned briefing.
For Amazon, the tragedy has prompted condolences and a pledge to cooperate fully.
For travellers, meanwhile, the crash caused widespread delays during one of America’s busiest holiday weekends.
A busy airport. A split-second disaster. And now, investigators must explain exactly what happened.

sources.news_title: At least five killed in Amazon Prime Air cargo plane crash in Miami
sources.text:
At least five killed in Amazon Prime Air cargo plane crash in Miami
Prime Air Flight 7598 overran the airport's diagonal runway and struck multiple vehicles on the ground
At least five people died when an Amazon Prime Air cargo flight overran a runway and crashed while landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday, local officials said.
Prime Air Flight 7598 overran the airport's diagonal runway shortly before 2pm EDT (1800 GMT) and struck multiple vehicles on the ground, officials said during a news conference on Sunday afternoon.
Five people were also injured in the crash, including three who are in critical condition, said Miami-Dade Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. At least two people were trapped in vehicles that were struck by the plane, and the pilot and co-pilot were trapped inside the plane by the crash, Jadallah said.
Officials declined to identify those who died.
More than 60 rescue units and about 200 personnel responded to the incident, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said in a statement. As of late afternoon, emergency personnel were still dealing with a fuel leak from the aircraft, Jadallah said.
Although the airport halted all flights immediately after the crash, flights had resumed by Sunday evening.
Read: Families of crew aboard crashed Pakistani cargo plane face agonising wait
The plane, which departed from San Juan, Puerto Rico, was a 32-year-old Boeing 767-300 freighter that had operated as a passenger jet for various airlines from 1994 to 2015, according to flight tracking service Flightradar24.
Cargo airline 21 Air operated the plane for Amazon, an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement.
"We are devastated by the accident involving one of our aircraft in Miami today," 21 Air said on its website. "Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives."
Reuters photos after the crash showed the jet with its nose on the ground and tail tilted up. The right side of the plane had what appeared to be scorch marks.
Flightradar24 said the plane was travelling at 112 knots(129 mph) when it exited the usable runway.
The National Transportation Safety Board, which investigates US civil aviation accidents, said it had sent a team led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy to investigate the accident and would hold its first media briefing in Miami on Monday.
Also Read: Air India A320 briefly lost key flight controls, Airbus analysis shows
Amazon is still gathering details about what happened, company spokesperson Kelly Nantel said. "We're working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened," Nantel said in a statement. "Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved."
Boeing and 21 Air said they would support the government investigations into the crash.
Video captured the moment an Amazon Prime plane overran a runway in Miami and crash landed, skidding into a carpark at the airport. At least five people were killed. pic.twitter.com/0DGemGGkM5
— Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) September 7, 2026
Sunday's incident is not the first time an Amazon Prime Air plane has been involved in a fatal crash. In February 2019, Atlas Air Flight 3591, a Boeing 767-300 freighter operating on behalf of Amazon Prime Air from Miami to Houston, entered a rapid descent and crashed into Trinity Bay, Texas. All three people on board were killed.
Miami, a major hub for trade with Latin America, is the third-busiest freight airport in the United States after Anchorage in Alaska and Louisville in Kentucky, according to the Airports Council International.
Freight shipments totalled nearly 3.5 million metric tons last year, and passenger traffic reached 55.3 million, the eighth-busiest airport in the nation, according to the airport in June.
In November, a UPS cargo plane crashed shortly after takeoff in Kentucky, killing 15 people, including three crew members and 12 on the ground.

sources.news_title: Investigators hunt for what went wrong after Amazon cargo plane crash in Miami kills at least 5
sources.text:
5 killed were all inside a van
MIAMI -- The five people killed when an Amazon cargo jet ran off a runway at Miami International Airport were all inside a van carrying seven people from a cleaning company, and an SUV hit outside of airport property, National Transportation Safety Board Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said Monday.
Homendy called the scene of Sunday’s crash “utter devastation.” She didn’t detail how many people were in the SUV or where the dead were located.
Homendy walked the route the Boeing 767 followed, noting tire marks from the pavement into the grass, the destroyed van carrying the cleaning crew, torn fencing, navigational equipment, and the crushed SUV outside airport property.
The debris included vehicle air bags, equipment from the vehicles, the airplane and the airport, and “fencing everywhere,” Homendy said.
“It’s pretty extensive. Hard to see and I’m sure it must have been very difficult for the responders as well,” Homendy said.
The airline, all told, traveled about 1,300 feet (396 meters) past the paved surface. Debris was everywhere, she said.
“I would describe it in one word as devastating, utter devastation,” Homendy said.
The van with seven people inside was “torn apart. It certainly must have been devastating,” she said. The van was owned by Professional Ocean Service Corp., an airline cleaning contractor.
Homendy said the NTSB would issue more information on Tuesday, including possibly information on speed that is confirmed by the flight data recorder.
Federal investigators examining the crash spent Monday determining whether the plane touched down too late to stop safely.
Video of Sunday’s landing appears to show the Boeing 767 remaining airborne well down the runway before touching down. Aviation experts said investigators will seek to determine exactly where the plane landed, whether it was beyond the normal touchdown zone, and why the pilots did not abandon the landing.
Investigators will also examine the plane’s speed and braking, weather and wind conditions, the aircraft’s mechanical condition and other factors that could have contributed to the deadly overrun.
The aircraft on Sunday flew from Cincinnati to Miami and then to San Juan, Puerto Rico. It was returning to Miami when it overran the runway around 2 p.m. and plowed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport.
Aside from the five who died, three people were critically injured and two others were hospitalized with less severe injuries, officials said.
The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.
The typical landing zone for a plane is within the first 3,000 feet (914 meters) of a runway, experts said. If the cargo jet was beyond that area, it should have aborted the landing and gone around for another try, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said.
Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former Inspector General of the Transportation Department, said video posted online shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.
It wasn’t raining at the time, but dark storm clouds loomed and strong winds were reported. Schiavo said that if the plane had a tail wind, that could have contributed to it floating further down the runway.
“A tail wind would certainly add to your troubles if you’ve already given up a good chunk of the runway by not touching down and landing right away,” Schiavo said.
The Miami airport is not equipped with arresting systems that the FAA says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide to safely stop planes that do go past the end of a runway. Those beds of lightweight, crushable material at the end of a runway have been credited by the FAA with helping save at least 497 lives aboard planes that overran runways.
Miami’s airport appears to be in compliance and wasn’t required to have an arresting system because it has a 1,000-foot safety buffer at the end of its runways, said Mike O’Donnell, the FAA’s former director of airport safety and accident investigations.
The requirement was prompted by American Airlines Flight 1420 overrunning a runway at Little Rock National Airport in Arkansas in 1999, killing nine.
The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semitrucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.
The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
Schiavo said the NTSB will also closely examine the maintenance history of this plane — particularly since it has a history of foreign ownership, including by a Russian company.
The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of Sunday afternoon and continued to hamper air travel into Monday.
Miami International Airport said that two of its four runways remained closed Monday and that operations were to be affected throughout the day because of aircraft and flight crews not arriving there due to Sunday’s cancellations after the crash.
An airport spokesperson said there were 160 cancellations and more than 300 delayed flights Sunday, plus another 69 canceled flights Monday through mid-afternoon. Flight tracking sites were reporting widespread delays at the airport.
Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport," the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
Last year, a UPS plane crashed after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport. The crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.
Levy reported from Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, and Collins reported from Columbia, South Carolina. Associated Press writer Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, contributed.

sources.news_title: Five killed after Amazon cargo plane overruns runway at Miami airport
5 Dead, 5 Injured After Amazon Cargo Plane Overshoots Runway at Miami Airport
sources.text:
At least five people have died and five others were injured after an Amazon Prime Air cargo plane overran the runway during landing at Miami International Airport (MIA), struck multiple vehicles on a nearby roadway, and burst into flames.
Runway Excursion and Crash Details
The incident occurred around 2:00 p.m. local time when Prime Air Flight 7598—a Boeing 767-300 operated by 21 Air arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico—was attempting to land.
According to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the aircraft failed to come to a stop on the designated runway, traveling off the airfield perimeter and colliding with several vehicles parked along an adjacent roadway, including semi-trucks and passenger cars. The impact sparked a severe fire, sending thick clouds of black smoke billowing into the sky visible across the airfield.
Massive Emergency and Technical Rescue Response
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue (MDFR) dispatched a massive emergency response to the crash site. Nearly 200 firefighters and 60 fire apparatuses responded to fight the blaze and search for survivors.
“A complex extrication with our technical rescue team [was required], including a search and rescue of the pilot and co-pilot that were trapped in this aircraft,” stated MDFR Chief Ray Jadallah. First responders conducted firefighting operations while simultaneously performing heavy rescue operations to free individuals pinned inside both the aircraft and the struck ground vehicles.
Five fatalities have been confirmed at the scene, with five additional victims transported to local hospitals for medical treatment.
Airport Operations and Investigation
In the immediate aftermath of the crash, the FAA issued a full ground stop, closing all runways and taxiways at Miami International Airport. While airport authorities lifted the ground stop later in the afternoon, officials warned that significant flight delays and reduced operational capacity will continue due to the disabled aircraft and ongoing emergency operations.
Both the FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) have launched investigations into the cause of the runway excursion. The NTSB announced that it has deployed a “Go Team” to the scene to examine weather conditions, flight data, mechanical systems, and air traffic control communications leading up to the landing.

sources.news_title: Amazon cargo plane overruns Miami runway, five killed
sources.text:
Amazon cargo plane overruns Miami runway, five killed (Video)
A routine cargo landing at one of America’s busiest airports turned deadly within seconds. Here’s exactly what happened.
An Amazon-branded cargo plane overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, striking multiple vehicles before bursting into flames.
The crash killed five people and injured five others, Miami-Dade officials confirmed.
Boeing 767-300 aircraft, operating as 21 Air Flight 7598 for Amazon’s Prime Air network, overran Runway 30 at around 14:00 local time while landing from San Juan, Puerto Rico.
How the crash unfolded
According to the Federal Aviation Administration, the aircraft overran the runway during landing.
It then continued beyond the airport boundary, crossed a road, and struck several vehicles near the 2100 block of Northwest 42nd Avenue.
The plane came to rest in an adjacent field, engulfed in flames with heavy smoke visible for miles.
More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units and roughly 200 personnel responded to the scene.
Rescue crews worked to free victims trapped in the struck vehicles, with one requiring specialised technical extrication.
They also searched for the pilots, whom officials said were trapped inside the cockpit.
Of the five people injured, three were taken to a trauma centre in critical condition, and two others were hospitalised with less severe injuries.
Miami-Dade Fire Chief Raied Jadallah also confirmed a fuel leak from the aircraft, which crews worked to contain.
Why the airport’s runway may have made things worse
The aircraft involved was a 32-year-old Boeing 767-300, originally built as a passenger plane before being converted to cargo use in 2015.
It had been operating on behalf of Amazon’s Prime Air network, flown by contracted carrier 21 Air, a North Carolina-based operator, since Amazon doesn’t hold its own air operator certificate for these routes.
Aviation analysts have pointed to a notable gap in Miami International’s safety infrastructure.
Unlike many major airports around the world, Miami’s runways don’t have an Engineered Material Arresting System.
This is a bed of crushable material designed specifically to stop an aircraft that overruns a runway.
Given how congested and densely built-up the area around the airport is, that absence has already drawn scrutiny.
The crash triggered a roughly three-hour ground stop at the airport, with average incoming flight delays reaching around six and a half hours before normal operations resumed.
The National Transportation Safety Board has sent a team, led by Chair Jennifer Homendy, to investigate.
Amazon’s response
An Amazon spokesperson said the company was “heartbroken” by the loss of life, adding: “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
This is a genuinely sobering reminder of how much can go wrong in the final seconds of a routine landing, and how much still depends on runway infrastructure most passengers never think twice about.

sources.news_title: Five dead after an Amazon cargo plane veers off MIA runway and smashes into cars
sources.text:
Five people died and five more were injured after an Amazon cargo plane crashed at Miami International Airport Sunday afternoon, causing a full ground stop that halted all flights for hours.
The Federal Aviation Administration said flight 7598 from Miami-based cargo transportation company 21 Air, a Boeing 767-300, departed from San Juan, Puerto Rico, earlier in the day. It overran the runway after landing at MIA around 2 p.m. The FAA will investigate the crash, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on X.
After crossing Northwest 67th Avenue, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said, the plane “struck multiple vehicles.” Photographs from the scene show crunched cars snarled in chunks of the wire fence that used to separate the airport from the road.
Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz confirmed Sunday evening in a press briefing with other officials that the crash killed five people and sent five others to the hospital, three of whom were in critical condition. Several of the casualties were on the ground, said Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Raied “Ray” Jadallah.
The plane crashed into “a couple” of vehicles, trapping people inside, Jadallah said. One of the victims was trapped underneath a car and had to be extracted by technical rescue personnel, the department said in a statement.
It was a “complex” search and rescue, extraction and fire, the chief said, emphasizing that it was a “very complex situation.” There was an active fuel leak, which was being addressed as officials briefed reporters around 6 p.m.
The pilot and co-pilot were also trapped in the plane, Jadallah said, although it was not clear how long — or the extent of crew members’ injuries.
The resulting fire from the crash sent large puffs of black smoke into the air. A firefighter was heard on the radio telling his colleagues, “The plane is on fire. The plane is on fire. Put your game faces on guys.”
Emergency radio dispatch traffic painted a chaotic scene facing the fire rescue workers among the 60 MDFR responding units.
Firefighters are heard scrambling to get hoses close enough to the plane to spray water to suppress the flames. The aircraft’s left engine was also still running as firefighters battled the fire, making it dangerous for them to enter the plane to check for patients inside.
Firefighters are also heard saying that the pilots told them they could not turn the engine off because they would need to “energize” the aircraft. So, firefighters had to flood the engine with water from their hoses to disable it.
Firefighters and paramedics working the road, meanwhile, were busy extricating seriously injured people from vehicles hit by the plane.
The crash froze all travel at MIA for hours on Sunday afternoon.
As of about 4:45 p.m., according to Flight Aware, MIA had 275 delays — 156 departures and 119 arrivals. The airport also had 82 canceled flights, slightly more departures than arrivals. Flights had begun resuming at some runways by 5 p.m.
Shortly after 5 p.m., Gaurav Sharma, 36, looked at the departures board at MIA for an update on his scrambled plans. His original British Airways flight to London scheduled for 5 pm was listed as canceled. Sharma, in Miami on business from his home in New Delhi, was already rebooked on another flight leaving for London at 7:40 pm. But first, that jet needs to get to Miami — and Sharma’s flight-tracking app showed its arrival time getting pushed back again and again. “I’m checking to see if that plane will get here,” he said. “It’s complicated.”
Shortly after 5 p.m., there were hints of MIA getting flights underway again. A few flights were listed as departed. Greg Chin, an MIA spokesman, confirmed the airport was starting to resume flight operations.
“Two of MIA’s four runways are now open,” Chin said.
The cause of the crash will be determined by the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board, Cordero-Stutz said.
The sheriff’s office will also investigate the five fatalities, Cordero-Stutz said. Her agency also has dedicated a hotline for family members of those who may have been killed or injured at 305-471-2400.
There “is no apparent threat to public safety,” she said.
Crews were on scene within 30 seconds of getting the call, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said. There were 60 fire apparatus with around 200 crew members involved in the operation.
Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said her “heart is with all the families who were affected.”
Possible causes?
Pablo Rojas is an aviation attorney with the Coral Gables law firm Podhurst Orseck, which has a history of representing plane crash victims back to the Eastern Airlines Dec. 29, 1972 crash that killed all 163 passengers and 13 crew members.
Knowing with certainly what happened Sunday is impossible to know so soon after the crash, Rojas said, but there are a number of possibilities that stand out to him. Chiefly, he said, the condition of the plane’s landing gear when it came to a rest.
“You can see it stops in this parking lot area with the landing gear collapsed,” Rojas told the Miami Herald. The nose is kind of dipping down. We don’t know if that’s something that happened late in the accident sequence or early enough to have caused the accident sequence.”
“You can imagine the incident being caused by something else and then the landing gear collapsing, but certainly if there was an issue with the landing gear early in the accident sequence, that’s going to be the first clue for investigators,” he said.
The stormy weather South Florida has been experiencing almost daily this week is also something that investigators will likely be looking at, Rojas said.
“A landing at an international airport is complex. The pilot needs to be communicating with air traffic control. Air traffic control needs to be minding the weather, and communicating that with the pilot. We know we’ve had rain in Miami recently. Air traffic control needs to help the pilot understand the condition of the runway,” Rojas said.
“Planes can land in nasty weather, but obviously, if the runway is slick that can sometimes cause air traffic control to pause or stop landings for a period of time,” he said.

sources.news_title: Five killed after Amazon plane overshoots runway at US airport
sources.text:
Five killed after Amazon plane overshoots runway at US airport
MIAMI — At least five people were killed after an Amazon cargo aircraft overran the runway during a landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, striking multiple vehicles and sending a thick black plume of smoke into the air as it caught fire.
Five others were injured in the crash, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Raied Ray Jadallah said during a news conference on Sunday evening. Three are in critical condition and were taken to a trauma center, while two others were taken to a local hospital, he said.
Several victims were trapped in the vehicles that were hit by the plane and had to be extricated, Jadallah said.
“The airplane did strike a couple of vehicles,” which left “a couple of victims that were actually trapped in the vehicles,” Jadallah said.
“A complex extrication with our technical rescue team” was needed, “including a search and rescue of the pilot and co-pilot that were trapped in this aircraft.”
Jadallah did not clarify whether the pilot or co-pilot survived, and officials declined to answer questions after brief statements were made.
Video showed thick smoke billowing from the blue and white Boeing 767 after it arrived at 1:58 pm (1758 GMT) from Puerto Rico, as fire trucks raced to the scene.
The plane operating as Prime Air Flight 7598 caught fire as a result of the “crash,” fire officials said.
“A total of 60 fire apparatuses arrived, just short, just shy of 200 men and women from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, to begin the actual search and rescue and firefighting,” Jadallah said.
“The actual cause of the incident will be determined by the FAA and the NTSB,” he added, referring to the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board.
In a statement posted to X Sunday evening, fire officials said they used foam to extinguish a fire in the engine compartment.
“One person was trapped under one of the involved vehicles and had to be extricated by specialized technical rescue personnel. Specialized hazardous materials (HazMat) units safely shut down the aircraft’s engine and worked to control a fuel leak,” the statement said.
The NTSB said in an X post on Sunday the B-767-300 cargo airplane was flying into Miami from San Juan, Puerto Rico and they have “launched a go team to investigate Sunday’s runway excursion accident.”
Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement the tech giant will cooperate with any investigation into the incident.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport. Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss,” Nantel said.
Miami Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz told reporters Sunday that her officers encountered a “really tragic scene,” but there was “no apparent threat to public safety.”
The airport closed all runways and taxiways because of the incident and posted an update to its website Sunday evening that travelers should check directly with their airline before heading to the airport.
After hours of holding all flights at the international airport Sunday, with numerous delays and canceled flights for commercial airline passengers, the Miami Herald newspaper reported that two of the airport’s four runways had reopened Sunday.
In a statement on X, Mayor Daniella Levine Cava thanked first responders for their speedy response, saying “our fire rescue team was there within seconds of the crash, so we’re deeply grateful.”

sources.news_title: Miami 767 left runway at 112 knots in fatal overrun
sources.text:
The Boeing 767-300 freighter that overran Runway 30 at Miami International Airport (MIA) on September 6, 2026, was still moving at 112 knots (roughly 129 miles per hour or 207 kilometers per hour) as it left the usable surface, according to tracking data.
The last speed logged by Flightradar24 was 69 knots. That energy was enough to carry the aircraft past the airfield boundary and onto a public road, where it struck vehicles and killed at least five people.
A 21 Air Boeing 767 operating for Amazon overran Miami’s Runway 30 this afternoon. Flightradar24 data shows a ground speed of 112 knots as it left the usable runway.
Downloadable flight data and updates available at https://t.co/uHIF4KdM17 pic.twitter.com/dnfX0uWjxt
An aircraft crossing the end of a runway at approach-adjacent speed indicates a stop that failed early, rather than one that fell marginally short. Flight 7598, operated by 21 Air for Amazon Air, had flown for two hours and eleven minutes from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, touching down at 13:53 local time.
The aircraft involved, registered N1997A, was a 32-year-old Boeing 767-33A(ER) converted from passenger to freighter configuration in 2015. Powered by two General Electric CF6-80C2 engines, it entered service with 21 Air in January 2025 and operated in Prime Air colors.
Thunderstorms and wet runway conditions face scrutiny
The METAR (METeorological Aerodrome Report) issued at the time of landing recorded thunderstorms over the field, winds from 190 degrees at 17 knots gusting to 26, and cumulonimbus at 2,000 feet.
Runway surface condition and braking performance are therefore likely early lines of inquiry, an area where the NTSB pressed the FAA in May 2026 to revise its wet runway guidance after reviewing 11 overruns between 2008 and 2022. Touchdown point, thrust reverser and spoiler performance, anti-skid function and landing weight are also to be examined.
Five dead and three critically injured
The aircraft crossed the runway safety area and perimeter fence before reaching the road, coming to rest beside two semi-trucks near a parking lot serving an Amazon warehouse.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue committed more than 60 units and around 200 personnel, treating ten patients and transporting five. One person was extricated from beneath a struck vehicle, and hazardous materials crews shut down an engine and contained a fuel leak.
Three of those transported were in critical condition. The two pilots survived. Authorities have not identified the dead or declared whether they were on board or on the ground.
It is the second US freighter accident in less than a year to kill people outside an airport perimeter, after UPS Flight 2976 came down in an industrial area beyond Louisville in November 2025, killing twelve on the ground.
NTSB investigation begins in Miami
An NTSB go-team led by Chair Jennifer Homendy is on site, with a first briefing scheduled for September 7, 2026. Boeing is supporting the investigation.
21 Air, based in Greensboro, North Carolina, flies contracted 767 services for Amazon and DHL. CEO Keith Winters said that the company was cooperating with federal investigators. Amazon holds no air operator certificate for these flights, the same contracting structure behind the 2019 loss of Atlas Air Flight 3591.
A ground stop imposed around 14:30 local time was lifted after roughly three hours, and two of four runways reopened, though average arrival delays reached about six and a half hours in the evening.

sources.text:
[Image: Facebook]
Five people have died after a Boeing 767 cargo aeroplane operating for Amazon’s Prime Air network overran the runway while landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, striking multiple vehicles before coming to rest near the airport perimeter.
The plane, flying as 21 Air Flight 7598, was arriving from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, when it failed to stop on the runway at around 2 p.m. local time.
According to preliminary tracking data, the plane was still travelling at close to 200 km/h when it ran off the usable portion of the runway.
From there, it struck several vehicles on a nearby roadway before coming to a stop in a field just outside the airport boundary. The impact and a subsequent fire caused significant damage, though officials say the aeroplane remained largely intact, resting on its belly.
Authorities have not yet said why the aeroplane was unable to stop in time, according to CNN. A review of air traffic control communications indicates the flight crew did not declare an emergency before landing.
Miami-Dade County officials confirmed five fatalities and at least five additional injuries, three of them serious enough to require transport to a trauma centre. Fire officials said some victims were trapped inside vehicles struck by the plane and had to be freed by specialised rescue crews.
Around 200 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue personnel responded to the scene, working simultaneously to search for survivors, extinguish the blaze, and contain a fuel leak from the wrecked aeroplane. The two pilots aboard the plane were pulled from the wreckage and taken in for treatment.
NBC reports that the crash forced a temporary halt to all airport operations, with runways and taxiways closed for several hours while first responders worked the scene. sources.news_title: 5 dead after Amazon cargo plane overruns runway at Miami airport
sources.text:
By Anthony Izaguirre, David Fischer and Josh Funk 
Associated Press
MIAMI — An Amazon cargo plane barreled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people and injuring five others as it struck vehicles and was engulfed in flames, authorities said.
The aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and plowed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalized with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference.
It wasn’t immediately clear if the pilots survived or those killed were all in vehicles when the plane struck.
The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.
The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon. Some 200 emergency personnel responded, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the department said. Firefighters used foam from specialized airport firefighting units to extinguish the fire, and crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane hours later.
The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semitrucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.
The cause had yet to be determined, and it was not clear if weather had played a role. Thunderstorms and wind gusts up to 30 mph (48 kph) were recorded in the area at the time, according to the National Weather Service.
The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
More than 160 flights were canceled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Officials from Orlando International Airport, more than 200 miles (320 km) north of Miami, said some flights were diverted there.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it was sending a team to Miami led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy to investigate.
Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska. Associated Press writers Tim Reynolds in Miami, Rio Yamat in Las Vegas and Wufei Yu in Phoenix contributed.

sources.news_title: Five Dead, Five Injured As Amazon Cargo Plane Crashes Into Vehicle In Miami
sources.text:
At least five people were killed when an Amazon cargo plane overshot a runway after it landed Sunday at Miami International Airport, crashed into vehicles and caught fire, officials said.
Miami-Dade County fire chief Ray Jadallah told reporters that in addition to five fatalities, three people were transported to trauma centers “in critical condition” and two more were treated at a local hospital.
“The airplane did strike a couple of vehicles,” which left “a couple of victims that were actually trapped in the vehicles,” Jadallah said.
“A complex extrication with our technical rescue team” was needed, “including a search and rescue of the pilot and co-pilot that were trapped in this aircraft.”
Jadallah did not clarify whether the pilot or co-pilot survived, and officials declined to answer questions after brief statements were made.
Video showed thick smoke billowing from the blue and white Boeing 767 after it arrived at 1:58 pm (1758 GMT) from Puerto Rico, as fire trucks raced to the scene.
The plane operating as Prime Air Flight 7598 caught fire as a result of the “crash,” fire officials said.
“A total of 60 fire apparatuses arrived, just short, just shy of 200 men and women from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, to begin the actual search and rescue and firefighting,” Jadallah said.
“The actual cause of the incident will be determined by the FAA and the NTSB,” he added, referring to the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board.
In a statement posted to X Sunday evening, fire officials said they used foam to extinguish a fire in the engine compartment.
“One person was trapped under one of the involved vehicles and had to be extricated by specialized technical rescue personnel. Specialized hazardous materials (HazMat) units safely shut down the aircraft’s engine and worked to control a fuel leak,” the statement said.

Miami Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz told reporters Sunday that her officers encountered a “really tragic scene,” but there was “no apparent threat to public safety.”
The airport closed all runways and taxiways because of the incident and posted an update to its website Sunday evening that travelers should check directly with their airline before heading to the airport.

Harrowing video circulating online shows the Prime Air-liveried freighter sliding at high speed through a parking area near warehouse operations, with smoke and fire billowing as bystanders look on. Miami-Dade officials said the plane left the pavement around 2 p.m. after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico. Flight-tracking data indicated it was still traveling about 112 knots, roughly 129 mph, as it exited the usable runway.
The 32-year-old converted freighter, registered N1997A and operated by 21 Air as Flight 7598, came to rest on its belly near parked cars and trucks outside the airport boundary. Fire crews described a “very complex fire” in the engine compartments and an active fuel leak hours later. More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units and about 200 personnel responded.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Raied “Ray” Jadallah said crews found people trapped in crushed vehicles and had to extract the two pilots from the cockpit. Three of the injured were in critical condition and taken to a trauma center; two others were hospitalized with less severe injuries. Officials have not publicly named the dead. Both crew members survived.
“Units arrived to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing,” Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said. Firefighters used airport foam units to knock down the blaze.
The National Transportation Safety Board launched a go-team. The FAA said it will investigate. Pilots did not declare an emergency on approach, according to air-traffic-control audio reviewed by outlets. Thunderstorms and gusty winds were in the area at the time; investigators have not determined a cause. Runway 30 is more than 9,000 feet long. An FAA spokeswoman said Miami’s runways are not equipped with an Engineered Materials Arresting System, or EMAS.
Amazon said it was “heartbroken” and cooperating with authorities. “Our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved,” a company spokesperson said. 21 Air also expressed condolences.
A full ground stop shut down Miami International during a busy holiday-weekend travel period. Hundreds of flights were delayed or canceled before some runways reopened later Sunday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned travelers to expect disruptions into Monday.
Miami-Dade Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said the community was “joined in prayers and grieving.” First responders ran into smoke and fire to pull people from vehicles and the cockpit. The NTSB is scheduled to brief the public as the investigation begins.

sources.news_title: Amazon Prime Air cargo plane crash claims at least five lives
sources.text:
At least 5 killed in Amazon Prime Air cargo plane crash in Miami
- By Reuters -
- Sep 07, 2026
At least five people died when an Amazon Prime Air cargo flight overran a runway and crashed while landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday, local officials said.
Prime Air Flight 7598 overran the airport’s diagonal runway shortly before 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) and struck multiple vehicles on the ground, officials said during a news conference on Sunday afternoon.
Five people were also injured in the crash, including three who are in critical condition, said Miami-Dade Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. At least two people were trapped in vehicles that were struck by the plane, and the pilot and co-pilot were trapped inside the plane by the crash, Jadallah said.
Officials declined to identify those who died.
More than 60 rescue units and about 200 personnel responded to the incident, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said in a statement. As of late afternoon, emergency personnel were still dealing with an active fuel leak from the aircraft, Jadallah said.
Although the airport halted all flights immediately after the crash, two of its four runways had been reopened by Sunday evening.
The plane, which departed from San Juan, Puerto Rico, was a 32-year-old Boeing (BA.N), opens new tab 767-300 freighter that had operated as a passenger jet for various airlines from 1994 to 2015, according to flight tracking service Flightradar24.
“We are devastated by the accident involving one of our aircraft in Miami today,” 21 Air said on its website. “Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives.”
Read more: Charter plane carrying 8 crashes near remote site in western Alaska, AP reports
Reuters photos after the crash showed the jet with its nose on the ground and tail tilted up. The right side of the plane had what appeared to be scorch marks.
Flightradar24 said the plane was traveling at 112 knots (129 mph) when it exited the usable runway.
The National Transportation Safety Board, which investigates U.S. civil aviation accidents, said it had sent a team led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy to investigate the accident and would hold its first media briefing in Miami on Monday.
Amazon is still gathering details about what happened, company spokesperson Kelly Nantel said. “We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened,” Nantel said in a statement. “Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved.”
Boeing and 21 Air said they would support the government investigations into the crash.
Sunday’s incident is not the first time an Amazon Prime Air plane has been involved in a fatal crash. In February 2019, Atlas Air Flight 3591, a Boeing 767-300 freighter operating on behalf of Amazon Prime Air from Miami to Houston, entered a rapid descent and crashed into Trinity Bay, Texas. All three people on board were killed.

sources.news_title: At Least 5 Killed As Plane Overshoots Miami Airport Runway
sources.text:
At least five people were killed and five others were injured after an Amazon cargo plane overshot the runway upon landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon.
Miami-Dade County officials said in an evening press conference that 21 Air Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-300 freighter operating on behalf of Amazon, crashed into several vehicles shortly before 2 p.m., local time.
The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration are investigating the incident. The Miami-Dade Sheriff’s office warned residents Monday morning to avoid the area, detailing that “the cargo plane crash remains active and has heavy law enforcement presence.”
"The airplane, which was operated by 21 Air, was attempting to land when this incident occurred,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement. “We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to learn more and will cooperate fully with any investigation.”
Nantel said the company’s “deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.” Amazon contracts out its cargo flights.
The incident has impacted operations in “America’s busiest airport for international freight and second busiest for international passengers,” according to the Miami airport’s website.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy advised travelers to anticipate significant delays and potential flight cancellations. A full ground stop had initially been issued, but has since been lifted.
Here’s what we know so far.
How it unfolded
According to the FAA, Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft, departed from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico.
Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said during the news conference that the crash happened at around 1:58 p.m. Data from tracking site Flightradar24 shows that the plane had a speed of nearly 130 mph when it left the usable portion of the diagonal runway.
It’s unclear what caused the plane to overshoot, and the NTSB and FAA are investigating. The airport’s runways and taxiways were closed, and the aircraft was left disabled at the northwest end of the airport. Some of the runways were later reopened.
According to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, more than 60 units and approximately 200 personnel responded to the scene, arriving at the airport “to find an airplane that had stopped beyond the airport operational boundary with heavy flames and smoke showing.” Photos and videos from the scene showed black smoke billowing from the plane.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue chief Raied Jadallah said in the news conference that several people were trapped in their vehicles.
“What we found was a very complex situation here,” Jadallah said, and added that responders also conducted search and rescue of the pilot and co-pilot who were trapped in the aircraft.
What we know about the victims
The authorities had not released the identities of the victims as of early Monday afternoon.
Jadallah said there were a total of 10 people involved in the crash: five were killed, three are in critical condition and were transported to the trauma center, and another two were transported to a local hospital.
It is not clear whether those killed and injured were on the plane or on the ground.
What we know about the carrier and the plane
North Carolina-based cargo airline 21 Air began operating Boeing 767-300 freighters on behalf of Amazon in 2024. The company was founded in 2014.
Keith Winters, the airline’s CEO, said in a statement on their website that they were “devastated by the accident” and that the company’s “deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives.”
Flightradar24 data shows the plane involved in the crash was a 32-year-old Boeing 767. The aircraft model is used for both passenger travel and freight delivery. The first Boeing 767 flew on Sept. 26, 1981, and started commercial operations in 1982 with United Airlines.
Amazon’s cargo flight history
Amazon Air’s cargo network oversees more than 100 aircraft and over 250 flights daily. It contracts all of its cargo flying to other operators. In its fleet are Boeing 737 and 767 planes, as well as the Airbus A330.
Citing details from aviation analytics firm Cirium, the New York Times reported that 21 Air runs eight planes for Amazon Air, while Air Transport International operates about 40 planes, and low-cost carrier Sun Country Airlines operates 22.
It’s not the first plane crash involving Amazon Air. In February 2019, Atlas Air Flight 3591, a cargo plane flying from Miami to Houston, crashed into Texas’s Trinity Bay. All three people onboard were killed, and a subsequent federal investigation attributed the crash to pilot error.
Sunday’s incident is the latest high-profile crash involving a cargo aircraft in the U.S. Last November, more than a dozen people were killed after a UPS plane crashed into an industrial area in Louisville, Ky. shortly after departing Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport.
Lawmakers share condolences
Floridian lawmakers expressed their sympathies with the victims of the crash as they thanked emergency services in the Miami area.
Republican Sen. Rick Scott said he and his wife were “heartbroken by this tragic loss of life” and credited “all the emergency personnel for responding so quickly to the scene and putting out the fire.”
Republican Rep. Carlos A. Giménez, a career firefighter and former Miami Fire Chief, shared that he was “extraordinarily proud” of the emergency services’ response and said he would be “praying for all victims and injured.”
Republican Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar said “Miami is with every family affected by this tragedy,” adding that “as we pray for the victims, their families, and those injured, we are also grateful for the Miami-Dade firefighters, police officers, sheriff’s deputies, and first responders who rushed to the scene and continue their work.”

Five dead, five injured after Amazon cargo plane overshoots Miami runway
Miami (AFP) – At least five people were killed when an Amazon cargo plane overshot a runway after it landed Sunday at Miami International Airport, crashed into vehicles and caught fire, officials said.
Issued on:
Miami-Dade County fire chief Ray Jadallah told reporters that in addition to five fatalities, three people were transported to trauma centers "in critical condition" and two more were treated at a local hospital.
"The airplane did strike a couple of vehicles," which left "a couple of victims that were actually trapped in the vehicles," Jadallah said.
"A complex extrication with our technical rescue team" was needed, "including a search and rescue of the pilot and co-pilot that were trapped in this aircraft."
Jadallah did not clarify whether the pilot or co-pilot survived, and officials declined to answer questions after brief statements were made.
Video showed thick smoke billowing from the blue and white Boeing 767 after it arrived at 1:58 pm (1758 GMT) from Puerto Rico, as fire trucks raced to the scene.
The plane operating as Prime Air Flight 7598 caught fire as a result of the "crash," fire officials said.
"A total of 60 fire apparatuses arrived, just short, just shy of 200 men and women from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, to begin the actual search and rescue and firefighting," Jadallah said.
"The actual cause of the incident will be determined by the FAA and the NTSB," he added, referring to the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board.
In a statement posted to X Sunday evening, fire officials said they used foam to extinguish a fire in the engine compartment.
"One person was trapped under one of the involved vehicles and had to be extricated by specialized technical rescue personnel. Specialized hazardous materials (HazMat) units safely shut down the aircraft's engine and worked to control a fuel leak," the statement said.
Investigation launched
The NTSB said in an X post on Sunday the B-767-300 cargo airplane was flying into Miami from San Juan, Puerto Rico and they have "launched a go team to investigate Sunday's runway excursion accident."
Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement the tech giant will cooperate with any investigation into the incident.
"We're heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today's incident at Miami International Airport. Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss," Nantel said.
Miami Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz told reporters Sunday that her officers encountered a "really tragic scene," but there was "no apparent threat to public safety."
The airport closed all runways and taxiways because of the incident and posted an update to its website Sunday evening that travelers should check directly with their airline before heading to the airport.
After hours of holding all flights at the international airport Sunday, with numerous delays and canceled flights for commercial airline passengers, the Miami Herald newspaper reported that two of the airport's four runways had reopened Sunday.

sources.news_title: NTSB Investigates Fatal Miami Runway Overrun of Amazon Prime Air Freighter
sources.text:
An Amazon Prime Air cargo plane overran a runway at Miami International Airport on September 6, 2026, crashing into ground traffic and resulting in at least five deaths. The aircraft, operated as 21 Air Flight 7598, broke through the airport perimeter and struck multiple vehicles before coming to a rest near Northwest 67th Avenue.
The Amazon cargo plane crash occurred shortly after the flight arrived from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. According to local officials, the five fatalities were primarily ground casualties located in the vehicles struck by the aircraft. Five other individuals were injured, including the pilot and co-pilot, who were initially trapped in the cockpit as the wreckage burst into flames.
Technical Details and Runway Overrun
The aircraft involved in the incident was a 32-year-old Boeing 767-300 freighter with registration N1997A. The plane holds significant historical value for the company, as it was the first aircraft to receive the Amazon Prime Air livery when the service launched in 2016, famously known as “Amazon One.”
Technical landing data indicates the aircraft was traveling at approximately 112 knots (130 mph) as it exited the usable area of Runway 30. Although Runway 30 at Miami International Airport is over 9,000 feet long, the aircraft failed to decelerate sufficiently before reaching the end of the pavement. Air traffic control audio from the final moments of the flight suggests the pilots did not declare an emergency prior to the landing attempt.
Investigation and Airport Operations
National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy arrived in Miami following the crash to lead the federal investigation. A formal media briefing is scheduled for Monday, September 7, to provide updates on the recovery of flight data recorders and the status of the investigation into the cause of the overrun.
The crash caused significant disruption to South Florida’s aviation hub. Emergency crews worked to secure the crash site and clear debris from the perimeter road. Investigators are expected to review weather conditions at the time of the landing and the mechanical state of the 32-year-old freighter as part of their probe.

An Amazon cargo plane barrelled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people as it struck vehicles and burst into flames, authorities said.
The aircraft overran the runway around 2 pm after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalised with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference.
AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
Miami officials said Sunday afternoon that it was too soon to determine whether the people who died were on board the plane or in the vehicles the plane hit.

The agency said another person was trapped under a vehicle. It also halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon. Fire crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane several hours after the crash, Jadallah said.
The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semi-trucks, images from the scene showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire. "Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss." Jackson Lee, who runs an electronics shop near the crash site, went outside with four colleagues after the crash and saw smoke rising near the airport's fences, Lee said. Amazon spokeswoman Kelly Nantel said an “Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land.” She added, “This is a fast-moving situation and we’re still gathering details.”
The Federal Aviation Administration said the Boeing 767-300 overran the runway around 2 p.m. after arriving from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan and that it would investigate. The National Transportation Safety Board also began gathering information.
Street closures followed along Northwest 67th Avenue as thick black smoke rose over the airport. Travelers were warned to expect major delays and cancellations even after limited operations resume. Additional details remained limited in the first hours after the crash, as investigators worked to determine why the aircraft failed to stop on a runway more than 9,000 feet long.

At least 5 dead, 5 injured after Amazon cargo plane went off runway at Miami airport
sources.text:
At least 5 dead, 5 injured after Amazon cargo plane went off runway at Miami airport
MIAMI— An Amazon cargo plane barreled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people and injuring five others as it struck vehicles and was engulfed in flames, authorities said.
The aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and plowed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalized with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference.
Miami officials said Sunday afternoon that it was too soon to say whether the people who died were on board the plane or in the vehicles the plane hit.
The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.
The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon. Some 200 emergency personnel responded, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the department said. Firefighters used foam from specialized airport firefighting units to extinguish the fire, and crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane hours later.
The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semi-trucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.
The cause had yet to be determined, and it was not clear if weather had played a role. Thunderstorms and wind gusts up to 30 mph (48 kph) were recorded in the area at the time, according to the National Weather Service.
The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
More than 160 flights were canceled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Officials from Orlando International Airport, more than 200 miles (320 km) north of Miami, said some flights were diverted there.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it was sending a team to Miami led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy to investigate.
Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
Last year, a UPS plane crashed after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport. The crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said that a 767 cargo aircraft would typically be staffed only by a pilot and copilot on domestic flights. A third pilot would be added for an international flight, and a long-haul international flight would require a fourth pilot.
Arroyo, a retired longtime United Airlines pilot, said he wants to know whether the Amazon plane landed in the touchdown zone of the runway, and if it was beyond that area why it didn’t simply abort that landing and go around to line up for another attempt. Typically, the landing zone is within the first 3,000 feet (914 meters) of a runway.
“Did the aircraft land within the required touchdown zone? If it did, what happened? Was it weather related or mechanical related?” Arroyo said. “If it did land beyond the touchdown zone, why didn’t it go around? That is a standing practice around the world.”
Jackson Lee, who runs an electronics shop near the crash site, went outside with four colleagues after the crash and saw smoke rising near the airport’s fences, Lee said.
“We hear planes taking off and landing every five minutes. I thought I’d got used to it,” Lee said. “I never thought it could come this close to us.”
———
Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska. Associated Press writers Tim Reynolds in Miami, Rio Yamat in Las Vegas and Wufei Yu in Phoenix contributed.
