MIAMI (AP) — The five people killed when an Amazon cargo jet ran off a runway at Miami International Airport were all inside a van carrying seven people from a cleaning company, and an SUV hit outside of airport property, National Transportation Safety Board Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said Monday.
Homendy called the scene of Sunday’s crash “utter devastation.” She didn’t detail how many people were in the SUV or where the dead were located.
Homendy walked the route the Boeing 767 followed, noting tire marks from the pavement into the grass, the destroyed van carrying the cleaning crew, torn fencing, navigational equipment, and the crushed SUV outside airport property.
The debris included vehicle air bags, equipment from the vehicles, the airplane and the airport, and “fencing everywhere,” Homendy said.
“It’s pretty extensive. Hard to see and I’m sure it must have been very difficult for the responders as well,” Homendy said.
The airline, all told, traveled about 1,300 feet (396 meters) past the paved surface. Debris was everywhere, she said.
“I would describe it in one word as devastating, utter devastation,” Homendy said.
The van with seven people inside was “torn apart. It certainly must have been devastating,” she said. The van was owned by Professional Ocean Service Corp., an airline cleaning contractor.
Homendy said the NTSB would issue more information on Tuesday, including possibly information on speed that is confirmed by the flight data recorder.
Federal investigators examining cause of deadly overrun
Federal investigators examining the crash spent Monday determining whether the plane touched down too late to stop safely.
Video of Sunday’s landing appears to show the Boeing 767 remaining airborne well down the runway before touching down. Aviation experts said investigators will seek to determine exactly where the plane landed, whether it was beyond the normal touchdown zone, and why the pilots did not abandon the landing.
Investigators will also examine the plane’s speed and braking, weather and wind conditions, the aircraft’s mechanical condition and other factors that could have contributed to the deadly overrun.
The aircraft on Sunday flew from Cincinnati to Miami and then to San Juan, Puerto Rico. It was returning to Miami when it overran the runway around 2 p.m. and plowed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport.
Aside from the five who died, three people were critically injured and two others were hospitalized with less severe injuries, officials said.
The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.
The typical landing zone for a plane is within the first 3,000 feet (914 meters) of a runway, experts said. If the cargo jet was beyond that area, it should have aborted the landing and gone around for another try, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said.
Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former Inspector General of the Transportation Department, said video posted online shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.
It wasn’t raining at the time, but dark storm clouds loomed and strong winds were reported. Schiavo said that if the plane had a tail wind, that could have contributed to it floating further down the runway.
“A tail wind would certainly add to your troubles if you’ve already given up a good chunk of the runway by not touching down and landing right away,” Schiavo said.
Miami airport appears compliant without updated system
The Miami airport is not equipped with arresting systems that the FAA says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide to safely stop planes that do go past the end of a runway. Those beds of lightweight, crushable material at the end of a runway have been credited by the FAA with helping save at least 497 lives aboard planes that overran runways.
Miami’s airport appears to be in compliance and wasn’t required to have an arresting system because it has a 1,000-foot safety buffer at the end of its runways, said Mike O’Donnell, the FAA’s former director of airport safety and accident investigations.
The requirement was prompted by American Airlines Flight 1420 overrunning a runway at Little Rock National Airport in Arkansas in 1999, killing nine.
The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semitrucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.
The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
Schiavo said the NTSB will also closely examine the maintenance history of this plane — particularly since it has a history of foreign ownership, including by a Russian company.
The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of Sunday afternoon and continued to hamper air travel into Monday.
Miami International Airport said that two of its four runways remained closed Monday and that operations were to be affected throughout the day because of aircraft and flight crews not arriving there due to Sunday’s cancellations after the crash.
An airport spokesperson said there were 160 cancellations and more than 300 delayed flights Sunday, plus another 69 canceled flights Monday through mid-afternoon. Flight tracking sites were reporting widespread delays at the airport.
Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
Last year, a UPS plane crashed after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport. The crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.
___
Levy reported from Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, and Collins reported from Columbia, South Carolina. Associated Press writer Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, contributed.

At least 5 killed in Amazon Prime Air cargo plane crash in Miami
CHICAGO >> At least five people died when an Amazon Prime Air cargo flight overran a runway and crashed while landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday, local officials said.
Prime Air Flight 7598 overran the airport’s diagonal runway shortly before 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) and struck multiple vehicles on the ground, officials said during a news conference on Sunday afternoon.
Amazon and the Miami-Dade Aviation Department earlier confirmed that an incident occurred as the plane was trying to land.
Five people were also injured in the crash, including three who are in critical condition, said Miami-Dade Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. At least two people were trapped in vehicles that were struck by the plane, and the pilot and co-pilot were trapped inside the plane by the crash, Jadallah said.
Officials declined to identify those who died.
More than 60 rescue units and about 200 personnel responded to the incident, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said in a statement. As of late afternoon, emergency personnel were still dealing with an active fuel leak from the aircraft, Jadallah said.

Although the airport halted all flights immediately after the crash, two of its four runways had been reopened by Sunday evening.
The plane was a Boeing 767-300 that had departed from San Juan, Puerto Rico, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Cargo airline 21 Air operated the plane for Amazon, an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement.
The cargo airline did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.
Reuters photos after the crash showed the jet with its nose on the ground and tail tilted up. The right side of the plane had what appeared to be scorch marks.
Amazon is still gathering details about what happened, company spokesperson Kelly Nantel said. “We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened,” Nantel said in a statement. “Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved.”
The Federal Aviation Administration said it will investigate the crash.
Sunday’s incident is not the first time an Amazon Prime Air plane has been involved in a fatal crash. In February 2019, Atlas Air Flight 3591, a Boeing 767-300 freighter operating on behalf of Amazon Prime Air from Miami to Houston, entered a rapid descent and crashed into Trinity Bay. All three people on board were killed.

sources.news_title: Five dead as a cargo jet operating for Amazon overruns the runway at Miami airport
sources.text:
At least five people were killed and five others injured on Sunday when a cargo aircraft operating for Amazon overran the runway on landing at Miami International Airport, broke through the perimeter fence and a service road and struck several vehicles before catching fire.
The aircraft, a 32-year-old Boeing 767-300 freighter, was operating 21 Air flight 7598 and had departed from Luis Muñoz Marín airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. It landed at around 2pm local time on runway 30, the northwest-facing diagonal, and failed to stop within the airfield boundary, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
Miami-Dade County sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz confirmed the five deaths at a press conference. County mayor Daniella Levine Cava reported five injured, among them both pilots, without specifying their condition. “My heart is with their families,” she said. More than sixty county fire units were deployed to tackle the blaze, which sent up a dense column of smoke visible from several parts of the city.
The airport closed all runways and taxiways from 3pm and imposed a ground stop, in the middle of the Labor Day weekend, one of the busiest for air travel in the United States.
The aircraft was operated by 21 Air, an independent US cargo carrier flying on behalf of Amazon Air. The technology company does not hold its own air operator certificate for these services and contracts external carriers. Amazon confirmed the flight was being operated on its behalf. Its air network runs around 250 flights a day at some 60 airports across four continents.
Airfield weather records show a thunderstorm at the time of landing, with winds of 17 knots gusting to 26 and cumulonimbus formations at 2,000 feet. The investigation has not begun and no connection with those conditions has been established.
The Federal Aviation Administration said it would investigate the accident. In the United States, civil aviation accident investigations are led by the National Transportation Safety Board, whose involvement is expected in incidents of this severity.
The most serious previous accident involving Amazon's cargo network occurred in February 2019, when a Boeing 767 operated by Atlas Air for the company crashed into a bay in Texas, killing its three crew. The investigation concluded the accident was caused by pilot error.

sources.text:
An Amazon-branded cargo plane overran the runway while landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, striking multiple vehicles and bursting into flames, killing five people and injuring five others, authorities said. The crash closed all runways and taxiways at one of the country's busiest airports for hours and triggered a National Transportation Safety Board investigation.
The Boeing 767-300 aircraft, identified by the Federal Aviation Administration as 21 Air Flight 7598, overran Runway 30 at approximately 1:58 p.m. local time after arriving from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. Miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said the plane struck multiple vehicles, including two semi-trucks, before coming to rest in a field beside a roadway near the northwest end of the airport. The aircraft came to rest on its belly, largely intact despite the fire that followed the impact.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Raied "Ray" Jadallah said three people were taken to a trauma center in critical condition and two others were hospitalized with less severe injuries. Several victims were trapped inside the vehicles struck by the plane and had to be extracted by a technical rescue team, while a separate search-and-rescue operation worked to free the plane's two pilots, who were trapped in the cockpit. More than 60 fire rescue units and roughly 200 personnel responded to the scene. A source with knowledge of the incident told local NBC affiliate NBC6 that the two pilots were taken to Jackson South hospital, with three others taken to Jackson Memorial Hospital. The identities of those killed and injured had not been released as of Sunday evening.
Amazon confirmed the aircraft was operated on its behalf by 21 Air, a North Carolina-based cargo carrier that flies Boeing 767s for companies including Amazon and DHL. "We're heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today's incident at Miami International Airport," Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement. "Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss. The airplane, which was operated by 21 Air, was attempting to land when this incident occurred. We're working closely with local authorities and officials to learn more and will cooperate fully with any investigation."
The Air Traffic Control System Command Center issued a ground stop at Miami International around 2:30 p.m., initially set to lift at 3 p.m. before being extended to 5:30 p.m. as first responders worked the scene. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the stop was necessary to allow emergency crews to assess the situation and warned travelers to expect "significant delays and potential cancellations." The Miami-Dade Aviation Department said all runways and taxiways were closed as of 3 p.m.; two of the airport's four runways had reopened by early evening, though a ground delay was expected to persist into Monday due to the disabled aircraft. According to FlightAware, roughly 250 flights were delayed at the airport by late Sunday afternoon. Inspection crews reported no aircraft parts or debris on the runway itself, though the plane damaged navigational equipment as it left the pavement, according to CNN.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it had launched a "go-team" to investigate the crash, while the FAA said it would separately investigate the circumstances that led the aircraft to overrun the runway. No cause has been determined. The aircraft involved was a 32-year-old Boeing 767 originally built to carry passengers; it flew for several airlines over more than two decades before being converted into a cargo configuration in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said the response effort had brought the immediate danger under control. "There is no apparent threat to public safety at this time," Cordero-Stutz said at a Sunday evening news conference, though she noted crews remained on scene addressing an ongoing fuel leak from the wrecked aircraft.
Runway overruns during landing are among the more common categories of commercial aviation accidents, typically involving a combination of factors such as excess landing speed, a wet or contaminated runway surface, mechanical issues with braking systems, or pilot response time — though investigators had not indicated which, if any, of those factors were under scrutiny in Sunday's crash. The NTSB's investigation is expected to include analysis of the aircraft's flight data and cockpit voice recorders, along with witness accounts and airport surveillance footage, a process that typically takes months before a preliminary report is issued.

sources.news_title: Chaos in Miami as an Amazon Cargo Plane Overruns the Runway Leaving At Least 5 Dead And Several Injured
sources.text:
A routine cargo flight turned into a catastrophic disaster on Sunday afternoon in South Florida. An Amazon Prime Air jet crashed after landing at Miami International Airport. The aircraft failed to stop on the runway around two in the afternoon. It burst through the airport boundary fence and crossed an active roadway. Thick black smoke and intense fire quickly erupted from the mangled wreckage.
Crash scene video
The aircraft was identified as 21 Air Flight 7598. It was a Boeing 767-300 converted cargo jet operating under Amazon Prime Air branding. The flight had just completed an international trip from San Juan, Puerto Rico. Eyewitnesses along perimeter roads reported hearing a loud roar followed by a heavy impact. The plane struck multiple vehicles on the roadway before grinding to a halt. Plumes of dark smoke could be seen rising into the sky for miles.
Emergency first responders rushed to the chaotic scene within minutes of the crash. More than sixty units from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue arrived to battle the flames. Firefighters poured heavy streams of foam and water onto the burning fuselage. Responders worked tirelessly under extreme heat to secure the perimeter and extinguish hot spots. Local law enforcement immediately cordoned off the entire perimeter to protect bystanders. Paramedics treated several wounded motorists on the roadside near the impact zone.
Casualty numbers began emerging soon after first responders contained the primary fire. Officials confirmed that at least five individuals tragically lost their lives. At least five other people sustained significant injuries and received emergency medical care. Miami Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz stated there was no ongoing public safety threat. However, she confirmed the scene remained an active multi-agency rescue and investigation zone.
The disaster triggered severe operational disruptions across South Florida and the nation. The Federal Aviation Administration immediately declared a full ground stop for Miami. Departures were halted across key airport hubs, including Atlanta, Houston, and Washington. Incoming flights were placed into holding patterns or diverted to nearby airports. Airport officials reopened one runway hours later, but travel delays remain widespread. Travelers faced packed terminals and stranded connections throughout the rest of Sunday.
Federal safety agencies have already mobilized to determine the cause of the fatal overrun. The Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board launched inquiries. Investigators will recover the cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder from the wreckage. They will examine runway conditions, aircraft braking systems, thrust reversers, and pilot communications. Amazon does not operate the planes directly; it uses contracted cargo carriers like 21 Air. Both Amazon and 21 Air are expected to cooperate fully with federal investigators.
Runway overrun accidents remain among the most dangerous scenarios in modern commercial aviation. When an aircraft breaches airport boundaries, external civilian infrastructure is at severe risk. This crash underscores the immense risks posed by airports located in dense urban areas. Families of the victims are now awaiting answers as forensic teams work the scene. Officials urge travelers flying through Miami to check airline schedules before heading out. This developing tragedy marks one of the darkest aviation accidents in South Florida history.

sources.text:
MIAMI — An Amazon cargo plane operated by 21 Air crashed at Miami International Airport Sunday afternoon, killing 5 people and injuring 5 others after overrunning a runway and striking multiple vehicles.
The plane was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, when it overran runway 30 just before 2 p.m. and came to rest in a field adjacent to the runway, the Federal Aviation Administration said.
WATCH BELOW: 5 dead after Amazon cargo plane overruns runway at MIA
Dark smoke filled the area surrounding the airport following the crash.
Miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz confirmed the details.
"A cargo plane crashed at MIA as it overran runway number 30. It came to rest at a field adjacent to the runway," Cordero-Stutz said.
The response and what we know about the victims
Approximately 200 first responders were called to the scene. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Raied "Ray" Jadallah described a complex rescue operation involving trapped crew members and active fires.
"A complex situation extrication with our technical rescue teams started to occur. In addition to that, we had a complex fire, engine compartments that were on fire — including a search and rescue of the pilot and copilot who were trapped in this aircraft," Jadallah said.
Of the five people injured, three were taken to a trauma center. It was not immediately clear whether those impacted were on board the plane or in the vehicles that were struck.
Miami-Dade Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said the focus remained on the families of those affected.
"We're deeply grateful for everything they have done and always do. And right now our focus is on the families and the ongoing response at MIA," Levine Cava said.

"We're heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today's incident at Miami International Airport. We're working closely with local authorities and officials to learn more and will cooperate fully with any investigation," Nantel said.

The crash triggered a ground stop at Miami International Airport, leading to flight cancellations and hours-long delays. The Bell family, visiting from Portsmouth, Virginia, learned their flight home was canceled shortly after speaking with Solache at the airport.
"It's challenging. So, we're coming up on five hours, which I got a feeling it's going to be later than that. So hopefully, I don't know, hopefully American steps up to the plate and hooks us up," traveler Mike Bell said.
What's next
The National Transportation Safety Board and the FAA are investigating the cause of the crash. Authorities said there is no other threat to the public.
A hotline has been established for loved ones of people involved in the crash: 305-471-2400.

sources.news_title: At least 5 dead after Amazon cargo plane barrels off runway at Miami airport
sources.text:
MIAMI — An Amazon cargo plane barreled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people and injuring five others as it struck vehicles and was engulfed in flames, authorities said.
The aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and plowed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalized with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference.
Miami officials said Sunday afternoon that it was too soon to say whether the people who died were on board the plane or in the vehicles the plane hit.
The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.
The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon. Some 200 emergency personnel responded, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the department said. Firefighters used foam from specialized airport firefighting units to extinguish the fire, and crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane hours later.
The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semi-trucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.
The cause had yet to be determined, and it was not clear if weather had played a role. Thunderstorms and wind gusts up to 30 mph were recorded in the area at the time, according to the National Weather Service.
The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it was sending a team to Miami led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy to investigate.
Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
Last year, a UPS plane crashed after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport. The crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said that a 767 cargo aircraft would typically be staffed only by a pilot and copilot on domestic flights. A third pilot would be added for an international flight, and a long-haul international flight would require a fourth pilot.
Arroyo, a retired longtime United Airlines pilot, said he wants to know whether the Amazon plane landed in the touchdown zone of the runway, and if it was beyond that area why it didn’t simply abort that landing and go around to line up for another attempt. Typically, the landing zone is within the first 3,000 feet (914 meters) of a runway.
“Did the aircraft land within the required touchdown zone?” he asked. “If it did, what happened?”
Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former inspector general of the Transportation Department, said that video posted online of the landing shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.
“It didn’t touch down right away, and so it lost a lot of critical real estate by just continuing to float over the runway. It was literally still flying,” Schiavo said.
She noted the Miami airport is not equipped with arresting systems that the FAA says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide to safely stop planes that do go past the end of a runway. Those beds of lightweight, crushable material at the end of a runway have been credited by the FAA with helping save at least 497 lives aboard planes that overran runways.

MIAMI (AP) — An Amazon cargo plane barreled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people and injuring five others as it struck vehicles and was engulfed in flames, authorities said.
The aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and plowed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalized with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference.
Miami officials said Sunday afternoon that it was too soon to say whether those who died were on board the Prime Air plane or in the vehicles the plane hit.
The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.
The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon. About 200 emergency personnel responded, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the department said. Firefighters used foam from specialized airport firefighting units to extinguish the fire, and crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane hours later.
The cause had yet to be determined, and it was not clear if weather had played a role. Thunderstorms and wind gusts up to 30 mph were recorded in the area at the time, according to the National Weather Service.
The flight was operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in Greensboro, North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
More than 160 flights were canceled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it is sending a team to Miami led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy to investigate.
“We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a social media post. “Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved.”

At least 5 dead after Amazon cargo plane crashed at Miami airport
At least five people were killed, and five others hospitalized after an Amazon cargo plane overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, Sept. 6, crashing into multiple vehicles and erupting in flames, authorities said.
Prime Air Flight 7598 overran an airport diagonal runway just before 2 p.m. local time, Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said during a news conference Sunday afternoon. The Federal Aviation Administration and Amazon confirmed the plane came down striking multiple vehicles.
According to Miami-Dade County fire officials, some victims were trapped inside the vehicles and at least three of the wounded are in critical condition. A video of the crash obtained by NBC News Miami shows fire and a black cloud of smoke billowing from the aircraft.
"We will continue to update you as soon as information is confirmed," Rosie Cordero-Stutz told reporters. "Our entire community is joined in prayers and grieving for those who are affected."
Miami-Dade County Fire Chief Raied Jadallah said the aircraft is leaking fuel and officials are working to contain it. Authorities were not immediately sure what caused the crash, and Cordero-Stutz declined to answer additional questions from reporters.
The incident forced the closure of one of the nation's busiest airports. All runways and taxiways are closed.
More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the scene. The fire department said the plane struck multiple vehicles and is "assessing patients." Officials did not immediately report on the condition of the people hospitalized.
The FAA issued a ground stop at the airport until at least 5:30 p.m. ET and said it will investigate the incident.
Air Flight 7598, an Amazon Air Boeing 767-300 jet, had departed San Juan, Puerto Rico, earlier in the day on Sept. 6. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said travelers using Miami International Airport should expect delays and potential cancellations.
"We're working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened," Amazon told USA TODAY in a statement. "Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved."
USA TODAY reached out to the flight's operator, 21 Air, for comment.
Deadly crash comes amid Labor Day travel
The deadly crash happened during the Labor Day travel rush at the South Florida hub.
According to FlightAware, a flight-tracking site, the airport had the most total cancellations and delays in the country following the deadly crash.
Nearly 200 flights headed into and out of the airport were canceled, according to FlightAware, and over 250 were delayed. Inbound flights were delayed about 6.5 hours, the site said.
The airport is one of the busiest in the country, seeing some 26 million passengers board flights out of the hub in 2025, according to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics. Airport officials said they expected to serve 900,000 passengers over Labor Day weekend in 2025.
Cargo plane crashes in the US
The crash is the latest in a series of high-profile aircraft accidents in the United States. In November 2025, a UPS cargo jet crashed shortly after takeoff from Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport in Kentucky, killing 14.
The National Transportation Safety Board found that the left engine detached from the plane and caught fire, the USA TODAY Network previously reported.
In January 2025, an American Airlines regional jet collided with an Army Black Hawk helicopter near Reagan Washington National Airport, killing all 67 people aboard the two aircraft. NTSB members later said the crash resulted from a "multitude of errors" and "systemic issues across multiple organizations."
This story has been updated to add new information.

sources.news_title: At least five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes in US
sources.text:
At least five people were killed when an Amazon cargo plane overshot a runway after it landed Sunday at Miami International Airport, crashed into vehicles and caught fire, officials said.
Miami-Dade County fire chief Ray Jadallah told reporters that in addition to five fatalities, three people were transported to trauma centres "in critical condition" and two more were treated at a local hospital.
"The airplane did strike a couple of vehicles," which left "a couple of victims that were actually trapped in the vehicles," Mr Jadallah said.
"A complex extrication with our technical rescue team" was needed, "including a search and rescue of the pilot and co-pilot that were trapped in this aircraft."
Mr Jadallah did not clarify whether the pilot or co-pilot survived, and officials declined to answer questions after brief statements were made.
Video showed thick smoke billowing from the blue and white Boeing 767 after it arrived at 1:58 pm (1758 GMT) from Puerto Rico, as fire trucks raced to the scene.
The plane operating as Prime Air Flight 7598 caught fire as a result of the "crash," fire officials said.
"A total of 60 fire apparatuses arrived, just short, just shy of 200 men and women from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, to begin the actual search and rescue and firefighting," Mr Jadallah said.
In a statement posted to X Sunday evening, fire officials said they used foam to extinguish a fire in the engine compartment.
"One person was trapped under one of the involved vehicles and had to be extricated by specialized technical rescue personnel. Specialized hazardous materials (HazMat) units safely shut down the aircraft's engine and worked to control a fuel leak," the statement said.
The NTSB said in an X post on Sunday the B-767-300 cargo airplane was flying into Miami from San Juan, Puerto Rico and they have "launched a go team to investigate Sunday's runway excursion accident."
Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement the tech giant will cooperate with any investigation into the incident.
"We're heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today's incident at Miami International Airport. Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss," Ms Nantel said.
The airport closed all runways and taxiways because of the incident for several hours before two of its runways reopened.

sources.news_title: US: Amazon cargo aircraft overruns runway in Miami, striking multiple vehicles - The Tribune
sources.text:
Florida [US], September 7 (ANI): An Amazon cargo aircraft operated by 21 Air overran the runway while landing at Miami International Airport in Florida on Sunday and struck multiple vehicles on a road surrounding the airport.
Confirming the development, Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson, issued a statement on X, "We can confirm that an Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land at Miami International Airport today. This is a fast-moving situation, and we're still gathering details. We're working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened. Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved. We're doing everything we can to support those affected."
According to CNN, citing Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, the aircraft caught fire, sending heavy flames and smoke into the air.
“Units arrived to find an aeroplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing,” Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said in a statement.
The Boeing 767, operating as an Amazon Prime Air flight, left the runway after landing at around 2 pm local time and damaged navigational equipment after entering the area beyond the pavement, according to the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).
More than 60 fire units were deployed to the scene to extinguish the fire and assess people who may have been affected.
Authorities had not immediately confirmed whether anyone was injured.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said it was gathering information about the crash, while the FAA is set to investigate the incident.
The reason the aircraft was unable to stop before reaching the end of the runway was not immediately known.
The incident prompted authorities to halt operations at Miami International Airport, with a full ground stop issued as emergency crews assessed the crash site.
US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the disruption was expected to affect travellers.
"We’ve issued a full ground stop at Miami International while first responders assess the scene after an Amazon cargo plane overran the runway. If you’re travelling through the area, please expect significant delays and potential cancellations," Duffy said in a post on X.
The FAA identified the aircraft as 21 Air Flight 7598, saying it had overrun the runway after landing at Miami International Airport.
“21 Air Flight 7598 overran the runway after landing at Miami International Airport around 2 p.m. local time,” the FAA said in a statement to CNN.
The aircraft, a 32-year-old Boeing 767, had flown from San Juan, Puerto Rico, to Miami. It landed on Runway 30, which is more than 9,000 feet long, according to FAA data, reported by CNN.
21 Air, a cargo carrier with its operations centre in Miami, conducts flights for companies including Amazon and DHL and operates Boeing 767 aircraft.
The incident involved what is known as a runway excursion, in which an aircraft departs the designated runway surface. According to CNN, citing data from the International Air Transport Association, runway excursions are the most common type of incident involving aircraft worldwide.
Miami International Airport, like many major airports, has designated safety areas beyond its runways that are intended to provide a buffer in the event an aircraft leaves the runway. (ANI)

An Amazon cargo plane is seen after it crashed at Miami International Airport on Sept. 6, 2026, in Miami, Florida. In a statement, the Federal Aviation Administration said Prime Air Flight 7598 overran the runway while landing around 2 p.m. after departing from Luis Munoz Marin International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, earlier Sunday. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
Five people are dead and five people are injured after an Amazon Air cargo plane from Puerto Rico overran a runway at Miami International Airport, Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said in a news conference Sunday evening.
The names of the deceased and the injured have not been released.
The National Transportation Safety Board said Sunday it is sending a team, led by NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy, to investigate the incident, which took place Sunday afternoon.
Both the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and Amazon confirmed the incident in separate statements.
"21 Air Flight 7598 overran the runway after landing at Miami International Airport around 2 p.m. local time on Sunday, Sept. 6. The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft departed from Luis Munoz Marin International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico," the FAA statement said.
"We can confirm that an Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land at Miami International Airport today," Kelly Nantel, a spokesperson for Amazon, said in a statement, adding that it was a "fast-moving situation" and that Amazon was "working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened."
"Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved. We're doing everything we can to support those affected," the statement added.
Preliminary data from Flightradar24 shows the plane was going approximately 128 mph as it went off the runway.
A ground stop at Miami International Airport was lifted around three hours after the incident, with two of the four runways now reopened, according to officials.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

LAST UPDATE | 16 hrs ago
AT LEAST FIVE people have died and five more were injured when an Amazon cargo plane overshot a runway as it landed at a Florida airport.
The plane crashed into vehicles and caught fire at Miami International Airport at around 2pm (7pm Irish time) on Sunday afternoon.
Video showed thick smoke billowing from the blue and white Boeing 767 plane.
The Federal Aviation Administration, which manages air travel in the United States, said in a statement on social media that the incident happened as the plane arrived at the airport from San Juan in Puerto Rico.
Miami-Dade County fire chief Ray Jadallah told reporters that around 60 fire apparatuses with just short of 200 men and women were working on the scene.
He said that in addition to five fatalities, three people were transported to trauma centres “in critical condition” and two more were treated at a local hospital.
“The airplane did strike a couple of vehicles,” which left “a couple of victims that were actually trapped in the vehicles,” Jadallah said.
“A complex extrication with our technical rescue team” was needed, “including a search and rescue of the pilot and co-pilot that were trapped in this aircraft.”
Jadallah did not clarify whether the pilot or co-pilot survived, and officials declined to answer questions after brief statements were made.
He said the cause of the incident will be determined by the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB).
In a post on X on Sunday evening, the NTSB said the B-767-300 cargo plane was flying into Miami from San Juan, Puerto Rico and they have “launched a go team to investigate Sunday’s runway excursion accident.”
In a statement, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the tech giant will cooperate with any investigation into the incident.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport. Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss,” Nantel said.
Miami Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz told reporters Sunday that her officers encountered a “really tragic scene,” but there was “no apparent threat to public safety.”
The airport closed all runways and taxiways because of the incident and posted an update to its website Sunday evening that travellers should check directly with their airline before heading to the airport.
After hours of holding all flights at the international airport Sunday, with numerous delays and cancelled flights for commercial airline passengers, the Miami Herald newspaper reported that two of the airport’s four runways had reopened Sunday.
In a statement on X, Mayor Daniella Levine Cava thanked first responders for their speedy response, saying “our fire rescue team was there within seconds of the crash, so we’re deeply grateful.”

sources.news_title: Amazon Air Boeing 767 Overruns Miami Runway, Crosses Street, Comes To Stop In Parking Lot
sources.text:
An Amazon Air Boeing 767 operated by cargo carrier 21 Air had an accident while landing at Miami International Airport (MIA) this afternoon, causing operations at the airport to stop for hours. Tragically, we’ve also now learned that there have been at least five fatalities. Ugh, that’s heartbreaking.
In this post:
Boeing 767 has accident landing in Miami, shuts down airport
This accident happened this afternoon (Sunday, September 6, 2026), at Miami Airport. It involves a 32-year-old Boeing 767-300 with the registration code N1997A. It was operated by 21 Air, a cargo airline that contracts out to Amazon Air (often referred to as Prime Air), which is Amazon’s air cargo operation.
Shortly before 2PM local time, flight 2I7598 was on approach to Miami after completing a routine roughly two hour flight from San Juan (SJU), and it was coming in to land on runway 30. This runway is quite long, at 9,360 feet (around 2,850 meters).
However, the plane didn’t come to a stop in time, so it overran the runway. We’re not just talking by a little bit, but instead, by around 2,000 feet, meaning it didn’t stop in the overrun area. It continued and crossed a street, and it came to a stop in a parking lot (not that there’s anything funny about this, but the parking lot happened to be right by an Amazon fulfillment center).
The plane caught on fire, with the right wing in particular suffering major damage, and basically not being recognizable anymore.
Authorities have now confirmed that there have been at least five fatalities, with more people being seriously injured. It’s not clear if the fatalities were all people on the ground, or if it involved any of the crew. It appears that the plane struck at least one vehicle (and possibly more) on the street, and that there were some fatalities there.My thoughts are with all of the people involved and their families. What a horrible tragedy.
The airport shut down following this accident, with dozens of flights diverting to Fort Lauderdale (FLL) and West Palm Beach (DJT). However, the airport reopened several hours later, in the evening.
What caused the Boeing 767 accident at Miami Airport?
Miami is my home airport, and Miami is also a city where the airport is pretty close to the city, and there are lots of high rises. So many in Miami could see the smoke and “scene” from their homes.
Obviously it’s too early to tell what caused this accident. A runway that’s nearly 10,000 feet long is plenty big for a Boeing 767 to land, even with less than ideal conditions, so what could’ve contributed to this?
At the time of the accident, there were somewhat gusty winds (at an angle that made for a crosswind for runway 30), thunderstorms, and some rain. So in terms of the gusts, it’s understandable that the pilots may have approached a bit faster than usual, and the precipitation made for a wet runway, which also isn’t ideal in terms of braking.
We’ve now also seen a video of the landing, and it sure explains a lot. According to Flightradar24 data, at the intersection of runway 27 and runway 30 (right near the typical landing point), the plane was at a speed of 177 knots. Just for context, the plane’s landing speed is only around 140 knots.
But the bigger issue is that the plane touched down really late, and then barely slowed down. Looking at Flightradar24 data, it seems that the plane was at a speed of around 110 knots when it went off the end of the runway, which is insanely fast.
In the video, you can see the plane landed really far down the runway, and it looked like the nose wheel made contact with the runway before the left main gear did, and as a result, the reverse thrusters didn’t deploy. Admittedly hindsight is 20/20, but I have no clue what the pilots were thinking here, and why they didn’t perform a go around.
Bottom line
A 21 Air Boeing 767 operating on behalf of Amazon Air had an accident while landing in Miami this afternoon. The plane overran the runway, and not just by a little. We’re talking around 2,000 feet, as the plane went through the airport perimeter fence, crossed a road, and ended up in a parking lot, at which point the plane burst into flames.
There are at least five fatalities as a result of this accident, which is incredibly tragic, and I’m keeping them in my thoughts. The airport was closed for hours following the incident. As of now, there are a lot more questions than answers, including how this happened, given that the plane exited the runway at a speed of around 110 knots.

sources.news_title: Plane smashes into vehicles in terrifying runway disaster
sources.text:
Amazon plane crash Miami International Airport: Five killed after plane crashes off runway, bursts into flames
Five people have been killed and several others rushed to hospital after an Amazon cargo plane careened off a runway at Miami International Airport, smashing into several vehicles before erupting in flames.
The dramatic crash unfolded about 2pm on Sunday after the Prime Air aircraft arrived in Florida from San Juan, Puerto Rico, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
The plane overshot the runway before eventually coming to a stop beside a roadway, where images shared on social media showed two semi-trucks nearby.
Pictures from the scene showed the aircraft resting on its belly and appearing largely intact despite a fire breaking out following the crash.
Five people have now been confirmed dead following the horror incident, while several others have been transported to hospital with injuries. The extent of their injuries remains unknown.
The emergency forced authorities to close all runways and taxiways at Miami International Airport, with a ground stop also put in place, an airport spokesperson confirmed.
A ground stop effectively brings airport operations to a halt, with flights prevented from departing or arriving until restrictions are lifted.
The Federal Aviation Administration has warned travellers to expect ongoing delays even after the airport reopens, with arrivals and departures expected to resume at a reduced rate.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said the aircraft struck multiple vehicles after running beyond the end of the runway.
Emergency crews responding to the crash arrived to find the plane on fire, prompting a major operation to bring the blaze under control.
About 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units were deployed to the scene and were working to extinguish the fire on Sunday afternoon, the agency said in a social media post.

sources.news_title: Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport after overshooting runway, fire erupts
sources.text:
At least five people have been killed, and five others were injured after an Amazon cargo plane overran a runway and crashed while landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday, striking multiple vehicles and bursting into flames. The incident forced the closure of all runways and taxiways, causing significant disruption at one of the busiest airports in the US.
Prime Air Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-300 operated by cargo carrier 21 Air, overran Miami International Airport’s diagonal runway at around 2 p.m. EDT, according to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).
The aircraft had arrived from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, before the crash. Airport officials said the plane came to rest at the northwest end of the airport and was disabled.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said the aircraft struck multiple vehicles after leaving the runway. Images from the scene showed the jet resting on its belly near a roadway, with its tail raised and scorch marks visible on the right side.
The crash triggered a major emergency response, with more than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units sent to the scene. Thick black smoke and heavy flames were reported as emergency crews worked to extinguish the fire and assess those involved.
Authorities had not immediately released a confirmed number of injuries or fatalities, although multiple patients were reportedly being assessed following the incident.
All runways and taxiways at Miami International Airport were closed from around 3 p.m. as emergency operations continued.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the FAA had ordered a full ground stop and warned passengers to expect significant delays and possible cancellations.
Amazon confirmed that one of its aircraft, operated by 21 Air, was involved in an incident while attempting to land in Miami.
“We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said. She added that the company’s priority was the “safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved.”
The FAA said it will investigate the incident, while the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said it was gathering information.
The circumstances that caused the Boeing 767 to overrun the runway remain unclear. Investigators are expected to examine the aircraft, runway conditions, weather, flight data and the plane’s landing sequence.
The aircraft involved was more than 32 years old, having first flown in June 1994. It originally operated as a passenger aircraft before being converted into a freighter.
The Boeing 767-300 was subsequently operated by several airlines, including Air Europa, Kenya Airways and Atlas Air, before becoming part of the cargo fleet.
21 Air began operating Boeing 767-300 freighters for Amazon in 2024. The aircraft type has become an important part of Amazon’s air-cargo operation, alongside larger Airbus A330 freighters and smaller Boeing 737 aircraft.
The Boeing 767 is no longer produced as a commercial passenger aircraft, although Boeing continues to manufacture variants of the aircraft for military refuelling missions.
The investigation into Sunday’s crash is ongoing.
(With Bloomberg, AP inputs)

What's next?
The airport issued a ground stop and closed the runways, which remains in effect.
At least five people are dead after an Amazon cargo plane barrelled off a runway at Miami International Airport, striking multiple vehicles and bursting into flames.
The crash sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky and forced the closure of all runways at one of the United States's busiest airports.
Five people were killed, three were critically injured and two others were taken to hospital with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference.

Five people are dead and five others are injured after an Amazon-branded cargo plane crashed just outside Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, officials said.

The plane overran Runway 30, struck multiple vehicles and came to rest at a field next to the airport, Miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said.
Three people were in critical condition and were taken to a trauma center, and two others were taken to a local hospital, Miami-Dade Fire Chief Raied Jadallah said.

sources.news_title: Amazon Prime Air Plane Overruns Runway at Miami International Airport, Strikes Vehicles and Catches Fire - FINCHANNEL
sources.text:
UPDATE: At least five people are dead after an Amazon cargo aircraft overran the runway during a landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, striking multiple vehicles and sending a thick black plume of smoke into the air as it caught fire.
Five others were injured in the crash, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Raied “Ray” Jadallah said during a news conference Sunday evening. Three are in critical condition and were taken to a trauma center, while two others were taken to a local hospital, he said.
Several victims were trapped in the vehicles that were hit by the plane and had to be extricated, Jadallah said. It’s not clear whether the victims who died were on the plane or on the ground.
The FINANCIAL — An Amazon Prime Air cargo plane operated by 21 Air overran a runway while landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday, Sept. 6, striking multiple vehicles and catching fire, according to the Federal Aviation Administration and Miami-Dade Fire Rescue.
The Boeing 767-300, operating as 21 Air Flight 7598, arrived from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, before the incident at Miami International Airport, or MIA, at about 2 p.m. local time.
The FAA said the aircraft overran the runway after landing and that it will investigate the incident.
Video obtained by NBC6 South Florida and other local media showed an aircraft in Amazon Prime Air livery beyond the runway with flames and thick black smoke rising from the scene.
Amazon plane crash at Miami airport
Miami International Airport identified the aircraft as Prime Air Flight 7598 and said it became disabled at the northwest end of the airport after overrunning the airport’s diagonal runway.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said the aircraft struck multiple vehicles after leaving the runway. More than 60 fire-rescue units responded to the scene as firefighters worked to extinguish the fire.
Local 10 reported that Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said multiple people were injured, although officials did not immediately provide the number of injured people or the severity of their injuries.
No verified official death toll had been released in the latest information available.
Reports circulating on social media have included unconfirmed claims about fatalities and the condition of the flight crew. Those claims have not been treated as confirmed information here.
FAA orders ground stop at Miami International Airport
The crash temporarily brought operations at MIA to a halt.
The FAA issued a ground stop because of a disabled aircraft on the runway. Miami International Airport said all runways and taxiways were closed following the incident.
The FAA said it expected significant delays even after the airport resumed operations, because arrivals and departures would initially operate at a reduced rate.
Reuters reported that all runways and taxiways were closed as of about 3 p.m. Eastern time and that information on injuries or fatalities was not initially available.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy also warned travelers to expect disruptions following the incident.
What happened to the Amazon plane?
The FAA said 21 Air Flight 7598 overran the runway after landing at Miami International Airport at approximately 2 p.m. Sunday.
The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft had departed from San Juan, Puerto Rico. The FAA has not released a cause for the runway overrun and said the agency will investigate.
CNN, citing the FAA, reported that the aircraft went off the runway after landing. Air traffic-control audio reviewed in CNN’s report included a ground vehicle reporting that an aircraft had overrun the runway.
The precise sequence of events that caused the aircraft to leave the runway remains under investigation.
There is currently no verified evidence establishing whether weather, aircraft performance, runway conditions, pilot actions or another factor contributed to the incident. Investigators will determine the cause.
Amazon confirms 21 Air-operated aircraft was involved
Amazon confirmed that an Amazon Air aircraft operated by 21 Air was involved.
In a statement provided to NBC6, Amazon said:
“We can confirm that an Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land at Miami International Airport today.”
Amazon said it was still gathering information and was working with local authorities and officials to determine what happened.
The company said its immediate priority was the “safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved” and that it was working to support those affected.
21 Air is an all-cargo airline that operates aircraft for customers including Amazon Prime Air. The company’s website lists a 24/7 Miami operations center and identifies Amazon Prime Air among its customers.
Flight 7598 was operating from San Juan to Miami
Flight-tracking information identifies 21 Air Flight 7598 as a San Juan-to-Miami service using a Boeing 767-300 freighter.
The flight departed Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan at about 11:42 a.m. Atlantic Standard Time and was recorded as landing in Miami at approximately 1:53 p.m. Eastern time, according to FlightStats.
The aircraft was an Amazon Air-operated Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft rather than a passenger flight. The plane was operated by 21 Air for Amazon Air.
Miami-Dade emergency crews respond
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue’s aviation operation is responsible for responding to aircraft incidents at Miami International Airport. The department operates dedicated airport fire stations at MIA.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said crews arrived to find the aircraft on fire after it struck multiple vehicles. Approximately 60 units were dispatched to fight the fire and assess people at the scene.
The department’s active-call system provides live information on emergency incidents, although the county notes that the online list is not a complete record of all incidents being handled by its crews.
Investigation underway
The FAA said it will investigate the Miami plane crash. The National Transportation Safety Board was also gathering information about the incident, according to AP.
Investigators are expected to examine the aircraft, runway and surrounding area, flight data, air-traffic-control communications, weather conditions and other evidence as they determine why the Boeing 767 overran the runway.
At this stage, authorities have not announced a cause.
The investigation is ongoing.
Amazon aircraft incidents in the United States
1. 2019 — Atlas Air Flight 3591, Texas — 3 killed
This is the most significant previous Amazon Air aircraft accident in the United States.
On Feb. 23, 2019, Atlas Air Flight 3591, a Boeing 767-375BCF, crashed into Trinity Bay in Texas while operating a domestic cargo flight for Amazon.com Services LLC. The flight had departed Miami International Airport and was bound for George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston.
All three people aboard — the captain, first officer and a non-revenue pilot riding in the jump seat — were killed.
The NTSB’s investigation found that the aircraft entered a rapid descent from about 6,000 feet. The board determined that the probable cause was the first officer’s inappropriate response to an inadvertent activation of the Boeing 767’s go-around mode, which led to spatial disorientation and nose-down control inputs. The captain’s failure to adequately monitor the aircraft’s flight path and intervene effectively was also identified as a contributing factor.
This accident is particularly relevant to the Miami incident because the 2019 Amazon flight also originated at Miami International Airport. The aircraft had been leased to Amazon and carried Amazon’s Prime Air livery.
Aircraft: Boeing 767-375BCF
Operator: Atlas Air
Customer: Amazon.com Services LLC
Flight: 3591
Route: Miami → Houston
Location: Trinity Bay, Texas
Date: Feb. 23, 2019
Fatalities: 3
Cause: Loss of control following inadvertent go-around-mode activation, according to NTSB
2. Sept. 6, 2026 — 21 Air Flight 7598, Miami
The newest incident is the Sept. 6, 2026, Miami International Airport runway overrun.
The FAA said 21 Air Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft operating for Amazon Air, overran the runway after landing at approximately 2 p.m. local time.
The aircraft had flown from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, to Miami. The FAA said it will investigate.
The aircraft reportedly left the runway, struck vehicles and caught fire. More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded, according to AP’s reporting.
Unlike the 2019 Texas crash, this was a runway excursion after landing, rather than a loss-of-control accident during flight.
The cause has not been established.
Aircraft: Boeing 767-300
Operator: 21 Air
Customer: Amazon Air
Flight: 7598
Route: San Juan → Miami
Location: Miami International Airport
Date: Sept. 6, 2026
Cause: Under investigation
Fatalities/injuries: Authorities were still establishing the casualty picture in the initial reports
Reuters reported that the incident forced MIA to close its runways and taxiways and impose a ground stop.
Amazon’s drone accidents are a separate category
The federal record becomes considerably larger if Amazon Prime Air delivery drones are included.
These aircraft are not conventional passenger or cargo airplanes. They are unmanned aircraft operated by Amazon.
3. November 2023 — Amazon MK27-2 drone, Oregon
On Nov. 10, 2023, an Amazon MK27-2 delivery drone crashed during a test flight at the Eastern Oregon Regional Airport in Pendleton, Oregon.
The NTSB classified the aircraft as an Amazon.com Services LLC MK27-2. It was substantially damaged, but there were no injuries.
The NTSB found that the drone’s battery was insufficiently charged. During the flight, the aircraft delivered a package and began climbing back toward its landing zone. It issued a low-voltage warning and initiated an emergency landing maneuver, but the battery depleted and the drone lost propulsion.
The NTSB determined the probable cause was the operator’s use of an insufficiently charged battery, resulting in loss of engine power and impact with terrain.
Aircraft: Amazon MK27-2
Location: Pendleton, Oregon
Date: Nov. 10, 2023
Damage: Substantial
Injuries: None
Cause: Insufficiently charged battery
4. September 2024 — Two Amazon MK30 drones collide in Oregon
On Sept. 6, 2024, two Amazon MK30 drones were involved in a midair collision during testing at the Pendleton UAS Range in Oregon.
The NTSB identified both aircraft as being owned and operated by Amazon.com Services LLC.
One aircraft, N213PA, was destroyed; the other, N282PA, sustained substantial damage. There were no injuries.
The incident occurred while Amazon was conducting simulated motor-out recovery procedures.
The NTSB found that both drones were diverted toward the same alternate landing pad, putting them on a collision course.
The board determined the probable cause was the operator’s failure to maintain separation between the two drones during simultaneous simulated engine-out recoveries.
Aircraft: 2 × Amazon MK30
Location: Pendleton, Oregon
Date: Sept. 6, 2024
Damage: One destroyed, one substantially damaged
Injuries: None
Cause: Failure to maintain separation during simulated emergency recoveries
5. May 2025 — Amazon MK30 drone crashes in Arizona
On May 21, 2025, an Amazon MK30 delivery drone made a forced landing on the front lawn of a residence in Tolleson, Arizona, in the Phoenix area.
The aircraft was N503PA and was registered to Amazon.com Services LLC. The Aviation Safety Network recorded no injuries and minor aircraft damage, although its entry is based on unofficial sources rather than an NTSB final determination.
This incident is important because it preceded the much more significant Arizona drone accidents later in 2025.
6. October 2025 — Two Amazon drones hit a crane in Arizona
This was another significant Prime Air drone incident.
On Oct. 1, 2025, two Amazon MK30 drones collided with a mobile crane in Tolleson, Arizona.
The NTSB’s preliminary report says both drones struck the crane’s boom, after which a battery fire occurred. No injuries were reported.
Reuters reported that the FAA and NTSB investigated the incident. Amazon temporarily paused drone deliveries in Arizona and subsequently said its internal review did not identify a problem with the drones or supporting technology. Amazon said it introduced additional landscape inspections to identify moving obstacles such as cranes.
Aircraft: 2 × Amazon MK30
Location: Tolleson, Arizona
Date: Oct. 1, 2025
Injuries: None reported
Event: Collision with crane
Investigation: FAA/NTSB
7. November 2025 — Amazon drone strikes Internet cable in Texas
On Nov. 18, 2025, an Amazon MK30 drone struck an overhead Internet cable in Waco, Texas, after completing a delivery.
According to the FAA, the agency investigated the incident. The NTSB said it was not investigating.
Amazon said the drone’s propeller became entangled in a thin overhead wire and that the aircraft then performed a “Safe Contingent Landing,” a procedure designed to bring the drone safely down after an abnormal event.
No injuries or widespread Internet outages were reported.
This is therefore better described as a drone safety incident, rather than a conventional aircraft crash.
8. January 2026 — Alaska Airlines cargo Airbus A330 operating for Amazon
There is another federal-record case worth mentioning because it demonstrates why simply searching for the words “Amazon plane crash” can produce misleading results.
On Jan. 28, 2026, an Alaska Airlines Airbus A330-343 operating a domestic cargo flight for Amazon.com Services LLC struck birds shortly after takeoff from Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport.
The aircraft was bound for Houston.
The NTSB preliminary report says the crew encountered a flock of geese at roughly 900–1,000 feet. Multiple birds struck the aircraft. There were no injuries to the two crew members.
This was not an Amazon-operated airline in the conventional sense; Alaska Airlines operated the aircraft for Amazon.

sources.text:
Five killed as Amazon plane overruns runway, hitting vehicles and bursting into flames
Updated ,first published
Miami: An Amazon cargo plane has barrelled off a runway at Miami International Airport, killing at least five people and injuring five others as it struck vehicles and was engulfed in flames, authorities said.
The aircraft overran the runway about 2pm on Sunday (4am Monday AEST) after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and ploughed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport.
Five people were killed, three critically injured, and two others hospitalised with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference.
It wasn’t immediately clear whether the pilots survived or whether those killed were all in vehicles when the plane struck.
The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.
The crash halted flights at the airport, a busy travel hub, for most of Sunday afternoon. Some 200 emergency personnel responded, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the department said.
Firefighters used foam from specialised airport firefighting units to extinguish the fire, and crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane hours later.
The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semi-trucks, according to images. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.
The cause had yet to be determined, and it was unclear if the weather had played a role. Thunderstorms and wind gusts up to 48 km/h were recorded in the area at the time, according to the US National Weather Service.
The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
More than 160 flights were cancelled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Officials from Orlando International Airport, more than 320 kilometres north of Miami, said some flights were diverted there.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it was sending a team to Miami, led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy, to investigate.
Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
Last year, a UPS plane crashed after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport. The crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said that a 767 cargo aircraft would typically be flown only by a pilot and copilot on domestic flights. A third pilot would be added for an international flight, and a long-haul international flight would require a fourth pilot.
Arroyo, a retired longtime United Airlines pilot, said he wants to know whether the Amazon plane landed in the touchdown zone of the runway, and if it was beyond that area, why it didn’t simply abort that landing and go around to line up for another attempt. Typically, the landing zone is within the first 914 metres of a runway.
“Did the aircraft land within the required touchdown zone?” he asked. “If it did, what happened?”
Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former inspector general of the Transportation Department, said that footage posted online of the landing showed the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.
“It didn’t touch down right away, and so it lost a lot of critical real estate by just continuing to float over the runway. It was literally still flying,” Schiavo said.
She noted that the Miami airport is not equipped with arresting systems, which the FAA says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide, to safely stop planes that go past the end of a runway. Those beds of lightweight, crushable material at the end of a runway have been credited by the FAA with helping save at least 497 lives aboard planes that overran runways.

sources.text:
Amazon cargo plane overshoots runway at Miami airport, killing five
MIAMI – An Amazon cargo plane overran a runway at Miami International Airport and burst into flames on Sept 6, killing at least five people and shutting down the airport’s runways.
The Boeing 767-300, operated by 21 Air as Prime Air Flight 7598, overshot the runway at around 2pm after arriving from Luis Munoz Marin International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, according to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).
The plane slammed into multiple vehicles near the airport, trapping some people inside, according to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, which reported heavy flames and smoke when it responded to the incident.
Along with the five people who were killed, another five were injured, three of whom were in critical condition, Miami-Dade Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said at a news conference.
“We’ll continue to update you as soon as information is confirmed, and tonight our entire community is joined in prayer and grieving for those who are affected,” she said.
“Prime Air Flight 7598 overran Miami International Airport’s diagonal runway and is disabled at the north-west end of the airport,” Indira Almeida-Pardillo, a spokeswoman for Miami International Airport, said in a statement.
She said all runways and taxiways were closed as at 3pm local time (3am on Sept 7, Singapore time) and a ground stop was in effect.
Several hours later, at least two of the runways had opened, said Greg Chin, another airport spokesperson.
There was “a very complex fire”, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue chief Ray Jadallah said at a news conference, and the engine compartments were on fire during the “search and rescue of the pilot and co-pilot who were trapped in this aircraft”.
A total of 60 fire units responded to the scene.
“They arrived within 30 seconds after getting a call,” he said.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned of significant delays and possible cancellations in a post on social media platform X.
21 Air, a Miami-based cargo airline, began operating Boeing 767-300 freighters on behalf of Amazon in 2024.
In a statement on its website, 21 Air said it was cooperating with the FAA, the US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and local authorities.
“Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives,” the company said.
Amazon confirmed that one of its planes, operated by 21 Air, experienced an incident while attempting to land in Miami.
“We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened,” Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokeswoman, said in a post on X.
“Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being and care of everyone involved,” she added.
The FAA said it would investigate the incident, and the NTSB said it was also starting a probe and would hold a media briefing on Sept 7.
Amazon’s in-house cargo airline has tilted its focus to larger aircraft that can handle longer distances and bulk shipping, with the 767 model that crashed in Miami now accounting for the largest portion of its fleet.
Amazon Prime also has 10 Airbus A330-300 freighters, as well as smaller narrow-body 737s for regional routes.
21 Air, which also provides dedicated transport for DHL Express, is owned by Jim Crane, the chairman of the Houston Astros baseball team, according to a 2021 letter to the Department of Transportation.
While the circumstances of the accident remain unknown, the crash stands to be the worst cargo-related incident since UPS Airlines Flight 2976 was destroyed on Nov 4, 2025, when it impacted the ground shortly after take-off at Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport in Kentucky, killing the three crew members on board and 11 people on the ground.
Freight planes make up only a small part of commercial air traffic, but cargo operations have been prone to proportionally more crashes over the years, partly because flights can be longer and planes are often older.
The most common accidents in the industry in 2025 were tail strikes, landing-gear malfunctions, runway excursions and ground damage, according to the International Air Transport Association’s 2025 Annual Safety Report.
The aircraft involved in the Miami crash was more than 32 years old, having first flown in June 1994.
Over the decades, it changed hands, including operations for Air Europa, Kenya Airways and Atlas Air, a cargo specialist, after being converted into a cargo aircraft in 2016, according to data compiled by the Planespotters website.
The Boeing 767 is no longer in production as a commercial aircraft but still widely flown.
The manufacturer still makes the plane in low numbers as military refuelling planes. BLOOMBERG
