An Amazon Prime Air cargo plane crashed after it overshot a runway at Miami International Airport
sources.text:
At least five people were killed, and five more injured, authorities said, after an Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767 cargo plane overshot the runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, striking multiple vehicles and erupting into a blaze.
Videos from the scene showed a fire and thick black smoke rising from the plane. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said in a Sunday evening statement that more than 60 of its units and about 200 personnel responded to the incident, arriving to find an airplane with "heavy flames and smoke showing."
At an afternoon news conference, Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said the fire had been contained and that there was no ongoing threat to the public.
It was not immediately clear on Sunday how many people were on the plane, and whether those killed were people on the ground. Officials did not identify the deceased.
An Amazon spokesperson said that "an Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land at Miami International Airport."
"This is a fast-moving situation and we're still gathering details," the spokesperson, Kelly Nantel, said in an X post around 4 p.m. "We're working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened."
Of the five people who were injured, three were taken to a trauma center, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said. The other two were taken to area hospitals.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said HazMat units safely shut down the plane's engine.
"Firefighters encountered a complex engine compartment fire and used foam from specialized airport firefighting units to extinguish the flames," the agency said. "The Crews also conducted search and rescue operations for the pilots and co-pilots inside the cockpit while locating and assessing patients throughout the scene."
What we know about the plane and the flight so far
The plane took off from Puerto Rico at noon and reached Miami around 2 p.m., according to data from the aviation tracking website Flightradar24. The website also showed the plane was traveling at 112 knots as it exited the usable part of the runway. Weather data shows there were thunderstorms and gusting winds at the time of the crash.
The plane involved was a Boeing 767-300 freighter, registered as N1997A, and first delivered as a passenger jet in 1994 to the now-defunct Belgian airline Sobelair. It passed through several more airlines before being converted into a freighter by a third party — not Boeing — and re-entering service in 2016. That means it had been operated and maintained by multiple companies over three decades before Sunday's crash.
"Boeing extends our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in the accident in Miami," Boeing said in a statement. "Our hearts go out to those injured and affected by this tragedy. Boeing is supporting the investigation led by the U.S National Transportation Safety Board."
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on X around 4 p.m. that a full ground stop was in place "while first responders assess the scene." The plane was left disabled at the northwest end of the airport. The airport has since partially reopened as of Sunday evening, but runway 30 remains closed, and passengers should expect delays of at least 6 hours, according to the FAA.
According to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue radio transmissions recorded on Broadcastify, the plane crossed 67th Avenue, a nearby road, before it struck a truck.
"We have a patient trapped," a first responder said, according to the recordings.
First responders scrambled to attain a reliable water supply as they sought to control the fire on the plane, according to the recordings.
A command dispatcher asked first responders several times to enter the plane, according to the recordings. The fire was largely extinguished by 2:08 p.m.
"I need you to start making entry with your crew so we can shut down the engine," the command dispatcher said, according to the recordings. "I believe the pilots are out of the aircraft."
A first responder said in the recordings that one pilot was with him in a parking lot. Another first responder said that the pilot was talking with firefighters at the scene to show them how to shut down the engine.
This is the second 767 cargo plane to crash in Amazon's Prime Air network. In 2019, an Atlas Air freighter flying on behalf of Amazon crashed into Trinity Bay near Houston, killing the three people on board. The NTSB said the cause of that accident was in-flight loss of control due to pilot error.

sources.news_title: Amazon jet goes off Miami runway, bursts into flames
sources.text:
MIAMI — An Amazon cargo plane barreled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people and injuring five others as it struck vehicles and was engulfed in flames, authorities said.
The aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and plowed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalized with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference.
It wasn’t immediately clear if the pilots survived or those killed were all in vehicles when the plane struck.
The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.
The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon. Some 200 emergency personnel responded, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the department said. Firefighters used foam from specialized airport firefighting units to extinguish the fire, and crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane hours later.
The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semitrucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.
The cause had yet to be determined, and it was not clear if weather had played a role. Thunderstorms and wind gusts up to 30 mph (48 kph) were recorded in the area at the time, according to the National Weather Service.
WATCH: Moments after a Prime Air Boeing 767 overshot the runway at Miami International Airport and crossed a road pic.twitter.com/kyCeeOpHdp
— BNO News (@BNONews) September 6, 2026
The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
More than 160 flights were canceled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Officials from Orlando International Airport, more than 200 miles north of Miami, said some flights were diverted there.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it was sending a team to Miami led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy to investigate.
Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
Last year, a UPS plane crashed after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport. The crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.
NEW ANGLE OF THE MIAMI CARGO JET INCIDENT 🚨✈️
The damage to the Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767 does NOT appear as severe as initially feared.
The aircraft reportedly suffered a runway excursion while landing at Miami International Airport after arriving from Puerto Rico.
The jet… pic.twitter.com/7Q0TdXajj8
— Shitik (@RitikV2) September 6, 2026
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said that a 767 cargo aircraft would typically be staffed only by a pilot and copilot on domestic flights. A third pilot would be added for an international flight, and a long-haul international flight would require a fourth pilot.
Arroyo, a retired longtime United Airlines pilot, said he wants to know whether the Amazon plane landed in the touchdown zone of the runway, and if it was beyond that area why it didn’t simply abort that landing and go around to line up for another attempt. Typically, the landing zone is within the first 3,000 feet (914 meters) of a runway.
“Did the aircraft land within the required touchdown zone?” he asked. “If it did, what happened?”
Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former inspector general of the Transportation Department, said that video posted online of the landing shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.
“It didn’t touch down right away, and so it lost a lot of critical real estate by just continuing to float over the runway. It was literally still flying,” Schiavo said.
She noted the Miami airport is not equipped with arresting systems that the FAA says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide to safely stop planes that do go past the end of a runway. Those beds of lightweight, crushable material at the end of a runway have been credited by the FAA with helping save at least 497 lives aboard planes that overran runways.
___
Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska. Associated Press writers Tim Reynolds in Miami, Rio Yamat in Las Vegas and Wufei Yu in Phoenix contributed.

sources.news_title: Miami Airport Issues Ground Stop After Amazon Prime Air Cargo Plane Overruns Runway
sources.text:
Miami Airport Issues Ground Stop After Amazon Prime Air Cargo Plane Overruns Runway
FAA investigates after Amazon-Branded Jet overruns runway, shutting down Miami Airport
A Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft operating for Amazon's Prime Air network overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, forcing a rare full ground stop and shutting all runways and taxiways at one of America's busiest hubs, the US Federal Aviation Administration has confirmed.
21 Air Flight 7598, flying from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, landed in Miami at around 2pm local time before running off the end of Runway 30.
Footage circulating on social media and local television appears to show the Amazon-branded jet beyond the airport perimeter, near Northwest 67th Avenue, with its fuselage resting in a field beside a highway.
Entire Airfield Brought to a Halt
Miami International Airport confirmed a 'disabled aircraft' on the runway and closed all runways and taxiways by approximately 3pm, with a ground stop enforced. The FAA said the measure was more typically associated with severe weather than a single aircraft incident.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue attended the scene. Images reviewed by local broadcaster WSVN showed dark smoke rising near the aircraft, though officials have not confirmed whether fuel or cargo contributed to it.
No injuries to the crew or anyone on the ground have been confirmed. As a cargo flight, there were no passengers aboard.
In a joint statement, airport officials and operator 21 Air said the aircraft 'overran Miami International Airport's diagonal runway and is disabled at the northwest end of the airport', adding that fire crews had responded. The jet remained disabled at the site.
Flight-tracking service FlightRadar24 showed movements at the airport coming to an abrupt halt as the ground stop took effect. Miami is one of the busiest gateways for Latin America and the Caribbean, and passengers on unrelated flights were left waiting on the tarmac or holding in the air while the disabled aircraft was dealt with.
FAA Opens Investigation as Unconfirmed Details Emerge
The FAA said its information remained preliminary and confirmed it would investigate the overrun. Regulators typically examine runway conditions, aircraft performance, braking action and crew decision-making in such cases, though no cause has yet been suggested by the agency or the airline.
Air traffic control recordings, picked up via LiveATC.com, captured a ground vehicle informing the control tower: 'Looks like we have an aircraft that overran the runway on 30.'
CNN said it had requested comment from Amazon regarding the incident and its safety procedures. Amazon had not issued a public response at the time of writing.
Details of what led to the overrun remain unclear, with no official confirmation yet on weather conditions or any mechanical or human factors involved. Investigators are expected to examine flight data recorders and interview crew members as part of the inquiry.
For now, the extent of the damage to the aircraft, and the full impact on Sunday's schedule at one of America's busiest airports, remains unconfirmed pending further statements from the FAA and Miami International Airport.
Passengers and airline operators at Miami International Airport face delays until the runway is cleared, with the FAA expected to provide an updated statement on Monday.

sources.news_title: At least five dead after Amazon cargo plane barreled off runway at Miami airport and smashed into cars, sheriff says
sources.text:
At least 5 dead after Amazon cargo plane barreled off runway at Miami airport
MIAMI (AP) — An Amazon cargo plane barreled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people and injuring five others as it struck vehicles and was engulfed in flames, authorities said.
The aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and plowed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalized with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference.
Miami officials said Sunday afternoon that it was too soon to say whether the people who died were on board the plane or in the vehicles the plane hit.
The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.
The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon. Some 200 emergency personnel responded, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the department said. Firefighters used foam from specialized airport firefighting units to extinguish the fire, and crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane hours later.
The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semi-trucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.
The cause had yet to be determined, and it was not clear if weather had played a role. Thunderstorms and wind gusts up to 30 mph (48 kph) were recorded in the area at the time, according to the National Weather Service.
The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
More than 160 flights were canceled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it is sending a team to Miami led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy to investigate.
Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said that a 767 cargo aircraft like this would typically be staffed only by a pilot and copilot on domestic flights. A third pilot would be added for an international flight, and a long-haul international flight would require a fourth pilot.
Arroyo, a retired longtime United Airlines pilot, said he wants to know whether the Amazon plane landed in the touchdown zone of the runway, and if it was beyond that area why it didn’t simply abort that landing and go around to line up for another attempt. Typically, the landing zone is within the first 3,000 feet (914 meters) of a runway.
“Did the aircraft land within the required touchdown zone? If it did, what happened? Was it weather-related or mechanical-related?” Arroyo said. “If it did land beyond the touchdown zone, why didn’t it go around? That is a standing practice around the world.”
Jackson Lee, who runs an electronics shop near the crash site, went outside with four colleagues after the crash and saw smoke rising near the airport’s fences, Lee said.
“We hear planes taking off and landing every five minutes. I thought I’d got used to it,” Lee said. “I never thought it could come this close to us.”

5 dead after Amazon cargo aircraft overruns runway in Miami, striking multiple vehicles
At least five people are dead after an Amazon cargo aircraft overran the runway during a landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, striking multiple vehicles and sending a thick black plume of smoke into the air as it caught fire.
Five others were injured in the crash, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Raied “Ray” Jadallah said during a news conference Sunday evening. Three are in critical condition and were taken to a trauma center, while two others were taken to a local hospital, he said.
Several victims were trapped in the vehicles that were hit by the plane and had to be extricated, Jadallah said.
“Guys, the plane’s on fire. Plane’s on fire. Put your game faces on,” a first responder said in Broadcastify audio.
Video below: Officials hold press conference after cargo aircraft crashes at Miami International Airport
Responders also said the pilots had been removed from the plane and were being treated.
“Our final patients are the pilots that were removed from the aircraft, so we need to get with them and get them treated,” one first responder said.
There is no apparent threat to public safety at this time, Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said during the news conference. The scene is still active as fire rescue crews respond to an ongoing fuel leak.
More than 60 “units arrived to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing,” an X post from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue says.
Video below: Aerial view of the scene
It’s not clear why the plane was unable to stop before the end of the runway. The plane was going nearly 130 miles per hour when it left the usable portion of the runway, according to data from tracking site Flightradar24.
A review of air traffic control audio by CNN shows the pilots did not declare an emergency before the landing.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson, said in a statement to CNN. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
“The airplane, which was operated by 21 Air, was attempting to land when this incident occurred,” the statement continues. “We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to learn more and will cooperate fully with any investigation.”
The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was flying from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and landed on runway 30, which is more than 9,000 feet long, according to FAA data.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it is gathering information about the crash and the Federal Aviation Administration will investigate.
Inspection crews reported there were no aircraft parts or debris found on the runway, but the plane damaged navigational equipment when it left the pavement.
A ground stop at the airport was lifted around 5 p.m. ET, and there’s a ground delay into Monday due to the disabled aircraft on the runway, according to the FAA.
The FAA said the 21 Air flight overran the runway around 2 p.m. local time.
The airline is a cargo carrier with an operations center in Miami that performs flights for companies like Amazon and DHL using Boeing 767 aircraft.
CNN has reached out to 21 Air for comment.
Runway excursions – when airplanes go off the runway – are the number one incident involving airplanes worldwide, according to data from the International Air Transport Association.
The runways at Miami International, like many airports, have a designated safety area that serves as a buffer in case excursions occur.
_____
CNN’s Sarah Dewberry, Amanda Jackson and Nayeli Jaramillo-Plata contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: At least five killed after Amazon cargo plane overruns runway in Miami
sources.text:
By ANTHONY IZAGUIRRE, DAVID FISCHER and JOSH FUNK
MIAMI (AP) — An Amazon cargo plane barreled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people and injuring five others as it struck vehicles and was engulfed in flames, authorities said.
The aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and plowed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalized with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference.
It wasn’t immediately clear if the pilots survived or those killed were all in vehicles when the plane struck.
The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.
The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon. Some 200 emergency personnel responded, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the department said. Firefighters used foam from specialized airport firefighting units to extinguish the fire, and crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane hours later.
Footage shows the moment that the 21 Air Flight 7598 overran the runway and crashed at Miami International Airport. Per reports, at least 5 individuals are dead with an unspecified number of injuries. pic.twitter.com/cOKhKwoTwh
— OSINTdefender (@sentdefender) September 7, 2026
The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semi-trucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.
The cause had yet to be determined, and it was not clear if weather had played a role. Thunderstorms and wind gusts up to 30 mph (48 kph) were recorded in the area at the time, according to the National Weather Service.
The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
More than 160 flights were canceled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Officials from Orlando International Airport, more than 200 miles (320 km) north of Miami, said some flights were diverted there.
Video showing the moment the Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767 landed at Miami International Airport. The aircraft appears to have come in fast and unstable, with the left main gear wheel not in contact with the runway after touchdown. pic.twitter.com/feHvvPDCkb
— Turbine Traveller (@Turbinetraveler) September 6, 2026
The National Transportation Safety Board said it was sending a team to Miami led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy to investigate.
Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
Last year, a UPS plane crashed after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport. The crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said that a 767 cargo aircraft would typically be staffed only by a pilot and copilot on domestic flights. A third pilot would be added for an international flight, and a long-haul international flight would require a fourth pilot.
Moments after a Prime Air Boeing 767 overshot the runway at Miami International Airport and crossed a road pic.twitter.com/DGDpk7iKPI
— 𝗝𝗥 (@malikjr0) September 6, 2026
Arroyo, a retired longtime United Airlines pilot, said he wants to know whether the Amazon plane landed in the touchdown zone of the runway, and if it was beyond that area why it didn’t simply abort that landing and go around to line up for another attempt. Typically, the landing zone is within the first 3,000 feet (914 meters) of a runway.
“Did the aircraft land within the required touchdown zone?” he asked. “If it did, what happened?”
Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former inspector general of the Transportation Department, said that video posted online of the landing shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.
“It didn’t touch down right away, and so it lost a lot of critical real estate by just continuing to float over the runway. It was literally still flying,” Schiavo said.
She noted the Miami airport is not equipped with arresting systems that the FAA says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide to safely stop planes that do go past the end of a runway. Those beds of lightweight, crushable material at the end of a runway have been credited by the FAA with helping save at least 497 lives aboard planes that overran runways.
___
Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska. Associated Press writers Tim Reynolds in Miami, Rio Yamat in Las Vegas and Wufei Yu in Phoenix contributed.

sources.text:
At least five people are dead after an Amazon cargo aircraft overran the runway during a landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, striking multiple vehicles and sending a thick black plume of smoke into the air as it caught fire.
Five others were injured in the crash, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Raied “Ray” Jadallah said during a news conference Sunday evening. Three are in critical condition and were taken to a trauma center, while two others were taken to a local hospital, he said.
Several victims were trapped in the vehicles that were hit by the plane and had to be extricated, Jadallah said. It’s not clear whether the victims who died were on the plane or on the ground.
The plane, a Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft, was flying from San Juan, Puerto Rico, when it overran the runway after landing in Miami around 2 p.m., the Federal Aviation Administration said.
It’s not clear why the plane was unable to stop. It was going nearly 130 miles per hour when it left the usable portion of the runway, according to data from tracking site Flightradar24. A review of air traffic control audio by CNN shows the pilots did not declare an emergency before the landing.
More than 60 “units arrived to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing,” an X post from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue says.
“Guys, the plane’s on fire. Plane’s on fire. Put your game faces on,” a first responder said in dispatch audio obtained by Broadcastify.
Responders said the pilots had been removed from the plane and were being treated. Their conditions are unknown.
The Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said it was in the process of confirming the identities of those who died and had established a dedicated family information phone line.
The National Transportation Safety Board and FAA will investigate. A team of FAA investigators was on the scene as of Sunday evening, according to the city’s mayor, and NTSB investigators were on their way.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson, said in a statement to CNN. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
Amazon said the plane was operated by 21 Air and that it “will cooperate fully with any investigation.”
21 Air is an all-cargo carrier headquartered in North Carolina, according to its website. It has a 24/7 operations center in Miami that dispatches planes for companies like Amazon and DHL using a fleet of Boeing 767 aircraft. According to aviation analytics company Cirium, 21 Air operates eight Boeing 767 planes for Amazon Air, the retailer’s cargo airline.
In a statement Sunday, 21 Air’s CEO Keith Winters said it was also cooperating with authorities, adding: “We are devastated by the accident involving one of our aircraft in Miami today. Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives.”
The incident occurred during Labor Day weekend, a busy time for air travel. More than 450 flights in and out of the airport were delayed or canceled as of Sunday night, according to FlightAware.com, as the crash prompted a roughly 3-hour ground stop. Flights are expected to be delayed into Monday due to the disabled aircraft on the runway, according to the FAA.
The 32-year-old Boeing plane landed on runway 30, which is more than 9,000 feet long, according to FAA data. Inspection crews reported there were no aircraft parts or debris found on the runway, but the plane damaged navigational equipment when it left the pavement.
David Soucie, a CNN safety analyst and former FAA safety inspector, told CNN’s Rosemary Church that planes typically land “nose up,” but video shows this one came in more level. He also noted that the direction of wind suddenly changed before the aircraft landed –– “at 190 degrees up to 26 knots of wind gusts” –– putting a “tailwind element” into the airplane.
When a plane is caught in a tailwind, gusts of air blow from behind the aircraft in the same direction the plane is flying.
“Now you have a tailwind which actually pushes the aircraft forward. So you’re picking up speed instead of bleeding speed off at that point,” Soucie added.
Investigators working to determine the cause of the incident are likely to look into four different areas: the piloting of the aircraft, the airfield, the weather and the condition of the plane, CNN Transportation Analyst Mary Schiavo told CNN’s Ben Hunte.
“Now, we do know that there were no Mayday calls before the landing – they didn’t report to Air Traffic Control that they had any problems with the aircraft,” Schiavo said. “But then some of those problems wouldn’t be known until the moment you touched down.”
The runways at Miami International are not equipped with Arrestor Beds, also known as an Engineered Material Arresting System (EMAS) – a pad of crushable material placed at the end of the runway to stop an aircraft from overrunning.
“We have those all over the United States, and they’re all over the world,” Schiavo said. “And for an airport as congested as Miami –– with population all around it –– buildings, freeways, et cetera, not to have any of this safety overrun system is a little surprising.”
CNN has reached out to the FAA and the airport for comment.
A Miami resident living roughly three miles from the airport told CNN affiliate WFOR he felt his home shake during the plane crash.
Jose Sanchez initially thought a truck had exploded. “But for the house to shake – it wasn’t normal,” he told WFOR.
Another resident living near the airport said the crash was a scary sight.
“I looked and saw the tail and there was a lot of emergency vehicles headed in this direction. It’s crazy,” the resident told CNN affiliate WSVN.
Some passengers departing from Miami airport have rebooked flights out of fear of further delays.
“We boarded — we were all sitting on the plane. 3:30 and they made an announcement that there was a ground stop and a plane went off the runway,” one traveler told WSVN.
“No one’s going to be leaving anytime soon. Everything is closed and delayed, so I re-booked out of Orlando for Tuesday.”
Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava was on the scene Sunday evening where she received a briefing from FAA officials.
“Our teams remain in close coordination with our federal partners, focused on caring for those affected, supporting our first responders and keeping our community safe,” she wrote in a post on X.
The Amazon Air cargo aircraft was one of more than 250 that the e-commerce giant operates daily to ship customer packages.
Amazon Air operates a fleet of more than 100 cargo aircraft, including the Boeing 737 and 767 and the Airbus A330. Cargo shipments may include anything from general merchandise, like a company’s flower bouquet orders, to dry ice, perishable medicines, parcels, fish, fruit and other goods.
Runway excursions – when airplanes go off the runway – are the No. 1 incident involving airplanes worldwide, according to data from the International Air Transport Association.

sources.news_title: Five dead after Amazon-branded cargo plane overruns runway at Miami airport, striking multiple vehicles
sources.text:
Five people are dead and five others are injured after an Amazon-branded cargo plane crashed just outside Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, officials said.
The Boeing 767-300 aircraft overran the runway just before 2 p.m. ET while it was landing, according to officials. The plane, 21 Air Flight 7598, was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
The plane overran Runway 30, struck multiple vehicles and came to rest at a field next to the airport, Miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said.
Three people were in critical condition and were taken to a trauma center, and two others were taken to a local hospital, Miami-Dade Fire Chief Raied Jadallah said.
A hotline has been set up for relatives of people who may have been involved in the accident. The scene remains active.
Video showed plumes of smoke billowing from the wreckage. The plane, Jadallah said, struck “a couple of vehicles.”
Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the flight was operated by 21 Air and was coming in to land when the incident occurred.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport. Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss,” Nantel said.
21 Air CEO Keith Winters said the crash has left the company “devastated” and that it is cooperating with federal investigators.
“Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives,” he said in a statement. “Our immediate priorities are supporting those affected, assisting the authorities, and ensuring that accurate information is communicated as it becomes available.”
All runways and taxiways at the airport were closed following a ground stop, an airport spokesperson said in a statement. After 5 p.m. ET, two of the four runways had reopened, the spokesperson said, and the airport was under a ground delay.
The delay was expected to continue through early Monday, according to Federal Aviation Administration airspace notices.
Fire and rescue personnel responded “within seconds,” Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said.
More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units went to the scene, where firefighters worked to extinguish a “very complex fire” that involved blazing engine compartments, Jadallah said.
A search-and-rescue operation was launched to retrieve the pilot and the co-pilot, who were trapped in the plane, and a technical rescue team conducted a “complex extrication” for people who were stuck inside the vehicles the plane hit, he said.
First responders were also addressing an active fuel leak at the crash site, Jadallah said Sunday evening.
Boeing described the aircraft as a 767-300 model delivered as a passenger jet in 1994 and later converted by a third party for use as a cargo plane.
“Boeing extends our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in the accident in Miami,” the aircraft manufacturer said in a statement. “Our hearts go out to those injured and affected by this tragedy.”
The National Transportation Safety Board said it has launched a team to investigate. Boeing said it was supporting the probe.
The FAA and the NTSB will determine the cause of the crash.

5 Dead, 5 Injured After Amazon Flight Crashes In FL: Authorities
The scene was active on Sunday afternoon, with over 60 fire and rescue agency units responding.
MIAMI — Five people are dead and another five are injured after an Amazon plane crashed Sunday at Miami International Airport, striking vehicles before coming to rest in a field, according to authorities.
Flight 7598 overran the runway after landing around 2 p.m. at the airport, hitting multiple vehicles near the 2100 block of Northwest 42nd Avenue, authorities said.
“Today is an incredibly difficult day for all of us here in Miami-Dade County,” Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said at a press conference Sunday evening streamed on YouTube by FOX 5 New York.

Details Of The Scene
Of the five surviving patients, three were taken to a local trauma center in critical condition and the other two were brought to area hospitals, according to authorities.
Crews also conducted search and rescue operations for the pilots and co-pilots, authorities said. A person was trapped under one of the vehicles and had to be extricated, according to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue.

A fuel leak remained active, Fire Chief Raied Jadallah said during the press conference.
In a video posted by NBC 6 News, a massive plume of smoke was coming from the aircraft, which appeared to be labeled with the Amazon logo, and fire was visible.
All runways and taxiways at the airport were closed as of 3 p.m. and a ground stop was in effect, according to the Miami-Dade Aviation Department. By later Sunday afternoon, one runway was open, according to the airport.
More than 160 flights were canceled and nearly 325 were delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Officials from Orlando International Airport, more than 200 miles north of Miami, said some flights were diverted there.
The scene was active on Sunday afternoon in Miami, with over 60 fire and rescue agency units and about 200 personnel responding, and the plane remained disabled at the northwest end of the airport.
Background On The Plane
The Federal Aviation Administration identified the plane as affiliated with cargo carrier company 21 Air, while the aviation department said the aircraft was conducting a Prime Air flight. 21 Air's website lists Prime Air among its customers.
"We can confirm that an Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land at Miami International Airport today," Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a prepared statement Sunday.
"This is a fast-moving situation and we're still gathering details. We're working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened. Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved. We're doing everything we can to support those affected."
The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft had departed from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, according to the FAA, which will investigate the incident.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it is sending a team to Miami led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy to investigate as well.
Initially a passenger plane, the 32-year-old aircraft involved in the crash was later converted to a freighter by a third party, according to Boeing.
"Boeing extends our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in the accident in Miami," the company said in a prepared statement. "Our hearts go out to those injured and affected by this tragedy. Boeing is supporting the investigation led by the U.S National Transportation Safety Board."
Anyone who believes they may have family involved in the crash is asked to call the sheriff's office at 305-471-2400, Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said at the press conference.

sources.news_title: Flights grounded after Miami plane incident triggers emergency response
sources.text:
Five people are dead and five more were injured after an Amazon Prime cargo plane overran a runway at the Miami International Airport on Sunday and hit vehicles, Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said during a press conference.
No further information on the identities of the deceased and injured were immediately provided.
The Miami-Dade Fire Rescue (MDFR) told Newsweek in a text that the department was treating "multiple patients" in a hazardous situation involving an aircraft that struck multiple vehicles near the 2100 block of Northwest 42nd Avenue.
"There were a total of 10 patients, and MDFR transported five patients by ground," the department told Newsweek. "Three were transported to a local trauma center. The other two were assessed and transported to local area hospitals."
The MDFR added: "More than 60 MDFR units and approximately 200 personnel responded, arriving to find an airplane that had stopped beyond the airport operational boundary with heavy flames and smoke showing."
Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel told Newsweek in an emailed statement that they are still working to gather details and are "working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened."
"Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved," Nantel said. "We're doing everything we can to support those affected."
Multiple videos circulating on social media appeared to show smoke billowing from an aircraft bearing the Amazon Prime Air logo near a roadway at or near the airport.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) told Newsweek in an email Sunday that 21 Air Flight 7598 overran the runway after landing at about 2 p.m. local time.
The agency said the Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft had departed from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, and that it will lead an investigation into the incident.
In a statement, Miami International Airport confirmed the incident that left the aircraft disabled at the northwest end of the airfield.
The FAA has referred questions about the aircraft and those on board to the airline.
MDFR told Newsweek that "firefighters encountered a complex engine compartment fire and used foam from specialized airport firefighting units to extinguish the flames," adding that "crews also conducted search and rescue operations for the pilots and co-pilots inside the cockpit while locating and assessing patients throughout the scene."
Officials said one person was trapped under a vehicle involved in the crash and "had to be extricated by specialized MDFR technical rescue personnel."
"Specialized MDFR hazardous materials (HazMat) units safely shut down the aircraft’s engine and worked to mitigate a fuel leak," MDFR explained.
Flights Resume with Delays
Air traffic has resumed at the airport after officials temporarily shut down all runways and taxiways.
Flights are expected to experience delays over six hours, the FAA airport status information website said.
"We’ve issued a full ground stop at Miami International while first responders assess the scene after an Amazon cargo plane overran the runway," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said earlier Sunday in a post on X. "If you’re traveling through the area, please expect significant delays and potential cancellations."
Airport officials advised travelers to check directly with their airlines for flight status updates before heading to the terminal.
Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Steve Mollman and Anthony Murray.

sources.news_title: NTSB arrives at Miami International Airport to begin investigation into deadly Amazon cargo plane crash
sources.text:
NTSB arrives at Miami International Airport to begin investigation into deadly Amazon cargo plane crash
Members of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) arrived at Miami International Airport on Monday to begin their investigation into what caused an Amazon cargo plane to overshoot a runway and slam into several vehicles before coming to a stop and bursting into flames on Sunday.
That crash, which left at least five people dead and five others injured, led to a roughly three-hour ground stop and forced officials to close all four runways at the South Florida airport.
Two of MIA's four runways have since been reopened, and the ground stop was lifted, but impacts for travelers remain and are likely going to continue for the next day or two.
That led Miami International Airport officials to urge passengers traveling to or from the facility to get in touch with their airline directly regarding a flight status before heading to the airport in case of a delay or cancellation.
Because of the ongoing situation at the airport, American Airlines said it was waiving change fees for travelers with flights to, from, or through MIA.
The airline posted more details on its website.
Many passengers who spoke with CBS News Miami said the situation had left them wondering what to do next as flight delays and cancellations mount, but said that they're keeping things in perspective given the fatal plane crash.
"It's sad what happened," Juana Paz said. "We just think of ourselves, but we don't think about other people who died, which is sad."
The NTSB held a news conference on Monday afternoon to provide more information about the fatal incident.
21 Air says it's "devastated" by crash at MIA
The Prime Air plane, which was being operated by North Carolina-based 21 Air, overran one of the airport's runways and came to a rest in an adjacent field, officials said at a Sunday news conference.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said the plane hit several vehicles near the 2100 block of Northwest 42nd Avenue, and more than 60 of its units responded to the crash. The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office said it also responded.
21 Air CEO Keith Winters said in a statement on Sunday that he was "devastated by the accident involving one of our aircraft."
"Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives," he said. "Our immediate priorities are supporting those affected, assisting the authorities, and ensuring that accurate information is communicated as it becomes available."
"We are cooperating fully with the National Transportation Safety Board, the Federal Aviation Administration, and local authorities," he said, adding that, "The circumstances of the accident are under investigation."
21 Air also added on Monday that it began a toll-free Family Assistance Line to "provide information directly to families of crew members and personnel involved in this event."
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue battles fire after plane crash, rescues victims
Of the five people who were injured, three were taken to a local trauma center in critical condition. Two others were assessed and taken to local hospitals. The names of the victims have not been released.
MDFR said when crews arrived, the plane was on fire and spewing out heavy smoke.
"What we found was a very complex situation," MDFR Chief Ray Jadallah said.
Crews used foam and specialized airport firefighting units to combat the flames, MDFR said. Crews also conducted search and rescue operations, including for the pilot and co-pilot inside the cockpit, while also locating and assessing patients throughout the scene, MDFR said.
Officials did not provide further information on the condition of the plane's crew. Officials have said it was too early to tell if the people killed were aboard the plane or on the ground.
Several people were trapped inside their vehicles and had to be removed using specialized MDFR technical rescue personnel, officials said.
Fuel leak reported at Amazon plane crash site
MDFR said there was an active fuel leak "occurring off of the aircraft that is being mitigated." Residents and motorists were urged to avoid the area of 67th Avenue and 25th Street, Commissioner Natalie Milian Orbis said.
Officials said there was no ongoing threat to public safety.
Amazon responds to cargo plane crash
Amazon confirmed one of its planes was involved in the crash.
"We're working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened. Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved. We're doing everything we can to support those affected," Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson, said.
Nantel said the company was "heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives" and that their "deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss."
Amazon will "cooperate fully with any investigation," Nantel added.
Is Miami International Airport still under a ground stop?
The Air Traffic Control System Command Center, part of the Federal Aviation Administration, issued the ground stop around 2:30 p.m. ET. Two of the airport's runways have since been reopened, according to Greg Chin, the communications director for the Miami-Dade Aviation Department. The ground stop was canceled after about three hours, and on Sunday night the average delay for a flight into the airport was more than six hours.
The FAA confirmed that a Boeing 767-300 that departed from San Juan, Puerto Rico, was involved in the crash. The 767 is 32 years old and had originally flown as a passenger plane for several airlines before it was converted into a cargo plane in 2015, according to Flightradar24.
Sean Duffy, secretary of the U.S. Department of Transportation, shared a brief statement on X, advising travelers of possible delays and cancellations.

sources.text:
5 dead, 5 injured after Amazon cargo plane overruns runway in Miami, striking multiple vehicles
By Amanda Musa, Pete Muntean, Aaron Cooper, Karina Tsui
(CNN) — At least five people are dead after an Amazon cargo aircraft overran the runway during a landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, striking multiple vehicles and sending a thick black plume of smoke into the air as it caught fire.
Five others were injured in the crash, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Raied “Ray” Jadallah said during a news conference Sunday evening. Three are in critical condition and were taken to a trauma center, while two others were taken to a local hospital, he said.
Several victims were trapped in the vehicles that were hit by the plane and had to be extricated, Jadallah said. It’s not clear whether the victims who died were on the plane or on the ground.
The plane, a Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft, was flying from San Juan, Puerto Rico, when it overran the runway after landing in Miami around 2 p.m., the Federal Aviation Administration said.
It’s not clear why the plane was unable to stop. It was going nearly 130 miles per hour when it left the usable portion of the runway, according to data from tracking site Flightradar24. A review of air traffic control audio by CNN shows the pilots did not declare an emergency before the landing.
More than 60 “units arrived to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing,” an X post from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue says.
“Guys, the plane’s on fire. Plane’s on fire. Put your game faces on,” a first responder said in dispatch audio obtained by Broadcastify.
Responders said the pilots had been removed from the plane and were being treated. Their conditions are unknown.
The Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said it was in the process of confirming the identities of those who died and had established a dedicated family information phone line.
The National Transportation Safety Board and FAA will investigate. A team of FAA investigators was on the scene as of Sunday evening, according to the city’s mayor, and NTSB investigators were on their way.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson, said in a statement to CNN. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
Amazon said the plane was operated by 21 Air and that it “will cooperate fully with any investigation.”
21 Air is an all-cargo carrier headquartered in North Carolina, according to its website. It has a 24/7 operations center in Miami that dispatches planes for companies like Amazon and DHL using a fleet of Boeing 767 aircraft. According to aviation analytics company Cirium, 21 Air operates eight Boeing 767 planes for Amazon Air, the retailer’s cargo airline.
In a statement Sunday, 21 Air’s CEO Keith Winters said it was also cooperating with authorities, adding: “We are devastated by the accident involving one of our aircraft in Miami today. Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives.”
The incident occurred during Labor Day weekend, a busy time for air travel. More than 450 flights in and out of the airport were delayed or canceled as of Sunday night, according to FlightAware.com, as the crash prompted a roughly 3-hour ground stop. Flights are expected to be delayed into Monday due to the disabled aircraft on the runway, according to the FAA.
The 32-year-old Boeing plane landed on runway 30, which is more than 9,000 feet long, according to FAA data. Inspection crews reported there were no aircraft parts or debris found on the runway, but the plane damaged navigational equipment when it left the pavement.
David Soucie, a CNN safety analyst and former FAA safety inspector, told CNN’s Rosemary Church that planes typically land “nose up,” but video shows this one came in more level. He also noted that the direction of wind suddenly changed before the aircraft landed –– “at 190 degrees up to 26 knots of wind gusts” –– putting a “tailwind element” into the airplane.
When a plane is caught in a tailwind, gusts of air blow from behind the aircraft in the same direction the plane is flying.
“Now you have a tailwind which actually pushes the aircraft forward. So you’re picking up speed instead of bleeding speed off at that point,” Soucie added.
Investigators working to determine the cause of the incident are likely to look into four different areas: the piloting of the aircraft, the airfield, the weather and the condition of the plane, CNN Transportation Analyst Mary Schiavo told CNN’s Ben Hunte.
“Now, we do know that there were no Mayday calls before the landing – they didn’t report to Air Traffic Control that they had any problems with the aircraft,” Schiavo said. “But then some of those problems wouldn’t be known until the moment you touched down.”
The runways at Miami International are not equipped with Arrestor Beds, also known as an Engineered Material Arresting System (EMAS) – a pad of crushable material placed at the end of the runway to stop an aircraft from overrunning.
“We have those all over the United States, and they’re all over the world,” Schiavo said. “And for an airport as congested as Miami –– with population all around it –– buildings, freeways, et cetera, not to have any of this safety overrun system is a little surprising.”
CNN has reached out to the FAA and the airport for comment.
A Miami resident living roughly three miles from the airport told CNN affiliate WFOR he felt his home shake during the plane crash.
Jose Sanchez initially thought a truck had exploded. “But for the house to shake – it wasn’t normal,” he told WFOR.
Another resident living near the airport said the crash was a scary sight.
“I looked and saw the tail and there was a lot of emergency vehicles headed in this direction. It’s crazy,” the resident told CNN affiliate WSVN.
Some passengers departing from Miami airport have rebooked flights out of fear of further delays.
“We boarded — we were all sitting on the plane. 3:30 and they made an announcement that there was a ground stop and a plane went off the runway,” one traveler told WSVN.
“No one’s going to be leaving anytime soon. Everything is closed and delayed, so I re-booked out of Orlando for Tuesday.”
Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava was on the scene Sunday evening where she received a briefing from FAA officials.
“Our teams remain in close coordination with our federal partners, focused on caring for those affected, supporting our first responders and keeping our community safe,” she wrote in a post on X.
The Amazon Air cargo aircraft was one of more than 250 that the e-commerce giant operates daily to ship customer packages.
Amazon Air operates a fleet of more than 100 cargo aircraft, including the Boeing 737 and 767 and the Airbus A330. Cargo shipments may include anything from general merchandise, like a company’s flower bouquet orders, to dry ice, perishable medicines, parcels, fish, fruit and other goods.
Runway excursions – when airplanes go off the runway – are the No. 1 incident involving airplanes worldwide, according to data from the International Air Transport Association.
This story has been updated with additional information.

At least 5 dead, 5 injured after Amazon Boeing 767 cargo plane crashes at Miami airport
sources.text:
At least 5 dead, 5 injured after Amazon Boeing 767 cargo plane crashes at Miami airport
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Add The New York Post on Google
A jumbo Amazon cargo jet overran the runway at Miami International Airport, killing at least five as it billowed smoke and barreled through vehicles on a nearby roadway, according to local officials and terrifying footage.
The wreck happened just before 2 p.m. Sunday as Prime Air flight 7598 – a Boeing 767 operated by 21 Air — was landing from Puerto Rico, and careened off the runway before plowing into “multiple vehicles” and bursting into flames, officials said.
Five people were confirmed dead and another five were injured — including three in critical condition — following the shocking crash, Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said, according to NBC 6 South Florida.
It remains unclear how the fatalities and injuries were spread between the plane’s crew and people struck by the wreck.
But the plane’s two pilots appeared to have been among the injured, as they were reportedly taken to a nearby hospital along with the other three wounded, NBC 6 reported.
Footage from the terrifying crash showed the huge jet lurched on its side as fires raged and huge plumes of black smoke filled the sky, while passersby looked on in horror.
“Oh my God!” people were heard as the wreck burned in one clip, while others captured officials waving people away and emergency responders descending on the fiery scene.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue confirmed the plane struck “multiple vehicles” in the wreck, and that 60 units had been dispatched along with personnel who were “assessing patients” on the scene.
“Units arrived to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing,” the agency said in a statement.
Despite the devastating wreck, the plane appeared largely intact where it lay on the road. Several semis were seen stopped on the roadway nearby, but it remains unclear if they were struck.
A ground stop was immediately ordered across the airport after the wreck. Airport officials closed all runways as the response continued.
Just two runways had been reopened after more than three hours.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
Cava also issued a statement sending condolences to the victims’ families.
“I am grateful to our Miami-Dade Fire Rescue teams and all the first responders who rushed to the scene,” the mayor said. “Our community stands together tonight with all those impacted as we continue to learn more.”
The Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board are investigating the crash.
Sunday’s disaster is just the latest incident of a cargo jet running into trouble near a major airport runway in the last year.
A UPS plane exploded in a ball of fire while taking off from Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport, with that fiery crash caught in jaw-dropping dashcam footage from a truck parked nearby.
And in May, a truck driving on the Jersey Turnpike was struck by a plane landing too low at Newark International Airport in an incident that was also caught on camera.

MIAMI INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT, FLA. (WSVN) - At least five people were killed and five others were injured after an Amazon cargo flying into Miami International Airport from San Juan, Puerto Rico, overran the runway and struck multiple vehicles, officials said, triggering a frantic race to rescue victims.
More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units and approximately 200 personnel responded near the 2100 block of Northwest 42nd Avenue, at around 2 p.m. on Sunday.
“Today is an incredibly difficult day for all of us here in Miami-Dade County, and now we know that five people lost their lives and five others were injured,” said Miami-Dade Mayor Daniella Levine Cava at a Sunday afternoon press conference.
The first group of responders arrived within 30 seconds of the plane crash.
Video obtained by WSVN shows the Boeing Prime Air 767-300 at the end of Runway 30 at the airport before it disappeared from view.
Another video captured the moments earlier as the plane began making its descent into the airport. It appeared to be having challenges on approach.
A third video clip captures the moment of distance, as the aircraft barreled into several vehicles just outside the airport’s perimeter. Part of the plane then burst into flames, leaving onlookers stunned.
Airport officials said Flight 7598, operated by by 21 Air on behalf of Amazon Air, was flying in from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport when it overran the diagonal runway and struck multiple vehicles near the airport.
Those who live near the airport said it was a scary sight.
“I looked and I saw, you know, the tail, and there was a lot of emergency vehicles that are heading in this direction. It’s crazy,” said Rohan Ellis.
“We live like right where flights come in, in the pattern, and all of a sudden no flights, and then we saw it’s a ground stop, and then sure enough, [fire rescue] shows up,” said Rory McNamara.
Fire crews doused the plane and its flames with foam as a search and rescue operation got underway.
The crash prompted officials to issue a ground stop, halting all flights in and out of MIA.
7Skyforce hovered above the scene, capturing the damaged plane on its belly with its right wing destroyed, apparent burn marks on the exterior of the plane, one of the vehicles that the aircraft struck wrecked in the field.
Pictures taken from the field captured a car engine ripped out and trees along the median destroyed.
Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah said some people were trapped inside vehicles. The pilot and copilot were also trapped in the plane.
“The airplane did strike a couple of vehicles — a couple of victims were trapped in the vehicles, so a complex extrication with our technical rescue team started to occur,” he said during Sunday’s press conference. “In addition to that, we had a very complex fire, engine compartments that were on fire, including a search-and-rescue of the pilot and co-pilot that were trapped in this aircraft.”
Body camera video captured the moment first responders found one of the crash victims alive among the wreckage.
“These incidents require seconds, not necessarily minutes,” said Jadallah.
Officials said crews managed to pull three people from the wreckage. They were transported as trauma alerts and their conditions remain unclear. The other two victims were taken to area hospitals.
According to the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office, Northwest 67th Avenue between 25th and 36th streets was shut down. Drivers experienced delays, and officials urge motorists to seek alternate routes.
In a statement the Federal Aviation Administration said:
21 Air Flight 7598 overran the runway after landing at Miami International Airport around 2 p.m. local time on Sunday, Sept. 6. The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft departed from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The FAA will investigate.
The cause had yet to be determined, and it was not clear if weather had played a role.
In a statement, an Amazon spokesperson said:
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport. Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss. The airplane, which was operated by 21 Air, was attempting to land when this incident occurred. We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to learn more and will cooperate fully with any investigation.”
The Federal Aviation Administration will investigate the incident. It remains unclear why the plane was unable to stop, but CNN reports data from the tracking site Flightradar24 shows the aircraft was going nearly 130 miles per hour when it left the unusable portion of the runway.
In addition, according to a review of air traffic control audio by CNN, the pilots did not declare an emergency before landing.
Officials said there is an ongoing fuel leak occurring from the plane and crews are working to contain it. They worked through the night around the wreckage.
“My heart is with all of the families who were affected and to everyone who is grieving tonight, and we’re also praying for the injured and for their families,” said Levine Cava.
On Monday afternoon, the National Transportation Safety Board provided additional details on the ongoing investigation.
“The flight was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico with two crew members onboard. This was the third flight for that aircraft [Sunday]. It went from Cincinnati to Miami, Miami to San Juan, then San Juan back to Miami,” said NTSB chair Jennifer Homendy.
Homendy added that the aircraft struck a white van that was owned by Professional Ocean Service Corporation, a contract cleaning company for airlines. Seven individuals were said to be inside the van when it was hit.
“The aircraft then traveled through a perimeter fence and impacted a Toyota Corolla Cross LE, which was traveling on Northwest 67th Avenue, and then continued into the grass and impacted another fence line which separated an area where Tesla robo-taxis were stationed,” said Homendy.
Investigators have recovered the aircraft’s flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder, which should provide critical details into the moments that led up to the crash.
“Prayers to the families, prayers to everyone that got hurt,” said a witness.
7News spoke to a family member of one of the hospitalized at Ryder Trauma Center. In Spanish, he said their loved one is doing OK.
Officials have released a Missing Family Hotline for those who may be looking for their loved ones. That number is 305-471-2400.
In a statement, a spokesperson for 21 Air, the aircraft’s owner, said:
We are devastated by the accident involving one of our aircraft in Miami today. Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives. Our immediate priorities are supporting those affected, assisting the authorities, and ensuring that accurate information is communicated as it becomes available. We are cooperating fully with the National Transportation Safety Board, the Federal Aviation Administration, and local authorities. The circumstances of the accident are under investigation.
Airport operations resumed several hours later, but as of Monday afternoon, only two of its four runways are currently operational.
Authorities have not released the identities of the victims, and it remains unclear whether or not the fuel leak has been capped.
As of Monday afternoon, the plane remains in the grassy area where it came to rest.
The NTSB is expected to provide further details into the investigation sometime Tuesday.

Five killed as Amazon cargo jet overruns runway at Miami airport, hits vehicles
MIAMI (AP) — An Amazon cargo plane barreled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people as it struck vehicles and burst into flames, authorities said.
The aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalized with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference. Miami officials said Sunday afternoon that it was too soon to determine whether the people who died were on board the plane or in the vehicles the plane hit.
The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said another person was trapped under a vehicle.
It also halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon. Fire crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane several hours after the crash, Jadallah said.
The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semi-trucks, images from the scene showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire. More than
The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
About 250 flights were delayed at the airport late afternoon Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it is sending a team to Miami led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy to investigate.
Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport," the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
Jackson Lee, who runs an electronics shop near the crash site, went outside with four colleagues after the crash and saw smoke rising near the airport’s fences, Lee said.
“We hear planes taking off and landing every five minutes. I thought I’d got used to it,” Lee said. “I never thought it could come this close to us.”
___
Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska. Associated Press writers Tim Reynolds in Miami, Rio Yamat in Las Vegas and Wufei Yu in Phoenix contributed.

sources.text:
A Boeing 767 cargo jet flying for Amazon’s Prime Air network skidded off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, tore through the airport’s perimeter fence, and slammed into vehicles on a nearby road, according to federal officials and video from the scene.
The Federal Aviation Administration said 21 Air Flight 7598 ran off the runway at roughly 2 p.m. after arriving from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The aircraft, a 30-year-old Boeing 767-300 freighter carrying Amazon’s Prime Air logo, was landing on Runway 30 when it failed to stop before reaching the end of the pavement, according to NBC News. It continued past the runway’s edge, breached the airport boundary, crossed a perimeter road, and came to rest after colliding with several vehicles.
Footage circulating online showed the jet resting against a chain-link fence with heavy black smoke pouring from the wreckage. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said more than 60 units responded and found the plane engulfed in flames; crews worked to contain the blaze and evaluate what the department described as multiple patients. The extent of injuries has not been confirmed.

sources.news_title: Flames seen after Amazon plane overshoots runway at Miami airport
sources.text:
Amazon plane crash near Miami airport kills at least 5, strikes vehicles
Five people were killed and multiple others injured when an Amazon cargo plane at Miami International Airport overshot the runway and struck multiple vehicles just outside the airport, according to Miami-Dade County Sheriff's Office.
First responders reported seeing heavy smoke and flames when they arrived at the crash site. In addition to the five people who were killed in the collision, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue reported five others were hurt and taken to area medical facilities for treatment.
Amazon Prime Air plane crashed at MIA (FOX Miami)
Amazon plane crashes at Miami International
What we know:
The Amazon Prime Air plane, operated by 21 Air, overran the runway shortly before 2 p.m. and struck multiple vehicles near the 2100 block of Northwest 42nd Avenue, eventually stopping outside the airport grounds, according to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue. The agency dispatched more than 60 units, consisting of about 200 individuals, to assist in the response.
The flight had just arrived from San Juan, Puerto Rico, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
"Units arrived to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing," MDFR said. "There are multiple patients."
MDFR explained that firefighters were able to knock down the flames using foam from specialized airport firefighting units as crews began searching for and trying to save the pilots and co-pilots in the cockpit, and helping any other patients at the scene, including one person who was trapped under a vehicle.
Video obtained by NBC 6 South Florida shows a Prime Air plane, a Boeing 767, crashed outside Miami International Airport. Flames and smoke could be seen coming from the aircraft.
The National Transportation Safety Board, the agency that investigates plane crashes, said a team led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy was heading to Miami to investigate.
Amazon issued the following statement at 4:10 p.m. ET Sunday:
"We can confirm that an Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land at Miami International Airport today. This is a fast-moving situation and we're still gathering details. We're working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened. Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved. We're doing everything we can to support those affected."
Ground stop issued
According to the Federal Aviation Administration, a full ground stop had been issued at Miami International Airport "while first responders assess the scene."
RELATED: Orlando International Airport receives diverted flights after plane crashes in Miami, officials say
"If you're traveling through the area, please expect significant delays and potential cancellations," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on X.
Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said her office is "closely monitoring" the situation.
"Right now, our focus is on everyone involved and making sure our first responders have what they need," she posted on X. "We will provide updates as we learn more."
What we don't know:
It's unclear what caused the plane to overrun the runway. The National Weather Service had reported thunderstorms with wind gusts up to 30 mph in the area at the time, but it is not known if that may have played a role.
The names of the victims have not been released. Authorities did not say whether those who died had been onboard the plane or on the ground.
Dig deeper:
The 32-year-old Boeing 767 involved in the crash was originally built for passenger flights and flew those routes for more than two decades before being converted into a cargo plane in 2015, according to the flight-tracking site Flightradar24. The flight was operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina.
The Source: This report includes information from the Federal Aviation Administration, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, NBC 6 South Florida, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
