sources.news_title: Prime Air 767 cargo aircraft overruns runway in Miami, striking multiple vehicles
sources.text:
Federal investigators said Monday they are committed to investigating a deadly plane crash that occurred at Miami International Airport Sunday afternoon.
Investigators are examining whether an Amazon cargo jet touched down too far down the runway to stop safely before crashing off a runway at the airport, killing five people and raising broader questions about runway safety, pilot decision-making and weather conditions during landing.
The National Transportation Safety Board and Federal Aviation Administration are investigating Sunday’s crash involving a Boeing 767 operated for Amazon Prime Air by North Carolina-based cargo carrier 21 Air.
“We are deeply, deeply committed to our duty, our responsibilities as an investigative agency, to determine how this accident occurred, why it happened, with one goal in mind – safety. And that's to prevent it from happening again,” NTSB Board Chief Jennifer Homendy said during a press conference Monday.
Video circulating online appears to show the aircraft remaining airborne longer than normal before touching down and overrunning the runway. The plane crossed a roadway near airport warehouses and slammed into multiple vehicles before catching fire.
At least five people were killed and several others injured. Homendy said the victims involved passengers in a van inside the airport and a small SUV outside the airport that were struck by the plane as to barreled past the runway.
Homendy said investigators will probe every aspect of the crash, from tire marks and flight crew experience training to policies and procedures for 21 Air and their “contractual relationship with Amazon,” as well as air traffic control.
“We'll have a group of investigators focused on operations and human performance. They will look at the history of the accident flight,” Homendy said. “We will not be determining probable cause while we are on scene. We are here to document the scene and to collect the perishable evidence.”
Experts told Scripps News investigators will also review what happened in the final moments before landing, including the aircraft speed, weather conditions, braking systems, and whether pilots should have aborted the landing and attempted a go-around.
“If you’re unstabilized at a certain point, it’s company policy that you conduct what we call a go-around,” Aviation safety expert Anthony Brickhouse told Scripps News. “Why this aircraft did not go around yesterday, these are questions that have to be answered.”
Investigators will likely examine whether the crash stemmed from human, environmental or mechanical factors — or some combination of the three, Brickhouse said.
One of the central questions investigators are expected to examine is whether the aircraft had enough runway remaining to stop safely after touchdown.
Brickhouse said investigators will also review weather conditions and possible tailwinds, which can increase landing speed and reduce stopping distance.
Investigators will also examine the aircraft itself, including maintenance records and braking systems. The plane involved was a 32-year-old Boeing 767, a passenger aircraft that was converted into a cargo jet in 2015.
RELATED STORY | Airplane pilot killed in collision with Pennsylvania police helicopter near runway
Another issue drawing attention is runway safety infrastructure. Miami International Airport does not have an Engineered Materials Arresting System, or EMAS, installed on the runway involved in the crash. The system uses crushable material designed to slow and stop an aircraft that overruns a runway.
“It's a safety system that was designed to try to keep airports as safe as possible,” Brickhouse said. “It would be perfect if airports were located in the middle of nowhere, but that's not the case. Most of our big airports are right in the middle of populated areas.”
In a Statement to scripps news, a spokesperson for the Miami-Dade Aviation Department said the airport meets FAA runway safety requirements and undergoes annual federal safety inspections.
“The full 1,000-foot Runway Safety Area mandated by the FAA,” the spokesperson said, adding that EMAS “are generally used at airports where space constraints prevent a full runway safety area from being provided.”
The spokesperson said the airport will cooperate fully with the ongoing NTSB and FAA investigation and review any resulting recommendations.
Investigators are expected to rely heavily on the aircraft’s cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder, which Homendy said were recovered, to reconstruct the final moments before the crash.
"Our whole goal as a safety agency is one thing. It's safety. It's to save lives. And that means our recommendations must be implemented, or we're going to be here again,” Homendy said.

Deadly Miami Plane Crash Disrupts Disney World Flights, Orlando Airport Impacted
sources.text:
Deadly Miami Plane Crash Disrupts Disney World Flights, Orlando Airport Impacted
Labor Day weekend is already a lot for anyone flying in or out of Orlando, with families racing to squeeze in one last Disney World or Universal trip before school takes over again. This year, that usual holiday scramble collided with something far more serious. A deadly plane crash in Miami has sent disruptions rippling straight into Orlando’s flight network, and travelers are caught right in the middle of it.
Here’s what’s going on:
- The details behind Sunday’s fatal Amazon cargo plane crash in Miami
- How that crash turned into hundreds of delayed and canceled Orlando flights
- What Orlando International Airport has said about the diverted flights
- Why the timing during Labor Day weekend makes this hit even harder
What Actually Happened in Miami
According to Click Orlando, federal investigators are looking into a deadly crash involving an Amazon cargo plane in Miami, and the fallout is already reaching passengers in Orlando through delays and cancellations. The plane overran the runway at Miami International Airport Sunday afternoon after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico. During landing, it crossed a road used by warehouse workers and nearby businesses around the airport. Officials confirmed five people died in the crash, with three others critically injured and two more hospitalized with less severe injuries.
The crash triggered a ground stop at Miami International Airport for most of the afternoon, and a lot of flights that were supposed to land there got rerouted to Orlando instead. By late Sunday, more than 160 flights had been cancelled outright, with nearly 325 more delayed because of it.
One Traveler Caught in the Middle of It
Cindy Noam had a flight booked to Miami for Monday, and she told Click Orlando it ended up delayed by at least an hour because of everything happening. “I received a message saying that my flight might be impacted because of the ground stop, but hopefully they have it all under control now,” she said. “It’s very concerning, but I think it’s safer to fly than it is to drive.”
Her experience sums up what a lot of people flying through Orlando dealt with this weekend, genuine uncertainty piling on top of an already packed holiday travel schedule.
The Timing Made a Bad Situation Worse
This whole thing hit at basically the worst possible moment, right as Orlando’s airport was already bracing for one of its busiest stretches of the entire year. Orlando International Airport was expecting 841,577 arriving and departing passengers between Thursday and Tuesday of Labor Day weekend, with Monday alone projected to bring in 78,336 passengers, the single busiest day of the whole stretch.
Stack a major diversion event on top of numbers like that, and you get a genuinely tough situation for both the airport and everyone trying to get through it. Orlando International Airport addressed it directly on social media after Sunday’s crash, saying, “We’re currently receiving diverted flights to support operations at MIA and assist our airline partners. Travelers on affected flights are encouraged to contact their airline directly for the latest information and instructions regarding their journey.”
What This Actually Means If You’re Flying In for Disney or Universal
If you’re flying into Orlando specifically for a Disney World or Universal trip this weekend, this kind of widespread disruption creates real problems beyond just a stressful airport day. A delayed or diverted flight can mess with park reservations, Lightning Lane bookings, dining reservations, even hotel check-in windows, especially if you built a tight, single day arrival schedule around limited Labor Day availability in the first place.
Since theme park trips tend to run on pretty tight arrival and departure windows, even a few hours of delay can mean missing an early dinner reservation or losing real time out of your first park day. If you’re connecting through Miami, or flying an airline that had planes diverted into Orlando as part of Sunday’s ground stop, it’s worth expecting some continued ripple effects over the next few days while airlines work to get planes and crews back into their normal rotations.
Getting Through This With Some Patience
Noam’s own take on the situation is genuinely useful advice for anyone dealing with travel this weekend. “I’ll tell you, carry on patience. That’s what we need to do is have patience. Especially when you’re traveling on a Labor Day weekend,” she said. Building in extra time at the airport, exactly what she did before her own delayed flight, is honestly one of the simplest ways to cut down on stress when the whole system’s already backed up.
If you’re heading into a Disney or Universal trip this weekend specifically, it’s smart to keep your arrival day plans a little loose instead of scheduling something tight right after landing. Keep your airline’s app open for real time updates, and reach out to them directly instead of just relying on airport announcements, that’ll help you stay ahead of anything else tied to the ongoing situation.
Keeping This in Perspective
Behind all the delayed flights and messed up vacation plans is a real tragedy. Five people died in Sunday’s crash, and investigators are still working through exactly what caused it. The travel disruptions hitting Orlando are a legitimate headache for anyone trying to get into the city this weekend, but they’re a pretty minor inconvenience compared to what the victims and their families are actually going through right now.
If you’re still dealing with a delayed or canceled flight this week, staying in touch with your airline and giving yourself extra patience is really the best way to handle it. And if your Disney World or Universal trip got affected by all this, both resorts have historically shown some flexibility with reservations during big regional travel disruptions, so it’s worth reaching out directly if your plans shifted in a major way.
Has your Labor Day trip to Orlando been affected by the delays and diversions from Sunday’s crash? Let us know in the comments how it’s impacted your plans and what’s actually helped you get through it.

The wreck triggered a massive emergency response and brought airport operations under severe strain.

County dispatch records placed the emergency call at roughly 1:55 p.m.
Officials said at least 10 victims were involved in the catastrophe.

Video that circulated Sunday appeared to show the aftermath, with the crashed plane visible outside the airport, according to NBC 6 South Florida. Separately, footage and local reports examined by The Aviation Hub showed heavy black smoke and flames rising from the freighter as crews arrived. The Federal Aviation Administration issued a ground stop at Miami International Airport at approximately 2:02 p.m. EDT, temporarily halting inbound air traffic while responders worked the scene, per the same outlet's reporting.
Ground Stop Snarls Air Traffic at Major Cargo Hub
The ground stop rippled across one of the country's busiest air cargo gateways. Miami International Airport functions as a critical logistics hub linking North American, Latin American, and Caribbean commercial routes, a role documented by FreightWaves. That volume of freight traffic underscores why even a single runway obstruction can cascade into broader delays across the airport's operations.
Air traffic control audio released Sunday captured real-time exchanges between controllers and emergency personnel as the runway overrun unfolded, according to Cedar News. The recordings offer an early window into how responders coordinated in the first moments after the aircraft left the pavement, though full details of the emergency communications have not been independently summarized beyond that release.
Aging Freighter Flew Under Third-Party Operator
The aircraft involved was registered N1997A, a 32-year-old Boeing 767 built in 1994 that originally flew as a passenger jet before its 2016 conversion into a cargo freighter, the aviation outlet reported. The plane was not operated directly by Amazon. Flight CSB7598 was flown by cargo carrier 21 Air on behalf of Amazon Prime Air, following 21 Air's addition to Amazon's transport network in November 2024 and the transfer of the aircraft's operating certificate in January 2025, according to reporting cited from FreightWaves.
That arrangement reflects how Amazon's Prime Air cargo brand relies on contracted airlines to fly its livery on widebody freighters, many of them converted from older passenger airframes. Key questions remain open, including whether any crew or ground injuries occurred, whether vehicles on NW 67th Avenue were affected as the jet departed the runway, and what caused the excursion in the first place, whether mechanical failure, brake trouble, or weather.
Federal Investigators to Examine Cause
Under standard protocol, the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board conduct joint investigations following commercial runway overruns, inspecting aircraft components, airport infrastructure, and flight recorder data, according to VINnews. Full preliminary findings from such investigations typically take several weeks to surface.
Sunday's incident is not the first cargo emergency tied to Miami International Airport in recent years. In January 2024, an Atlas Air Boeing 747-8 cargo jet bound for Puerto Rico suffered an inflight engine fire shortly after takeoff from MIA, forcing an emergency return landing with no injuries reported, according to Business Insider. And in February 2019, an Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767-300 freighter operated by Atlas Air crashed into Trinity Bay near Houston after departing Miami, killing all three crew members aboard, according to Wisner Baum, which noted that NTSB investigators in that case focused on crew spatial disorientation.

sources.news_title: Amazon's Twin Headwinds: A Miami Runway Tragedy and the $220 Billion Cloud Gambit
sources.text:
The image of a Boeing 767-300 sheared against a Miami parking lot is not the kind of publicity Amazon typically courts. Yet as investigators sift through the wreckage of Sunday’s fatal landing, the company’s leadership is simultaneously wrestling with a different kind of turbulence: how to fund an unprecedented $220 billion infrastructure splurge without losing its operational footing.
A Landing Gone Wrong in Florida
The accident unfolded around 2 p.m. local time when Flight 7598, operated by 21 Air on behalf of Amazon Prime Air, touched down at Miami International Airport. The 32-year-old aircraft, arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, failed to decelerate in time. It tore through the airport perimeter fence, struck multiple vehicles on an adjacent roadway, and came to rest on a parking lot, where a fire erupted near the right wing shortly after impact.
Local media, citing CNN and Bloomberg, reported five fatalities and five additional injuries. Both the FAA and the NTSB have launched comprehensive investigations into the crash. Early indications suggest the aircraft crossed the threshold at roughly 170 knots — well above the standard approach speed of 135 to 140 knots. Airport operations ground to a halt temporarily as emergency crews responded.
The tragedy lands at an awkward moment for the e-commerce giant, which has been eager to project an image of operational precision while scaling its logistics empire and cloud ambitions simultaneously.
The Price of AI Dominance
Even before the Miami incident, Amazon’s calculus was shifting. The company now plans to boost capital expenditures for 2026 from an initially projected $200 billion to approximately $220 billion — a 10 percent increase earmarked primarily for new data centers and proprietary AI chip development. The bet reflects a conviction that generative AI workloads will soon dwarf traditional cloud demand.
That conviction is already showing up in the numbers. Amazon’s AI-related revenue run rate stands at $25 billion annually, growing at triple-digit rates. The company’s deepening partnership with Anthropic — a commitment exceeding $100 billion over ten years — underscores how seriously it takes the competitive threat from rivals who are also building their own silicon.
Geographic expansion continues apace as well. A new cloud region in Saudi Arabia is slated to go live in December, representing investments of more than $5.3 billion.
Two Giants, Converging Paths
Amazon is not alone in this arms race. Microsoft, its fiercest cloud competitor, has been equally aggressive in pursuing vertical integration. Reports suggest Microsoft could unveil its Maia 300 chip as early as this autumn, a move designed to reduce dependence on external suppliers. The two companies, historically locked in a winner-take-all rivalry, recently announced a partnership to simplify multicloud connectivity — private high-speed links between AWS and Azure that acknowledge a marketplace reality: enterprise customers increasingly distribute workloads across multiple providers.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Amazon?
The financial profiles of the two companies reflect their divergent DNA. Amazon’s diversified model — retail, logistics, cloud — produces robust revenue but thinner, more volatile margins. Microsoft’s software fortress, anchored by Office 365 and Windows, generates the kind of recurring, high-margin cash flow that institutional investors prize; its debt ratio of just 0.07 signals exceptional balance-sheet strength. Year-to-date, Amazon shares have climbed roughly 12 percent, outpacing Microsoft’s 4 percent gain, though Microsoft’s typical net margins above 30 percent remain the envy of the industry.
Regulatory Clouds Gather
Operational momentum notwithstanding, Amazon faces a thickening regulatory fog. In Washington, policymakers are debating whether to force a breakup of AWS, the highly profitable cloud division that effectively subsidizes the company’s broader ambitions. CEO Andy Jassy has stated he sees no clear advantage in such a separation but has indicated the company would comply with any government directive. A separate FTC lawsuit alleging hidden advertising fees running into the billions adds further pressure.
These legal entanglements, combined with the Miami investigation, give investors pause. The stock closed Friday at €222.55, up 13 percent since the start of the year but roughly 11 percent below its 52-week high of €249.00 set on August 3.
The Long Game
For all the near-term noise, the strategic question remains whether Amazon can convert its enormous capital outlays into durable competitive advantage. The company’s flywheel logic is straightforward: AI services attract developers, developers consume more compute, and that consumption strengthens the AWS ecosystem. The same dynamic applies to Microsoft, which is reorganizing around its “Agents and Infra” initiative and plans to report Azure revenue separately starting in fiscal 2027 — a transparency move that will invite direct comparison with AWS.
Both companies face the same fundamental challenge: translating AI pilot projects into recurring revenue while absorbing the depreciation and energy costs of aggressive data-center expansion. Amazon’s retail efficiency provides one source of funding; Microsoft’s software margins provide another. Neither path is easy, and both carry execution risk.
The Miami crash serves as a grim reminder that Amazon’s ambitions span physical and digital worlds simultaneously — and that both carry inherent dangers. As the NTSB investigation unfolds and regulatory proceedings advance, the market will be watching whether Amazon can keep its eyes on the runway ahead while managing the wreckage in its rearview mirror.

sources.text:
At least five people were killed when an Amazon cargo plane overshot a runway after it landed Sunday at Miami International Airport, crashed into vehicles and caught fire, officials said.

“The airplane did strike a couple of vehicles,” which left “a couple of victims that were actually trapped in the vehicles,” Jadallah said.
“A complex extrication with our technical rescue team” was needed, “including a search and rescue of the pilot and co-pilot that were trapped in this aircraft.”
Jadallah did not clarify whether the pilot or co-pilot survived, and officials declined to answer questions after brief statements were made.
Video showed thick smoke billowing from the blue and white Boeing 767 after it arrived at 1:58 pm (1758 GMT) from Puerto Rico, as fire trucks raced to the scene.
Officials investigate the scene where a Prime Air cargo plane overran the runway and crashed into other vehicles at Miami International Airport at Miami International Airport in Miami, Florida, on September 6, 2026.
The plane operating as Prime Air Flight 7598 caught fire as a result of the “crash,” fire officials said.
“A total of 60 fire apparatuses arrived, just short, just shy of 200 men and women from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, to begin the actual search and rescue and firefighting,” Jadallah said.
“The actual cause of the incident will be determined by the FAA and the NTSB,” he added, referring to the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board.
In a statement posted to X Sunday evening, fire officials said they used foam to extinguish a fire in the engine compartment.
“One person was trapped under one of the involved vehicles and had to be extricated by specialized technical rescue personnel. Specialized hazardous materials (HazMat) units safely shut down the aircraft’s engine and worked to control a fuel leak,” the statement said.

sources.news_title: Amazon Prime Air Cargo Crash: At Least Five Killed In Miami
sources.text:
At least five people died when an Amazon Prime Air cargo flight overran a runway and crashed while landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday, local officials said.
Prime Air Flight 7598 overran the airport’s diagonal runway shortly before 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) and struck multiple vehicles on the ground, officials said during a news conference on Sunday afternoon.
Five people were also injured in the cargo crash, including three who are in critical condition, said Miami-Dade Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. At least two people were trapped in vehicles that were struck by the plane, and the pilot and co-pilot were trapped inside the plane by the crash, Jadallah said.
Officials declined to identify those who died.
Flights Resume
More than 60 rescue units and about 200 personnel responded to the incident, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said in a statement. As of late afternoon, emergency personnel were still dealing with a fuel leak from the aircraft, Jadallah said.
Although the airport halted all flights immediately after the crash, flights had resumed by Sunday evening.
The plane, which departed from San Juan, Puerto Rico, was a 32-year-old Boeing 767-300 freighter that had operated as a passenger jet for various airlines from 1994 to 2015, according to flight tracking service Flightradar24.
Cargo airline 21 Air operated the plane for Amazon, an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement.
“We are devastated by the accident involving one of our aircraft in Miami today,” 21 Air said on its website. “Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives.”
Reuters photos after the crash showed the jet with its nose on the ground and tail tilted up. The right side of the plane had what appeared to be scorch marks.
Flightradar24 said the plane was traveling at 112 knots (129 mph) when it exited the usable runway.

Boeing and 21 Air said they would support the government investigations into the crash.
Sunday’s incident is not the first time an Amazon Prime Air plane has been involved in a fatal crash. In February 2019, Atlas Air Flight 3591, a Boeing 767-300 freighter operating on behalf of Amazon Prime Air from Miami to Houston, entered a rapid descent and crashed into Trinity Bay, Texas. All three people on board were killed.
Miami, a major hub for trade with Latin America, is the third-busiest freight airport in the United States after Anchorage in Alaska and Louisville in Kentucky, according to the Airports Council International.

sources.news_title: Amazon cargo plane crash claims five lives
sources.text:
MIAMI-(MaraviPost)-Five people have been killed and five others seriously injured after an Amazon Air cargo aircraft overshot the runway while landing at Miami International Airport, striking vehicles on the ground and erupting into flames in a crash that caused widespread disruption at one of the United States’ busiest airports.
According to the BBC, the Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft, operated by North Carolina-based charter carrier 21 Air, was attempting to land shortly before 14:00 local time on Sunday after departing from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico.
The aircraft continued beyond the usable section of the runway before coming to rest near a parking area serving an Amazon warehouse and other businesses.
Five confirmed dead as rescue operation unfolds
Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava confirmed that five people died in the crash, while five others were injured.
Miami Fire Chief Raied Jadallah said three of those injured were in critical condition.
Emergency crews encountered a complex rescue operation after people became trapped inside or beneath vehicles struck during the crash. Firefighters worked to remove victims while battling the aircraft fire.
More than 200 firefighters responded to the scene.
The blaze was eventually extinguished, although officials said a fuel leak remained at the crash site.
Cause of crash remains unknown
Authorities have cautioned against speculation over what caused the aircraft to leave the runway.
The National Transportation Safety Board is expected to lead the investigation into the crash and plans to provide an update on Monday.
Investigators will examine the aircraft, runway conditions, weather, flight data and other factors that could help establish how the accident unfolded.
Initial flight-tracking information from FlightRadar24 indicated that the aircraft was travelling at approximately 112 knots, or about 129mph (207km/h), when it exited the usable runway.
The tracking service also reported light thunderstorms and gusting winds in Miami around the time of the incident.
Those conditions alone do not establish the cause of the accident, and investigators will have to determine whether weather, mechanical problems, operational factors or a combination of circumstances contributed to the crash.
Amazon expresses condolences
Amazon said it was cooperating with local authorities and the investigation.
Kelly Nantel, Amazon’s director of corporate global media relations, expressed condolences to those killed and to their families.
The company confirmed that the aircraft was operated by 21 Air and was attempting to land when the incident occurred.
The BBC said it had contacted 21 Air for comment but had not received a response.
Miami airport operations disrupted
The crash triggered major disruption at Miami International Airport during one of the busiest travel periods in the US calendar.
The Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights as emergency services responded to the burning aircraft.
Passengers reported delays and cancellations, while long queues developed at airline counters as travellers attempted to rearrange their journeys.
Some passengers told the BBC they faced the possibility of remaining in Miami overnight because of the disruption.
The incident occurred during the Labor Day holiday weekend, traditionally one of the busiest periods for travel in the United States.
The Transportation Security Administration had projected that about 17 million travellers would pass through US airports during the week leading up to the holiday Monday, with approximately 2.3 million people expected to fly on Sunday alone.
Miami International Airport’s strategic importance
The accident occurred at an airport that plays a major role in both US passenger travel and international freight.
Miami International Airport is located close to downtown Miami and serves as a major gateway between the United States, Latin America and the Caribbean.
The airport describes itself as the country’s busiest airport for international freight and a major international passenger hub.
Its importance to cargo operations makes the crash particularly significant for aviation and logistics companies operating through South Florida.
Investigation will determine what happened
The immediate priority following the crash has shifted from emergency response to preserving evidence and establishing the sequence of events.
Investigators are expected to examine the aircraft’s flight-data and cockpit-recording systems, maintenance history, runway conditions, weather information, air-traffic communications and operational procedures.
The central questions will include why the Boeing 767 failed to stop within the usable runway area and what factors contributed to its collision with vehicles beyond the runway.
Until the NTSB completes its investigation, officials have not identified a definitive cause.
For the families of those killed and injured, however, the technical investigation comes after an immediate human tragedy.
The Miami crash has left five people dead, several others critically injured and a major international airport facing significant operational disruption as investigators begin the painstaking process of determining how an Amazon cargo flight ended in disaster.

sources.news_title: Amazon cargo plane crashes in Miami, kills 5, injures 5 as NTSB launches investigation
sources.text:
At least five people were killed and five others injured after an Amazon cargo plane overshot the runway, crashed into vehicles and burst into flames while landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday.
The Boeing 767, operating as Prime Air Flight 7598 from San Juan, Puerto Rico, was involved in the crash shortly after touching down at about 1:58 p.m.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Ray Jadallah said three victims were taken to trauma centres in critical condition, while two others were treated at a local hospital.
“The airplane did strike a couple of vehicles,” Jadallah said, adding that “a couple of victims that were actually trapped in the vehicles.”
He said firefighters carried out “a complex extrication with our technical rescue team,” including efforts to rescue the pilot and co-pilot who were trapped inside the aircraft.
About 200 firefighters and 60 emergency vehicles responded to the scene, using foam to extinguish the fire and hazardous materials teams to contain a fuel leak.

Miami Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz described the scene as “really tragic,” but said there was “no apparent threat to public safety.”
The airport temporarily closed all runways and taxiways after the crash, causing major flight disruptions before two of its four runways were later reopened.

sources.news_title: Fatal Crash at Miami Airport: Amazon Air Cargo Jet Overshoots Runway, Five Dead
sources.text:
Key Points
- Five fatalities confirmed after Amazon Air cargo aircraft overran runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday
- Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-300 operated by 21 Air, was inbound from San Juan, Puerto Rico
- Aircraft collided with ground vehicles after departing runway, igniting a massive fire
- Five individuals sustained injuries, with three reported in critical condition
- Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board have initiated full investigations
A cargo aircraft operating under Amazon Air’s banner overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, resulting in at least five deaths and five additional injuries.
The incident involved Prime Air Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-300 freighter operated by contract carrier 21 Air. The aircraft was completing its journey from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico when it failed to stop on the runway at approximately 2 p.m.
After exiting the runway, the cargo jet collided with several ground vehicles in the vicinity of the airport. Emergency responders from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue encountered significant flames and dense smoke upon their arrival.
Multiple individuals became trapped within the vehicles impacted by the aircraft. The emergency response mobilized 60 fire units, with first responders reaching the crash site within half a minute of receiving the emergency call.
Fire Chief Ray Jadallah of Miami-Dade Fire Rescue characterized the situation as “a very complex fire,” noting that engine compartments were engulfed in flames while rescue teams worked to extract the pilot and co-pilot who remained trapped inside the cockpit.
Mayor Daniella Levine Cava of Miami-Dade County verified the death toll of five individuals, with an additional five sustaining injuries. Among the wounded, three remain in critical condition, while two others were admitted to hospitals with injuries of lesser severity.
Miami International Airport implemented a complete shutdown of all runways and taxiways starting at 3 p.m. Operations partially resumed several hours afterward, with at least two runways returning to service.
Statements from Amazon and Contract Carrier
Amazon acknowledged the accident through an official statement published on X. Company spokesperson Kelly Nantel emphasized that the organization is collaborating extensively with local officials and that “the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved” remains their foremost concern.
21 Air, headquartered in Miami and operating Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft, has provided services for Amazon since 2024. Company representatives have not yet responded to media inquiries regarding the incident.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy advised passengers to anticipate disruptions and potential cancellations due to the airport closure.
Federal Probe Launched
The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed it will conduct a comprehensive investigation into the accident. The National Transportation Safety Board has similarly deployed investigators and announced plans for a press briefing scheduled for Monday.
Initial reports indicated an active fuel leak from the damaged aircraft, which emergency crews were working to contain.
Records show the Boeing 767 involved in the crash was manufactured over three decades ago, entering service in June 1994. The aircraft’s operational history includes service with Air Europa, Kenya Airways, and Atlas Air before undergoing conversion to cargo configuration in 2016.
Boeing discontinued commercial production of the 767 passenger variant, though limited manufacturing continues for military aerial refueling tankers.
Aviation experts are drawing parallels to the UPS Airlines Flight 2976 disaster in November 2025, which resulted in three crew fatalities and 11 ground casualties following departure from Louisville.
The Boeing 767 constitutes the backbone of Amazon’s air cargo operations, representing the majority of its fleet composition. The e-commerce giant supplements its 767 fleet with Airbus A330-300 freighters for long-haul routes and smaller Boeing 737 aircraft serving regional destinations.
Investigators have not yet determined what caused Sunday’s runway overrun as the inquiry progresses.

AP reported that it crossed onto a road used by warehouse workers and other airport-area businesses, ploughing into vehicles in its path.
Three of the injured were listed in critical condition, with two others admitted to hospital with less severe injuries.
Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah said the pilot and co-pilot were trapped in the cockpit, while several vehicle occupants were also unable to free themselves.
Rescue personnel additionally had to extricate one person who had become pinned beneath a vehicle.
Some 200 emergency responders arrived to find the plane engulfed in heavy flames and thick black smoke rising from the engine compartment.
Specialised airport firefighting units deployed foam to bring the fire under control. Hours after the initial crash, crews were still managing a fuel leak aboard the aircraft.
Images from the scene showed the plane resting on its belly alongside a roadway near two semitrucks. Despite the intensity of the fire, the aircraft remained largely structurally intact.
The Boeing 767 involved in the crash is 32 years old. Originally constructed as a passenger jet, it operated with several commercial airlines over more than two decades before being converted to a cargo configuration in 2015, according to flight-tracking service Flightradar24.
The flight was operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier headquartered in North Carolina.

sources.text:
US3 min(s) read
Audio released after fatal Miami plane crash left 5 people dead
Emergency audio has been released after an Amazon cargo plane crashed off a runway at Miami International Airport around 2:00PM on Sunday, leaving five people dead and five others injured.
Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-300 operated by cargo carrier 21 Air, had arrived from San Juan, Puerto Rico, before overrunning the airfield. Flight-tracking data indicated that the aircraft exited the usable runway at approximately 129 mph during severe thunderstorms and strong wind gusts.
The jet smashed through the airport perimeter fences and ploughed directly into vehicles on a busy nearby road, coming to rest near a parking lot.
Emergency radio transmissions captured the chaotic moments as first responders arrived at the scene within 30 seconds of the call. Firefighters struggled to contain a massive fire while dealing with an active fuel leak and an operational hazard that hindered their ability to enter the aircraft.
The left engine of the plane remained running after the impact, preventing crews from immediately searching the interior for survivors. Pilots informed rescuers via radio that they could not shut down the engine because they needed to "energize" the aircraft.
Firefighters eventually flooded the running engine with water to disable it and safely continue their operations.
Emergency response and rescue efforts
Approximately 200 firefighters and 60 emergency units responded to the site. Beyond tackling the burning fuselage, crews worked to extricate victims from destroyed cars along the roadway. One individual was pinned under a vehicle and required specialized rescue equipment to be freed.
Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz confirmed the five fatalities. Five additional individuals were rushed to local hospitals, with three reported to be in critical condition.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Raied "Ray" Jadallah noted that both the pilot and co-pilot were initially trapped inside the plane, though authorities have not released details regarding the duration of their rescue or their physical conditions. Official identities of the deceased and injured have not been made public.
Impact on airport operations and official statements
The severe collision forced Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy to issue a full ground stop, halting air traffic at the hub for hours. Hundreds of flights experienced delays or cancellations before authorities managed to reopen two of the airport's four runways later on Sunday evening.
Student pilot Rohan Ellis, 34, observed the scene from across the airfield and described the hit vehicles as "mangled."
Amazon released an official statement regarding the accident: "[We are] heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport."
The company added: "Our deepest condolences go out to the families, loved ones and all those affected by this devastating loss. We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to learn more and will cooperate fully with any investigation."
21 Air CEO Keith Winters expressed similar sentiments, stating the organization was "devastated" by the event. "Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives," Winters said.
"Our immediate priorities are supporting those affected, assisting the authorities and ensuring that accurate information is communicated as it becomes available."
Investigative teams from the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board have launched a formal inquiry into the exact cause of the runway overrun. The NTSB is scheduled to issue a public briefing on the investigation status on Monday.

"We've issued a full ground stop at Miami International while first responders assess the scene after an Amazon cargo plane overran the runway. If you're traveling through the area, please expect significant delays and potential cancellations."
All runways and taxiways were closed following the incident, and about 250 flights had been delayed by late Sunday afternoon. The FAA said that even after the airport reopens, arrivals and departures will operate at a reduced rate.
Miami International Airport incident: Amazon and Boeing respond
In a statement to NBC, Amazon confirmed the aircraft belonged to its cargo arm and was operated by 21 Air. The company said it was working with local authorities to establish what happened, adding: "Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved. We're doing everything we can to support those affected."
Boeing also issued a response, offering condolences to the families of those killed. A company spokesperson said Boeing was supporting the investigation being led by the US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB).
The NTSB confirmed it was gathering information about the crash.
Aircraft dismantled at Lagos airport over indebtedness
Legit.ng earlier reported that a Boeing 737-700 operated by Arik Air is being dismantled at the Murtala Muhammed Airport in Lagos amid a dispute over an alleged debt owed to Access Bank.
The aircraft, located between the Civil Aviation Flying Unit hangar and the Air Force helicopter hangar at the airport’s domestic wing, has reportedly been undergoing dismantling for about a month.

sources.news_title: Amazon Prime Air Plane Overruns Miami Runway, Hits Vehicles And Catches Fire
sources.text:
Five people were killed and five others injured after Amazon Prime Air Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft operated by 21 Air, overran a runway while landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday, September 6. The aircraft had arrived from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and crossed beyond the runway before striking multiple vehicles and catching fire.
Three of the injured were critically hurt, while the pilot and co-pilot were among those trapped following the crash, according to Miami-Dade Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units and around 200 emergency personnel responded as crews battled the fire and a fuel leak.
The crash forced the closure of all runways and taxiways and triggered a ground stop, causing widespread flight disruptions. Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the company was working with authorities to understand what happened, while the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) began investigations. The cause of the crash remains unknown.
Crash Triggers Massive Rescue Operation
The aircraft overran Miami International Airport’s diagonal runway shortly before 2 p.m. local time and continued beyond the airport boundary, where it struck several vehicles on the ground before coming to rest and catching fire. Images from the scene showed the Boeing 767 with its nose down and tail raised, while thick smoke rose above the airport.
Emergency crews faced a difficult rescue operation involving the burning aircraft, damaged vehicles and a fuel leak. Fire Chief Ray Jadallah said the pilot and co-pilot were trapped inside the aircraft, while at least two people were trapped in vehicles hit by the plane.
Five people died and five were injured, including three in critical condition. The identities of those killed and injured had not been publicly released in the latest updates.
Amazon said its “absolute priority” was the “safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved” and that it was working closely with local authorities to establish what happened. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy also warned travellers to expect “significant delays and potential cancellations” following the crash.
Investigators Examine Landing Sequence
While the exact cause remains under investigation, preliminary flight-tracking information and weather conditions are likely to form part of the inquiry. Reuters reported that Flightradar24 data showed the aircraft landing at around 1:53 p.m. and travelling at approximately 112 knots, or 129 mph (207 km/h), when it left the usable runway area.
Thunderstorms were present around Miami, with wind gusts reportedly reaching about 30 mph. Aviation experts cited by AP said investigators will examine where the aircraft touched down, how much runway remained, its braking performance and the crew’s decisions during the landing.
Experts have also raised questions about whether weather or a possible tailwind may have affected the approach. However, none of these factors has been established as the cause of the crash. Investigators are expected to examine the aircraft’s systems, maintenance history, flight data, cockpit communications, air-traffic-control records and runway conditions before drawing conclusions.
The aircraft was a roughly 32-year-old Boeing 767 that had previously operated as a passenger aircraft before being converted for cargo use; its age alone does not establish any link to the accident.
The Logical Indian’s Perspective
An aviation accident of this scale is a tragedy not only because of the loss of lives but also because people on the ground were caught in an incident they could not have anticipated. At this stage, it is important to resist speculation and allow investigators to establish what happened through evidence rather than social-media footage or premature claims.
The families of those who died deserve compassion, while those injured, including the flight crew and people caught in the path of the aircraft, deserve care and support. Authorities, the airline, Amazon and airport operators must be transparent about the findings and ensure that any safety lessons are acted upon.

sources.news_title: Australian National Review - Harrowing Audio Reveals Fire Crews Racing to Amazon Cargo Plane Crash in Miami that Left Five Dead and Five Injured
sources.text:
Harrowing Audio Reveals Fire Crews Racing to Amazon Cargo Plane Crash in Miami that Left Five Dead and Five Injured
By MELISSA KOENIG, US REPORTER and ELISHA FIELDSTADT and ALYSSA GUZMAN, US NEWS REPORTER
First responders could be heard in distressing audio scrambling to extinguish a massive blaze after an Amazon cargo plane overshot a runway in Miami and collided into cars on a busy roadway, killing five people and leaving five others injured.
Flight 7598 was landing at Miami International Airport from San Juan, Puerto Rico when it overran the runway on Sunday at around 2pm and ‘struck multiple vehicles’ on Northwest 42nd Avenue, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue told the Daily Mail.
When firefighters arrived at the scene within just 30 seconds of receiving an emergency call, they found people trapped inside their vehicles, Fire Chief Raied Jadallah said at a news conference Sunday evening.
They also found the Boeing 767-3000 on fire, with heavy flames and smoke.
‘The plane is on fire. The plane is on fire,’ a firefighter could be heard in emergency radio dispatch obtained by the Miami Herald. ‘Put your game face on guys.’
Firefighters could also be heard on the emergency radio dispatch struggling to get hoses close enough to the plane to spray water to suppress the flames.
Making matters worse, the aircraft’s left engine was still running when firefighters battled the blaze, making it dangerous for them to enter the plane to check for patients inside.
The firefighters could be heard in the radio traffic saying the pilots onboard told them they could not turn the engine off because they would need to ‘energize’ the aircraft, leaving firefighters on the scene forced to flood the engine with water.
Five people were killed, and five others were left injured after an Amazon cargo plane crashed after overrunning the runway at the Miami International Airport on Sunday
The plane caught on fire as a result of the crash and killed five as it collided into vehicles
Images from the scene shared by NBC Miami show the plane, with Amazon branding, precariously close to a building. Smoke can be seen billowing from the aircraft.
At least five people were killed in the tragedy, while three others remain in critical condition at a local trauma center.
Two others were also transported to the hospital with unspecified injuries. Authorities have not yet identified the deceased nor the victims taken to the hospital.
Flight data from tracking site FlightRadar24 shows the cargo flight, operated by North Carolina-based 21 Air, was traveling at 129mph as it exited the ‘usable runway’ amid thunderstorms and gusting winds.
It then came to a rest near a parking lot that services an Amazon warehouse and other businesses, with photos from the scene showing the plane largely intact behind two semitrucks.
Meanwhile, Rohan Ellis, 34, a student pilot who was on the other side of the airport when the Prime Air plane crashed, described the vehicles on the road as ‘mangled’ to The New York Times.
One person was then left trapped underneath one of the struck vehicles and had to be extricated by specialized rescue personnel, fire crews told the Daily Mail as they continued to try to stop a fuel leak at the scene.
A spokesperson for the airport also told the Daily Mail that the plane ‘overran Miami International Airport’s diagonal runway and is disabled at the northwest end of the airport.’
The plane crashed into multiple vehicles after it overran the runway, leaving them ‘mangled’
The plane’s mangled wing could be seen leaning over cars at the scene
It remains unclear what may have caused the plane to overrun the runway.
But Robert A Clifford, founder of Clifford Law Offices in Chicago and a recognized leader in aviation law, said it ‘appears to be a classic tailwind landing mistake where a pilot mistakenly or over-confidently decides to land with a tailwind instead of a headwind.’
Doing so causes excessive touchdown speed and leaves an inadequate distance for the airplane’s braking and reverse thrust systems, he explained.
Clifford pointed to Miami’s own Automated Surface Observation System, which reports that the plane had tailwinds of 20 knots to 30 knots amid thunderous conditions.
Automatic Dependent Surveillance broadcast data also shows the plane touched down on Runway 30 at about 167 knots, or about 192mph, and went off the runway at over 120mph.
‘The highway vehicles stood no chance against the 300,000-pound Boeing 767-300 crashing into them at that speed,’ he noted.
Investigators will now examine the pilot’s decision to land with such high tailwinds, said Clifford, whose firm represents 15 victims and their families who were killed or injured when a UPS cargo jet crashed shortly after takeoff last year.
‘Certainly, the [National Transportation Safety Board] will examine that issue fully, along with the failure to declare an emergency,’ he said. ‘Also, to be examined, will be the performance of the engines to see if the reverse thrusters were properly deployed.’
Smoke billowed into the sky after the Prime Air plane crashed into a busy road
It remains unclear what caused the Prime Air plane to overrun the runway
A damaged vehicle is seen in pieces outside Miami International Airport following the crash
Pablo Rojas, an aviation attorney in the Miami-area, also told the Miami Herald there are a number of details about the crash that stand out to him.
‘You can see it stops in this parking lot area with the landing gear collapsed,’ he said. ‘The nose is kind of dipping down. We don’t know if that’s something that happened late in the accident sequence or early enough to have caused the accident sequence.
‘You can imagine the incident being caused by something else and then the landing gear collapsing, but certainly if there was an issue with the landing gear early in the accident sequence, that’s going to be the first clue for investigators,’ he continued, adding that the investigators will also look at the stormy weather conditions.
‘A landing at an international airport is complex,’ Rojas declared. ‘The pilot needs to be communicating with air traffic control. Air traffic control needs to be minding the weather and communicating that with the pilot.
‘We know we’ve had rain in Miami recently. Air traffic control needs to help the pilot understand the condition of the runway,’ he said.
‘Planes can land in nasty weather, but obviously if the runway is slick, that can sometimes cause air traffic control to pause or stop landings for a period of time.’
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) spokeswoman Hannah Walden further confirmed to The New York Times that runways at Miami International Airport are not equipped with an Engineered Materials Arresting System – crushable concrete designed to bring planes that overshoot the runway safely to a stop.
The FAA has long recommended that airports install the system, but it is not mandated and airports are able to use other FAA-approved methods of mitigating runway overruns instead.
Officials are seen investigating the runway incursion on Sunday evening
Following the crash, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy issued a full ground stop at the airport.
‘If you’re traveling through the area, please expect significant delays and potential cancellations,’ he posted on social media.
Miami International Airport has since reopened two of its four runways, but flights are still being impacted, with about 250 flights delayed at the airport late Sunday afternoon, according to FlightAware.
In a statement, Amazon said it was ‘heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport.
‘Our deepest condolences go out to the families, loved ones and all those affected by this devastating loss.’
‘We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to learn more and will cooperate fully with any investigation.’
21 Air CEO Keith Winters also said the crash left his company ‘devastated’ and that it is cooperating with federal investigators.
‘Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives,’ he said in a statement.
‘Our immediate priorities are supporting those affected, assisting the authorities and ensuring that accurate information is communicated as it becomes available.’
Investigators from both the FAA and NTSB are now at the scene, with NTSB officials set to hold a news conference on the crash on Monday.

sources.news_title: Five Die As Amazon Cargo Jet Overruns Runway, Engulfs Vehicles In Flames At Miami Airport
sources.text:
Miami: At least five people died and five others were hurt when an Amazon Prime Air cargo jet skidded off the runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, slamming into vehicles on a perimeter road and erupting in fire, AP reported.
The Boeing 767-300 freighter, operated by 21 Air for Amazon, arrived from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and overran Runway 30 around 2 p.m. local time, officials said. Miami-Dade County officials told reporters that five people were killed, three were critically injured and two others were hospitalized with less severe injuries. They cautioned that it was too soon to say whether the dead were aboard the aircraft or in the vehicles it hit.
Firefighters Douse Blaze, Free Trapped
The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.
Some 200 emergency personnel responded, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the department said. Firefighters used foam from specialized airport firefighting units to extinguish the fire, and crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane hours later.
The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semi-trucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.
Cause Unclear
Investigators had not pinpointed a cause and said it was too early to tell if weather was a factor. At the time of the accident, the Miami area saw thunderstorms with wind gusts as high as 30 mph (48 kph), the National Weather Service reported.
The service was being provided by 21 Air, a cargo operator headquartered in North Carolina. Data from Flightradar24 show the 32-year-old Boeing 767 spent more than 20 years flying passengers for multiple airlines before being reconfigured as a freighter in 2015.
By late Sunday, FlightAware counted more than 160 cancellations and nearly 325 delays tied to the shutdown. Orlando International Airport, located over 200 miles (320 km) north of Miami, said it took in several diverted flights.
NTSB Team Sent; Amazon Pledges Cooperation
The National Transportation Safety Board announced it was dispatching a “go team” to Miami, with Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy serving as the board member on scene.
Amazon said it would fully cooperate with the investigation.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”

മിയാമി: അമേരിക്കയിലെ മിയാമി അന്താരാഷ്ട്ര വിമാനത്താവളത്തിൽ ചരക്കുവിമാനം റൺവേയിൽനിന്ന് നിയന്ത്രണംതെറ്റി സമീപത്തെ പാർക്കിങ് മേഖലയിലേക്ക് ഇടിച്ചുകയറി തീപിടിച്ചുണ്ടായ അപകടത്തിൽ അഞ്ച് പേർ മരിച്ചു. അപകടത്തിൽ അഞ്ചുപേർക്ക് പരിക്കേൽക്കുകയും ചെയ്തു. ആമസോൺ പ്രൈം എയറിന്റെ ചരക്കുവിമാനമാണ് അപകടത്തിൽപ്പെട്ടത്. റൺവേ മറികടന്ന വിമാനം റോഡരികിൽ പാർക്ക് ചെയ്തിരുന്ന വാഹനങ്ങളിലേക്ക് ഇടിച്ചുകയറുകയായിരുന്നു.
പ്യൂർട്ടോറിക്കോയിലെ സാൻ ഹുവാനിൽനിന്ന് പുറപ്പെട്ട പ്രൈം എയർ ഫ്ലൈറ്റ് 7598 വിമാനമാണ് അപകടത്തിൽപ്പെട്ടത്. ഞായറാഴ്ച ഉച്ചയ്ക്ക് പ്രാദേശിക സമയം രണ്ട് മണിയോടെ മിയാമി വിമാനത്താവളത്തിൽ ഇറങ്ങുന്നതിനിടെയായിരുന്നു അപകടം. ലാൻഡിങ്ങിനിടെ ചരിഞ്ഞ റൺവേ മറികടന്ന് വിമാനം റൺവേയ്ക്ക് പുറത്തേക്ക് തെന്നിമാറുകയായിരുന്നു. തുടർന്ന് സമീപത്തെ സ്ഥാപനങ്ങളിലെയും വെയർഹൗസുകളിലെയും ജീവനക്കാർ ഉപയോഗിക്കുന്ന പാർക്കിങ് ഏരിയയിലുണ്ടായിരുന്ന വാഹനങ്ങളിലേക്ക് ഇടിച്ചുകയറി. ഇടിയുടെ ആഘാതത്തിൽ വിമാനത്തിന് തീപിടിക്കുകയും ആകാശത്തേക്ക് കറുത്ത പുക ഉയരുകയും ചെയ്തു.
അപകടത്തെ തുടർന്ന് പൈലറ്റും കോ-പൈലറ്റും വിമാനത്തിന്റെ കോക്പിറ്റിൽ കുടുങ്ങിപ്പോയിരുന്നു. റൺവേയ്ക്ക് സമീപം പാർക്ക് ചെയ്തിരുന്ന വാഹനങ്ങളിലുണ്ടായിരുന്നവരക്കം നിരവധിപേർ കുടുങ്ങിയിരുന്നു. രണ്ട് പേരെ വാഹനങ്ങളിൽനിന്നും ഒരാളെ വിമാനത്തിനടിയിൽ നിന്നുമാണ് അഗ്നിരക്ഷാ സേനാംഗങ്ങൾ രക്ഷപ്പെടുത്തിയത്.

sources.news_title: Five Dead, Five Hurt In Miami Cargo Plane Accident
sources.text:
A Boeing 767-300 cargo plane overran a runway while landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing five people and injuring five others after it struck multiple vehicles and caught fire, officials said.
The aircraft, operating as 21 Air Flight 7598 under Amazon‘s Prime Air brand, had departed San Juan, Puerto Rico. Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz told reporters the plane went down around 1:58 p.m. ET, moments after it ran off the end of Runway 30.
Flight-tracking data put the plane’s speed at close to 130 miles per hour as it ran out of runway, and a review of the air traffic control recording found no indication the crew flagged trouble before touching down. The jet continued past the airfield boundary near Northwest 42nd Avenue and struck several vehicles. Two semi-trucks sat near where the wreckage finally stopped, in a field bordering the road, its tail draped over a perimeter fence. A fuel leak fed a large fire involving the engine compartments, Fire Rescue Chief Raied Jadallah said.
Fire rescue sent more than 60 units to the scene. The wreckage trapped the two pilots, who had to be extracted before being taken to area hospitals. Of the five injured, three were rushed to a trauma center in critical condition. The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a ground stop that lasted about three hours, and two of the airport’s four runways reopened within hours of the crash. By evening, flights arriving at the airport were running about six and a half hours behind schedule on average.
The National Transportation Safety Board, led by Chair Jennifer Homendy, is sending an investigative team, and the FAA is conducting its own review. The plane itself dated back 32 years — it carried passengers early in its life before operators converted it to cargo duty in 2015.
Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the company was “heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives.” Amazon has no air operator certificate of its own, relying on contract carriers such as 21 Air to fly under the Prime Air brand.

sources.text:
A Boeing 767 freighter was still moving at 112 knots, roughly 129 miles per hour, when it ran off the end of a Miami International Airport runway on September 6, according to ADS-B data captured by Flightradar24. The overrun killed five people on the ground and injured five others, including both pilots.
A 21 Air Boeing 767 operating for Amazon overran Miami’s Runway 30 this afternoon. Flightradar24 data shows a ground speed of 112 knots as it left the usable runway.
Downloadable flight data and updates available at https://t.co/uHIF4KdM17 pic.twitter.com/dnfX0uWjxt
— Flightradar24 (@flightradar24) September 6, 2026
The aircraft, 21 Air Flight 7598, had arrived from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, and touched down around 2 p.m. local time, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said. It overran Runway 30, crossed the airfield boundary, struck several vehicles on the road outside, and came to rest near a parking lot serving an Amazon warehouse before catching fire.
Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said five people were killed and five were hospitalized, three of them in critical condition. Fire Chief Raied Jadallah said some victims were trapped inside their vehicles and that both pilots were trapped in the aircraft. Crews were still working to contain a fuel leak hours after the crash.
The speed at the runway’s end points investigators toward the landing itself. The jet was still traveling at 112 knots as it exited the usable runway area, with a final recorded telemetry speed of 69 knots before tracking stopped, Flightradar24 data showed. Runway 30 measures more than 9,000 feet, according to FAA data.
Weather at touchdown was active. The airport’s METAR reading logged a thunderstorm over the field, winds at 17 knots gusting to 26, and a peak wind of 26 knots recorded one minute before landing. A LATAM Cargo 767 had landed on the same runway about 20 minutes earlier, Flightradar24 noted. A runway excursion, in which an aircraft departs the runway surface, is the most common category of aviation incident worldwide, according to the International Air Transport Association.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy ordered a full ground stop while responders worked the scene. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue deployed more than 60 units and about 200 personnel. The airport reopened one runway roughly an hour later.
The 32-year-old aircraft, registered N1997A, was delivered as a passenger jet in 1994 and flew for carriers including Vietnam Airlines, Air Europa, and Kenya Airways before conversion to a freighter in 2015, according to Flightradar24. It is powered by two General Electric CF6-80C2B6F engines. 21 Air, based in Greensboro, North Carolina, flies contracted 767 services for Amazon and DHL. Amazon does not hold its own air operator certificate for these flights.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) launched a Go Team led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy and scheduled its first briefing for September 7. Boeing said it is supporting the investigation.

Amazon Plane Crash Miami Kills Five, Injures Several Others
Cargo jet from Puerto Rico bursts into flames after skidding off runway at Miami International Airport
Miami – (Special Correpondent/Web Desk) – An Amazon plane crash Miami left five people dead and five others hurt on Sunday afternoon, after a cargo jet skidded off the runway at Miami International Airport and burst into flames.
The aircraft, Prime Air Flight 7598, was flying in from San Juan, Puerto Rico. It touched down just before 2pm and failed to stop in time, running past the edge of the runway and slamming into several vehicles parked nearby.
Officials say the plane came to rest near the northwest side of the airport. Thick black smoke rose into the sky within moments, and the jet quickly caught fire.
More than sixty Miami-Dade Fire Rescue crews rushed to the scene. Firefighters worked for hours to put out the flames, which one fire chief called extremely difficult to control because parts of the engine were still burning.
Five people were taken to hospitals. Three of them are in critical condition, while the other two suffered less serious injuries. Rescue teams had to cut through wreckage to free people trapped inside vehicles that were struck by the plane.
The Boeing 767-300 involved in the crash is over three decades old. It first flew as a passenger jet before being turned into a cargo freighter back in 2015. It was being flown by 21 Air, a cargo airline based in North Carolina that operates flights for Amazon.
A fuel leak was also reported at the crash site. Emergency crews spent hours working to contain it and keep the area safe.
Miami International Airport shut down all its runways right after the crash happened. This forced a full ground stop, meaning no planes could take off or land for a while. Airport officials say two of the four runways have since reopened, but delays are expected to continue into Monday.
Hundreds of flights were delayed, and many others got cancelled entirely. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned travellers to prepare for major disruptions in the days ahead.
Amazon released a short statement saying it is working closely with local authorities to figure out exactly what went wrong. A company spokesperson said the situation is still unfolding and that the safety of everyone involved remains the top concern.
The head of 21 Air also spoke out, saying the company is devastated by what happened. He offered condolences to the families of those who lost their lives and confirmed the airline is cooperating fully with investigators.
Both the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board are now looking into the crash. Investigators have already started collecting evidence from the site, though it may take time before a clear cause is known.
For now, officials are simply asking the public to stay patient as the airport works to get back to normal. Flight delays are likely to continue for at least another day, and passengers are being urged to check their flight status before heading to the airport.
This remains a developing story, and more updates are expected as investigators learn more about what caused the crash.

sources.news_title: Five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport
sources.text:
An Amazon Air cargo plane overshot the runway while attempting to land at Miami International Airport, killing five people and seriously injuring five more.
The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft crashed just before 14:00 local time (19:00 GMT) after departing from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The flight also hit several vehicles on the ground.
Amazon said that it is “working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened”.
All flights were ordered grounded by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) as fire crews raced to the smoking crash site. The crash comes over Labor Day weekend, one of the busiest travel times of the year.
“At least five people have lost their lives, and five others are injured,” Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said at a news conference on Sunday evening.
She added that rescue crews arrived at the scene within “seconds” of the crash.
“Right now, our focus is on the families, those who were injured, and the ongoing response,” she continued.
Three of the five people injured are in critical condition, said Miami Fire Chief Raied Jadallah. The mayor said they were all taken to hospital with “unknown injuries”.
Several of the injured were trapped inside or under vehicles on the ground, and needed to be extricated by fire and rescue crews, said Jadallah.
Officials say it is too early to know the cause of the crash, and that it will be investigated by the National Transportation Safety Board. The federal agency, which investigates all air crashes in the US, plans to hold a news conference on Monday.
The Amazon flight operated by 21 Air, a charter company based in North Carolina, “overran Miami International Airport’s diagonal runway and is disabled at the northwest end of the airport,” the airport said in a statement.
Miami Dade Fire Rescue said crews “arrived to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing”.
Over 200 firefighters responded to the crash. The flames were extinguished, but there is still a fuel leak at the site, said Jadallah.
Amazon issued a statement saying that it is working closely with authorities and offering condolences to the victims.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” said Kelly Nantel, Amazon’s Director of Corporate Global Media Relations.
“Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.
“The airplane, which was operated by 21 Air, was attempting to land when this incident occurred. We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to learn more and will cooperate fully with any investigation.”
The BBC has emailed 21 Air about the incident, but has not received a response.
Flight data from tracking site FlightRadar24 shows that the Amazon cargo flight was travelling at 112 knots (129mph, 207km/h) as it exited the “useable runway”.
In a blog post, the site says the plane came to rest near a parking lot that services an Amazon warehouse and other businesses.
There were light thunderstorms and gusting winds in Miami at the time of the incident, the site says.
The crash comes during one of the busiest travel weekends of the year in the US.
Passengers at Miami International Airport airport told the BBC they were frustrated by the lack of information coming from officials, with many flights cancelled or delayed as a result of the incident.
There were long lines at airline counters as people tried to reschedule travel plans, with some saying they would be forced to stay in Miami an extra night.
The Transportation Safety Administration (TSA) said there would be 17 million travellers passing through US airports in the week leading up to Monday’s Labor Day holiday.
The TSA, which screens passengers flying in the US, predicted that 2.3 million people would fly on Sunday alone.
Miami International Airport (MIA) is located near downtown Miami, and is one of the busiest airports in the country.
“Founded in 1928, MIA is America’s busiest airport for international freight and second busiest for international passengers, offers more flights to Latin America and the Caribbean than any other US airport,” according to their website.
About 60% of all international visitors to Florida arrive at this airport, it says.

sources.news_title: Amazon Cargo Plane Crashes at Miami Airport, Killing at Least Five
sources.text:
An Amazon cargo plane overran the runway while landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday, struck multiple vehicles, and burst into flames, killing at least five people and injuring five others in one of the more serious cargo aviation incidents at a major US airport in recent years.
What Happened
The Federal Aviation Administration said Prime Air Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-300 freighter operated by North Carolina-based 21 Air, overran one of the airport’s runways at approximately 2 p.m. local time while landing after departing from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The aircraft crossed a road beyond the airfield boundary, struck several vehicles, and came to rest in an adjacent field, catching fire in the process.
Miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz confirmed five deaths, with five additional people injured, three of them in critical condition and taken to a local trauma center. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Ray Jadallah said more than 60 fire rescue units responded to the scene, battling heavy flames and thick black smoke while working to mitigate an active fuel leak from the aircraft, though officials said there was no ongoing threat to broader public safety.
All runways and taxiways at Miami International Airport were closed following the crash, prompting a roughly three-hour ground stop and grounding departures as emergency crews worked the scene. Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the company was “heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident,” extending condolences to the families and loved ones affected and confirming Amazon would “cooperate fully with any investigation.”
Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767-300 has run off the runway and onto a highway at Miami International Airport pic.twitter.com/SNTBrMWutm
— SAY CHEESE! 👄🧀 (@SaycheeseDGTL) September 6, 2026
Why It Matters
The crash represents a significant disruption to one of the busiest airports in the country, with the extended ground stop affecting flight operations well beyond the immediate emergency response, illustrating how a single cargo aircraft incident can ripple through broader commercial aviation schedules at a major hub.
The specific circumstances, a large cargo freighter overrunning a runway and continuing beyond the airport perimeter into an area with vehicle traffic, raise questions about runway safety margins and airport perimeter design that federal investigators will likely examine closely as part of the formal inquiry into the crash’s causes.
For Amazon’s Prime Air cargo operation, which has expanded significantly in recent years to support the company’s delivery network, the crash represents a serious safety incident that is likely to draw scrutiny of the broader cargo aviation sector’s safety practices, even though the aircraft was operated by a separate contracted carrier rather than Amazon directly.
Context and Background
21 Air, the company operating the aircraft on Amazon’s behalf, is a cargo airline based in North Carolina that has partnered with Amazon’s Prime Air network to support the company’s air cargo logistics operations, a common industry arrangement in which retailers and logistics companies contract specialized cargo carriers to operate branded aircraft.
Miami International Airport ranks among the busiest airports in the United States for both passenger and cargo traffic, given its role as a major gateway for flights connecting the US with Latin America and the Caribbean, making any significant runway closure there likely to have outsized effects on broader regional air travel and cargo logistics.
Runway overrun incidents, while relatively rare, have occurred periodically at airports worldwide and are typically investigated closely by aviation safety authorities given their potential to reveal broader issues involving aircraft braking systems, runway conditions, pilot procedures, or airport design that could carry implications beyond the specific incident.
Analysis
Aviation safety analysts note that runway overrun incidents involving cargo aircraft, while statistically less common than passenger aircraft accidents, can be equally serious given the size and fuel load of large freighter aircraft like the Boeing 767, factors that likely contributed to the severity of Sunday’s fire and the resulting fatalities.
Some aviation experts point to the aircraft coming to rest beyond the airport’s perimeter fence and striking vehicles on an adjacent roadway as a particularly concerning detail, suggesting investigators will likely examine both the specific factors that caused the runway overrun and whether existing safety buffer zones around the airport were adequate for an aircraft of this size and speed.
Industry analysts note that the National Transportation Safety Board’s involvement, expected in incidents of this severity, will provide the most authoritative eventual accounting of the crash’s causes, though such investigations typically take months to reach preliminary conclusions and longer for a final report.
What Happens Next
The FAA and NTSB are expected to lead a formal investigation into the crash’s causes, a process that will likely take an extended period before preliminary findings are released. Miami International Airport is expected to resume full operations following the completion of the immediate emergency response and runway safety assessments.
Amazon and 21 Air are likely to face continued scrutiny regarding cargo aircraft safety protocols as the investigation proceeds, with the airline industry broadly likely to review its own runway overrun prevention and response procedures in light of Sunday’s fatal incident.
