sources.news_title: Five killed after Amazon cargo plane barrels off runway
sources.text:
Five killed after Amazon cargo plane barrels off runway
ANTHONY IZAGUIRRE, DAVID FISCHER and JOSH FUNK |
An Amazon cargo plane has barrelled off a runway at Miami International Airport, killing at least five people as it struck vehicles and burst into flames.
Prime Air Flight 7598 from San Juan, Puerto Rico overran the airport’s diagonal runway at about 2pm on Sunday (4am Monday AEST) and was disabled at the airport’s northwest end, officials said.
Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalised with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference.
Miami officials said it was too soon to determine whether the people who died were on board the plane or in the vehicles the plane hit.
The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and co-pilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah.
The agency said another person was trapped under a vehicle.
It also halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon. Fire crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane several hours after the crash, Jadallah said.
All runways and taxiways at the Miami airport were closed as of 3pm EDT. Travelers should “expect significant delays and potential cancellations”, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a post on x.
The plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semi-trucks, images from the scene showed.
The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.
The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina.
The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
About 250 flights were delayed at the airport late on Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it is sending a team to Miami led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy to investigate.
Amazon said in a statement that it would co-operate with any investigation.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said.
“Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
AP

sources.news_title: Amazon Air 767 Crash Kills Five; Investor Read-Through Awaits the Cause
sources.text:
An Amazon Air cargo jet operated by 21 Air overran a runway in Miami on Sunday. At least five people were killed, and five others were injured. The Boeing 767-300 struck vehicles and caught fire after arriving from San Juan at about 14:00 EDT. The details were reported by the Associated Press and in a Federal Aviation Administration statement published by ABC News.
The National Transportation Safety Board sent investigators led by Chair Jennifer Homendy. No cause had been assigned as of 18:18 EDT on September 6. That uncertainty is central to the stock analysis.
Amazon.com NASDAQ:AMZN provides the brand and the freight network. 21 Air operated Flight 7598. The Boeing Co. NYSE:BA made the aircraft, which was built 32 years ago as a passenger jet and converted for cargo service in 2015. Those are separate layers of responsibility, and Sunday’s evidence does not yet connect the overrun to any one of them.
The accident happened while U.S. markets were closed. Amazon shares finished Friday at $258.51, down 0.15%, at 16:00 EDT. Boeing closed at $212.25, up 0.83%.
Those prices contain no reaction to the crash. The NYSE is also closed Monday for Labor Day, making Tuesday’s premarket the first equity test.
One aircraft, a larger oversight question
Amazon says its air network uses more than 100 aircraft and operates more than 250 flights a day. It also says carrier partners operate every flight. On that published base, one aircraft is less than 1% of the fleet count. One disrupted flight is less than 0.4% of daily activity.
That is capacity arithmetic, not a loss estimate. The fatalities, injuries, property damage and potential claims are unresolved. Amazon has not disclosed the aircraft’s ownership, insurance allocation, cargo value or any contract action involving 21 Air.
Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the company was working with authorities and that care for those involved was its immediate priority, the AP reported. Investors still need to know whether Amazon temporarily removes 21 Air aircraft, reroutes volume or reviews contractor controls.
| Confirmed fact | Current stock read-through | What would change it | 
|---|---|---|
| 21 Air operated the flight for Amazon | Direct operating scrutiny starts with the carrier; Amazon retains brand and vendor-oversight exposure | A suspension, contract change or evidence of a broader control failure | 
| The jet was one of more than 100 aircraft in Amazon’s published network | A single-aircraft capacity loss looks manageable | A fleet inspection or grounding affecting multiple aircraft | 
| The 767 was built in 1994 and converted in 2015 | It is not representative of Boeing’s current new-build output | Evidence of a design or structural problem shared across the 767 fleet | 
| The NTSB investigation has just begun | Any allocation of fault is premature | Recorder data, maintenance records and an initial investigative update | 
The direct network hit also looks small beside Amazon’s business scale. North America sales reached $116.2 billion in the second quarter, with $9.1 billion of segment operating income. A single aircraft loss would not alter that earnings base by itself.
A prolonged service interruption would be different. About 250 flights across Miami International Airport were delayed by late Sunday afternoon, the AP reported. That count covers the airport, not Amazon’s network. It should not be treated as Amazon volume lost.
Boeing exposure needs a technical link
The Boeing read-through is narrower for now. Aircraft age is relevant to maintenance history, but age alone does not establish cause. Nor does a runway overrun automatically point to the airframe.
Investigators will examine the approach and landing performance. They will also review weather, crew decisions and maintenance records. Brakes and tires are other likely evidence.
Boeing’s exposure would rise if investigators identify a design or manufacturing issue common to other 767s. It would fall if the facts remain specific to this flight, operator or aircraft.
A prior Amazon-contracted 767 loss shows why the distinction matters. The NTSB found that the 2019 crash of Atlas Air Flight 3591 followed the first officer’s inappropriate response to an inadvertent go-around mode activation and spatial disorientation. The agency also cited deficiencies in Atlas Air’s pilot-selection and performance-measurement practices.
Its official findings did not identify a systemic 767 design failure. That case does not explain Sunday’s crash; it shows how far an investigation can move responsibility from the aircraft maker.
The evidence that matters next
The first useful signals will be operational. Watch for an Amazon or 21 Air fleet action, an FAA airworthiness directive, and any continuing limits at Miami. None had been announced in the authorities’ initial accounts reviewed Sunday evening.
The NTSB’s on-scene update should clarify the aircraft’s condition and the evidence recovered. Flight-data and cockpit-voice recorders, runway measurements, weather records and maintenance documents can then narrow the cause. A preliminary report may establish facts, but it will not necessarily assign probable cause.
Tuesday’s first trades may produce a headline reaction. They will not settle the investment case. The threshold for a lasting move is evidence that expands this from one fatal flight into a wider operating, contractual or fleet problem.

sources.news_title: Tesla Sees Dozens of Cybercabs Narrowly Escape Amazon Cargo Jet Crash
sources.text:
An Amazon Air Boeing 767 freighter that overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday nearly hit dozens of Tesla Cybercab robotaxis, photographs and video from the scene show.
Rows of the gold two-seaters, are visible in images of the wreckage within a few car-lengths of the aircraft’s nose, with a Miami-Dade Fire Rescue crash tender positioned between them and the fuselage.
Neither Tesla nor Miami-Dade Fire Rescue had said as of 5 p.m. Eastern time whether any of the vehicles was struck or damaged, and the fire department has identified the vehicles it says the plane hit only as “multiple vehicles.”
The Crash
Prime Air Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-300 registered N1997A and operated for Amazon by 21 Air, overran the airport’s diagonal runway on landing at about 2 p.m. after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
The aircraft left the airfield, struck vehicles and caught fire, and came to rest on its belly beside a perimeter road; Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said more than 60 units responded and that there were “multiple patients,” without giving a count or describing injuries.
The fire department placed the struck vehicles near the 2100 block of Northwest 42nd Avenue.
One of the airport’s four runways reopened by late afternoon after a full ground stop, and the airport said it was still “experiencing impacts.”
The FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board are investigating, and Amazon said it was “still gathering details” and working with authorities.
“We can confirm that an Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land at Miami International Airport today,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement posted on the company’s news site on Sunday.
“This is a fast-moving situation and we’re still gathering details. We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened. Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved. We’re doing everything we can to support those affected,” the company added.
The statement did not address the condition of the crew, the cargo, or the vehicles the aircraft struck.
The Lot
Tesla launched unsupervised Robotaxi service in Miami on July 3 with a handful of Model Ys in a geofenced zone in the western suburbs.
Within days, industry analyst Grayson Brulte of The Road to Autonomy reported finding a staging lot “on the fringe of Miami International Airport,” about two miles from the main terminal entrance, holding about 21 Cybercabs on Florida license plates alongside Model Y robotaxis.
Tesla’s investor and most followed X content creator Sawyer Merritt posted video on Saturday of what he counted as 35 Cybercabs at the same lot, and on Sunday wrote that the crash occurred “right where all those Cybercabs/Teslas were parked,” adding that the cars’ Sentry Mode cameras were likely to have recorded the accident.
Photographs from the scene show a fenced lot of mixed vehicles, dozens of them the gold-painted Cybercabs, bordered by a logistics warehouse marked 3320, with a Miami-Dade Fire Rescue vehicle and the aircraft’s nose immediately beyond the fence line.
The Cybercabs visible in the images appear intact, but the photographs cover only part of the lot and the impact area on the far side of the aircraft is obscured by the fuselage and by semi-trailers.
Tesla
Cybercabs have not entered commercial service in Miami; Tesla’s Florida fleet in operation consists of Model Ys, and the company gave the first public Cybercab rides in Austin only last week, at an invitation-only event that was not livestreamed.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened an audit query on Friday into Tesla’s self-certification of a vehicle with no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors, and Tesla shares fell 6.5% that day.
Tesla has listed installed Cybercab capacity above 125,000 units a year and has said the car will be sold to consumers for under $30,000 before 2027; Ark Invest has estimated production cost at about $18,000 a unit, which would put the value of 35 cars at roughly $630,000 at cost.
If any of the vehicles were struck, it would be the first loss of Cybercabs to an external event.
The model’s only reported collision to date, in May, was a minor incident that Tesla-focused accounts on X said was not the car’s fault.

sources.news_title: An Amazon Boeing 767 cargo is on fire after reportedly overrun the runway at Miami Airport
sources.text:
MIAMI — An Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767 cargo aircraft overran the runway upon landing and struck multiple vehicles at Miami International Airport (MIA) on Sunday, September 6, 2026, crossing a nearby roadway and catching fire.
Flight tracking data indicates that the aircraft, a Boeing 767-300F registered as N1997A, was operating a scheduled cargo flight from San Juan, Puerto Rico, to Miami. The incident occurred at approximately 05:54:20 PM UTC, when the aircraft veered off Runway 30 during touchdown.
Overrun and Fire Response
Footage captured at the scene showed heavy black smoke billowing from the frame of the wide-body freighter.According to eyewitness reports and preliminary video, the aircraft cleared the airfield boundaries and came to a stop adjacent to a perimeter roadway, sustaining major damage, including losing its right wing before catching fire.
Emergency response teams from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue arrived rapidly to extinguish the blaze. Fire crews deployed foam streams to suppress the flames fueled by residual jet fuel.
Impact on Airport Operations
The incident occurred during a busy holiday weekend, prompting aviation authorities to temporarily ground departures and issue a ground stop at Miami International Airport.
- Status of the Crew:Authorities have not yet officially confirmed the condition of the flight crew aboard the freighter.
- Runway Closures: Runway 30 and adjacent taxiways remain closed while emergency teams secure the site and fuel containment procedures continue.
Investigation Launched
Federal agencies, including the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), have launched a joint investigation into the cause of the runway excursion. Investigators will evaluate weather conditions at the time of arrival, aircraft telemetry, runway surface conditions, and flight recorder data.
Neither Amazon Air nor the operating carrier has issued a final statement pending official updates from airport authorities and federal investigators.
UPDATE
At least five people have died and five others were injured.

sources.news_title: Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport after it overshoots runway
sources.text:
An Amazon cargo plane crashed at Miami international airport in Florida on Sunday afternoon after the flight, which was arriving from Puerto Rico, overshot the runway, striking several vehicles and resulting in at least five deaths.
The plane erupted in flames as dark smoke billowed into the sky, bringing operations at one of the busiest airports in the US to a halt. The pilot and copilot were trapped in the cockpit as a result of the crash, said the Miami-Dade rescue fire chief Ray Jadallah.
The mayor Daniella Levine Cava of Miami-Dade county said at a news conference on Sunday that in addition to the five people who were killed, five others were injured. Miami-Dade fire rescue confirmed during the same conference that ten total people were involved, with five deaths, three people in critical condition and two taken to a local hospital.
Jadallah, described the incident as a “very complex situation” where the plane crashed into multiple vehicles as it ran off the tarmac, trapping several people inside their vehicles.
The National Transportation Safety Board has assembled a team to investigate, the agency said in a social media post on Sunday evening. They are scheduling a media briefing for Monday.
Videos posted online show heavy plumes of smoke surrounding an aircraft bearing the Amazon arrow logo on its tail. Unconfirmed reports suggest there may be casualties, but details about injuries or fatalities remained unclear.
The plane was a Boeing 767 flying for Amazon Prime Air.
The Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) confirmed the crash in a statement to the Guardian, saying: “21 Air Flight 7598 overran the runway after landing at Miami International Airport around 2 pm local time on Sunday, September 6. The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft departed from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The FAA will investigate.”
The plane overran the airport’s diagonal runway and was disabled at the north-west end of the airport, a spokesperson for Miami international airport said.
An air and ground stop has been issued at the airport, preventing all other flights from landing or taking off at the busy south Florida hub. Fire crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane several hours after the crash, Jadallah said.
“All runways and taxiways at MIA are currently closed as of 3pm and a ground stop is in effect,” the airport said, adding: “Miami-Dade Fire Rescue has responded to the scene.”
About 250 flights were delayed at the airport late afternoon on Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.
More than 60 units from the Miami-Dade fire rescue services appeared on scene, with units arriving “to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing”, the fire department said, with the post adding that the plane had struck multiple vehicles near the airport.
Firefighters were “working on extinguishing the fire and assessing patients”, the post said.
US transportation secretary Sean Duffy said on social media that responders would “assess the scene after an Amazon cargo plane overran the runway”.
“If you’re traveling through the area, please expect significant delays and potential cancellations,” he added.
Meanwhile, the Miami-Dade sheriff’s office announced street closures due to the crash, saying: “NW 67th Avenue between NW 25th Street – NW 36th Street is currently closed. Expect delays and seek alternate routes.”
Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson told the Guardian in a statement: “We can confirm that an Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land at Miami International Airport today.”
Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami international airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
Courtesy: theguardian

Breaking: Amazon Cargo Jet Overruns Miami Runway, Ground Stop
sources.text:
An Amazon-branded Boeing 767 overran a runway at Miami International Airport Sunday, prompting a ground stop. The FAA is investigating.
According to reports, a cargo aircraft carrying Amazon’s Prime Air branding overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, September 6, 2026 prompting a ground stop and disrupting flights.
Early reports described a possible crash. There is now a more concrete account: the FAA says a Boeing 767-300 operating as 21 Air Flight 7598 (tail N1997A) overran the runway after landing around 2:11 pm local time (EDY). The flight originated in San Juan, Puerto Rico. Amazon often operates under charter or utilizes another carrier to operate and staff flights.
WATCH: Moments after a Prime Air Boeing 767 overshot the runway at Miami International Airport and crossed a road pic.twitter.com/kyCeeOpHdp
— BNO News (@BNONews) September 6, 2026
What Happened In Miami
According to an FAA statement reported by WSVN, the cargo flight arrived from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport before running beyond the runway.
WSVN reports that video shows the Prime Air aircraft leaving the end of Runway 30, crossing the airport perimeter road and Northwest 67th Avenue, and stopping in a field. The news outlet reported that departures had been halted as of 2:30 p.m EDT.
Separately, NBC 6 reported that Miami International Airport confirmed a ground stop because of a disabled aircraft.
The FAA will investigate.
What We Still Don’t Know
At the time of writing, the reports cited here do not establish the number of people aboard (likely two but could be more), who the injured parties were (crew, on the ground or a combination), nor does it speculate as to the cause of the overrun. I will update as details emerge.
I would be careful about drawing conclusions from where the aircraft stopped. That tells us something about the outcome. It does not tell us why the aircraft failed to stop on the runway. Audio from the flight recorders will take weeks if not months to release, but FlightRadar24 might have communications. It wasn’t immediately available at the time of publication.
For now, there is no verified basis in these reports to attribute the overrun to weather, a mechanical problem or a crew decision.
What The Ground Stop Means For Travelers
A ground stop can affect travelers who have not yet reached Miami. Under the FAA’s definition, flights destined for an affected airport can be held at their departure airports until the restriction is lifted.
That is separate from the reported pause in departures from Miami itself. Together, those restrictions can disrupt both sides of a connection. If you are traveling through Miami, check your airline’s flight status before heading to the airport and keep an eye on the onward flight as well. A departure that still appears on time is not much comfort if the flight bringing you to it cannot leave. Expect delays.
Following ground stops takes a while to correct before service returns to normal. Aircraft and crews may still need to get back into position, and the effect on an individual itinerary can outlast the initial restriction.
Updates will follow as available.

sources.news_title: Amazon Air Boeing 767 crashes after runway overrun at Miami International Airport
sources.text:
An Amazon Air Boeing 767 freighter crashed after apparently overrunning runway 30 at Miami International Airport on Sunday, with the aircraft coming to rest outside the airport perimeter and catching fire.
The aircraft was operating Amazon Air flight CSB7598 from San Juan, Puerto Rico, to Miami when the accident occurred. Videos from the scene show the Boeing 767 beyond the runway environment, with a large plume of black smoke and flames visible around the aircraft.
The aircraft has been identified as Boeing 767-33AER(BDSF), registration N1997A. The 767 is operated by 21 Air for Amazon Air. Aviation records identify the aircraft as MSN 27310. Photographic records also show N1997A previously operating Amazon services from Miami under Atlas Air. This 767 was initially delivered from the factory to Sobelair as OO-SBY on 24 June 1994.
Initial reports described the aircraft as having gone off or overrun Runway 30, although the precise sequence of events remains to be established. Images from the scene indicate that the aircraft travelled beyond the runway and across a road before coming to rest.
Emergency services responded in large numbers, with firefighters tackling a fire involving the aircraft. The full extent of the damage has not yet been established.
Casualties being investigated
The number and condition of people involved in the accident has not yet been officially confirmed.
Unverified reports circulating on social media have referred to multiple casualties, but these figures have not been independently confirmed by Miami-Dade authorities, the FAA or the National Transportation Safety Board. Aviation24.be will update this article as soon as reliable casualty information becomes available.
The aircraft was carrying a two-person flight crew, according to the type of operation.
Miami International Airport experienced operational disruption following the accident, with emergency crews requiring access to the runway and surrounding areas.
The cause of the accident is currently unknown. Investigators will examine the aircraft’s approach and landing, weather conditions, runway surface and braking performance, as well as any possible technical or operational factors.
The FAA and NTSB are expected to investigate the accident.
The crash is particularly notable because the aircraft was operating for Amazon Air, whose US cargo network relies on aircraft operated by partner airlines. It also recalls the February 2019 crash of Atlas Air Flight 3591, another Boeing 767 freighter operating for Amazon, which crashed near Houston while flying from Miami. All three people aboard that aircraft were killed.
This is a developing story. Further information on the crew, possible ground casualties, the aircraft’s final approach and the cause of the accident is expected as authorities investigate.

sources.news_title: Amazon Boeing 767 Crashes Near Miami Airport, Erupting in Flames Along Roadway
sources.text:
Five Dead After Amazon Cargo Jet Overruns Miami Airport Runway, Slams Into Vehicles
At least five people were killed and five others hospitalized after an Amazon Prime Air cargo jet overran a runway while landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, plowing into several vehicles and erupting in flames in a major accident that temporarily shut down one of the nation’s busiest airports.
Three of the injured were in critical condition, while two others were hospitalized with less serious injuries, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Ray Jadallah said. Authorities had not identified the five people killed or disclosed whether they were aboard the aircraft or on the ground.
The aircraft, Prime Air Flight 7598, was a Boeing 767-300 cargo plane operated by 21 Air on behalf of Amazon. The flight had originated at Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, and was attempting to land in Miami when it went off the airport’s diagonal runway shortly before 2 p.m.
The plane continued beyond the runway and struck multiple vehicles near Northwest 42nd Avenue before coming to rest in an area adjacent to the airport. Flames and heavy black smoke poured from the aircraft as emergency crews converged on the scene.
Jadallah described the scene confronting rescuers as “a very complex situation.” Some people were trapped inside vehicles struck by the aircraft, while another person was found trapped beneath a vehicle. The plane’s pilot and co-pilot were also trapped inside the cockpit and had to be rescued.
More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units and roughly 200 emergency personnel responded to the disaster. Hours after the crash, crews were still working to control an active fuel leak from the Boeing 767.
Images from the scene showed the freighter largely intact but resting with its nose on the ground and its tail elevated. Scorching was visible along the aircraft, while other images showed the jet near a roadway and vehicles outside the airport perimeter.
The aircraft involved was approximately 32 years old. It was originally built as a passenger aircraft and spent more than two decades carrying passengers before being converted into a freighter in 2015.
Amazon confirmed that the aircraft was flying for its Amazon Air operation but was being operated by 21 Air, a North Carolina-based cargo carrier with an operations center in Miami.
“This is a fast-moving situation and we’re still gathering details. We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened,” Amazon spokeswoman Kelly Nantel said.
“Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved. We’re doing everything we can to support those affected.”
The crash immediately brought operations at Miami International Airport to a halt. The Federal Aviation Administration imposed a ground stop, and all of the airport’s runways and taxiways were initially closed while firefighters, rescue workers and investigators responded.
The shutdown caused widespread disruption to air travel. Roughly 250 flights had been delayed by late Sunday afternoon, and federal officials warned travelers to expect significant delays and cancellations. Airport operations gradually resumed, with two of Miami International’s four runways reopened by Sunday evening.
The National Transportation Safety Board has launched an investigation and is sending an investigative team to Miami led by NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy. The FAA is also investigating. Authorities have not yet announced what caused the aircraft to overrun the runway.
Among the central questions investigators are expected to examine are the aircraft’s condition, its approach and landing, runway conditions, braking and other aircraft systems, crew actions and flight data. At this stage, however, officials have offered no conclusion about the cause, and there is no confirmed indication that any particular mechanical problem or crew action was responsible.
The accident marks another fatal crash involving a Boeing 767 freighter operating for Amazon. In February 2019, Atlas Air Flight 3591, another Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft flying on behalf of Amazon Prime Air, plunged into Trinity Bay near Houston while traveling from Miami. All three people aboard that flight were killed.
Sunday’s accident is now the subject of an extensive federal investigation, while authorities work to identify the dead and determine exactly who was aboard the aircraft and inside the vehicles it struck.
As of the latest official reports, the toll stands at five dead and five hospitalized — three in critical condition and two with less serious injuries. Authorities have not publicly identified the victims or clarified how many of the fatalities occurred aboard the plane and how many occurred on the ground.

sources.news_title: Boeing 767 Cargo Plane Reportedly Overruns Runway At Miami International Airport
sources.text:
The reported incident occurred as the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) imposed a temporary inbound ground stop at Miami International Airport due to runway and surface constraints.
A Boeing 767 cargo aircraft operated by Prime Air has reportedly overrun a runway at Miami International Airport (MIA) in Florida, according to aviation platform FL360aero.
FL360aero reported the incident in a post on X on Sunday, saying emergency response crews were at the scene.
“Details regarding possible injuries, aircraft damage and the circumstances of the incident remain unclear as the situation develops,” the platform said.
The reported incident occurred as the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) imposed a temporary inbound ground stop at Miami International Airport due to runway and surface constraints.
According to the FAA's Air Traffic Control System Command Center, the restriction was in effect from about 2:02 p.m. to 3:00 p.m. EDT on Sunday.
The FAA subsequently listed a traffic management programme for flights arriving at the airport due to a “RWY-TAXI / DISABLED AIRCRAFT.”
It said departure traffic destined for Miami International Airport would not be allowed to depart until 3:00 p.m. EDT.
The FAA said arriving flights were experiencing airborne delays of 15 minutes or less.
While reports of a possible cargo aircraft runway overrun circulated on social media, official details regarding the incident, including possible injuries or damage to the aircraft, remained unclear as of the latest update.
